 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX , appeal s pursuant to subsection  63(4) of the 
Immigration and Refugee Protection  Act1 (IRPA ) from the decision dated September 13, 2017  of 
the immigration officer determining that he has  not met the residency obligations pursuant to 
subsection  28(2) of the IRPA .  
[2] The issue is the legal validity of the immigration officer’s decision and whether 
humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special relief in all the circumstances of 
the case.2   
DECISION  
[3] There was  no legal challenge to the immigration officer’s decision. After  reviewing  the 
evidence in this appeal, the Panel finds that the immigration officer’s  decision  is valid in law. 
Furthermore , having considered the evidence and submissions, the Panel finds that the appellant 
has not proven on a balance of probabilities that there are sufficient humanitarian and 
compassionate considerations to warrant special relief. The appeal is dismissed.  
BACKGROUND  
[4] On September 11, 2017 , the appellant’s application  for a permanent resident travel  
document  (PRTD) to return to Canada from Vung Tau, Vietnam3, where he  reside s, was received 
at the Canadian Consulate General in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. After the appellant’s 
application  for a PRTD was  considered, the immigration officer was not satisfie d that he  had met 
the residency obligation requirements, as well as noting that there were insufficient humanitarian 
and compassionate considerations, taking into account the best interests of a child directly 
affected by the determination, to justify rete ntion of permanent resident status and overcome the 
breach of the residency obligation s.4

[5] The appel lant gave his evidence at the appeal hearing  via tele -conference from his home 
in Vung Tau, Vietnam . On appeal, the appellant filed one exhibit  of documenta ry evidence in 
support of the appeal  being allowed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.  
[6] The respondent , the Minister of Immigration , Refugees and Citizenship Canada, appeared 
at the hearing and relied on the Record.  
[7] The appellant obtained permanent  residence of Canada on May 4, 20065 as a result of 
being successfully sponsored to Canada by his sister as he was a dependent of his parents.  While 
in Canada the appellant engaged in English as a Second Language programs and studied at 
George Brown College . The appellant also worked part -time while studying at George Brown 
College.  
[8] After arriving in Canada , the appellant’s father stayed for four to five weeks before his 
return to Vietnam as his father he was 85 years of age and not well. The appella nt’s mother 
remained in Canada for three to four months before returning to Vietnam. The appellant’s 
paternal grandfather passed away approximately six to eight months thereafter and as a result the 
appellant’s father remained in Vietnam to run a business.  The appellant’s parents have not 
returned to Canada to re -establish permanent residence since they left 12 years ago.  
[9] The appellant  however remained in Canada for seven years, save for summer visits of 
three  weeks duration  to Vietnam . The appellant return ed to Vietnam on April 11, 2013 as his 
father was sick with colon cancer. The appellant was very concerned about his father’s health as 
well as the construction business his father was operat ing.  
[10]  The appellant married his wife in Vietnam  on October 20, 201 3 and they have two 
children born of their marriage on July 23, 2014 and December 4, 2016. The appellant has not 
returned to Canada to re -establish permanent residence since leaving on April 10, 2013.

ANALYSIS  
[11]  A permanent  resident must comply  with a resid ency obligation by being physically  
present  in Canada for 730 days of a five -year period.6 
[12]  The  appellant  bear s the burden of proof. To all ow this appeal , the appellant must satisfy 
the Panel  on a balance of probabilities that the immigration officer’s deci sion was wrong in law 
or fact, or mixed law and fact and taking into account the best interests of a child directly 
affected by the decision, that sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant 
special relief in light of all the circumsta nces of the case.  
[13]  The appellant  submits  that the appeal  should be allowed on humanitarian and 
compassionate  grounds as he returned to Vietnam to care for his father and manage the family 
business . He did not return to Canada as he did not know the law and had personal commitments  
to tend to.   
[14]  The Minister on the other hand asks the Panel to dismiss the appeal  as the refusal is valid  
in law and  that insufficient humanitarian  and compassionate ground s exists to allow the appeal . 
The Minister provides that while the appellant may have returned to Vietnam to care for his 
father, he remained, married after six months of his return, had children, worked in his father’s 
construction business and expanded t he business. As such , the appellant re -establishes himself in 
Vietnam as opposed to returning to Canada and doing the same . There is no evidence of hardship 
if the appeal is dismissed  
Residency obligation and circumstances  
[15]  The  residency obligations provide  some flexibility by requiring permanent residents to be 
physically  present in Canada for 730 days out of any five years under consideration. However, 
the broader objectives of residency are to facilitate settlement, establishment and contribution to 
Canad ian society, while also enriching Canada through the benefits of immigration.

[16]  In the five -year assessment  period, that being September 11, 2012  to September 11, 2017 , 
the immigration officer calculates the appellant’s physical presence in Canada in the amo unt of 
115 days during the assessment period; however, the Panel does note an error in the immigration 
officer’s calculation. The appellant has 211 days of physical presence during the assessment 
period. The appellant is short of the minimum number of phys ical presence in Canada  by 519 
days . 
[17]  After considering  all the evidence, the Panel is satisfied that the decision to refuse the 
appellant  a PRTD  is legally valid. Since the appellant has  not  been  physically present  in Canada 
for at  least 730 days, the more days he  need s to meet the residency obligations, the higher  degree 
of evidence would be needed with respect to consideration on humanitarian and compassionate 
grounds or special relief.   
Special relief  
[18]  In considering  whether spec ial relief is appropriate, the Panel considered a number of 
factors7 and took into account additional evidence that was not before the immigration  officer .8 
The Panel is cognizant of the immigration objectives, especially “to see that families are reunited  
in Canada”;9 “to promote the successful  integration of permanent residents into Canada”10 and to 
have “consistent standards and prompt processing”.11 
[19]  In Hawthorne ,12 Justice XXXXXX  wrote that t he likely degree of hardship to the child 
caused by the removal is to be weighed with other  factors, including public policy considerations  
that either favor  or disfavor the granting of special relief:  
[6]  … For all practical purposes, the officer's task is to determine, in the 
circumstances of each case, th e likely degree of hardship to the child caused by 
the removal of the parent and to weigh this degree of hardship together with other

Immigration) (1970), 4 IAC 338 (IAB).

factors, including public policy considerations, that militate in favour of or against 
the removal of the parent.  
 
[20]  The  test for humanitarian and compassionate grounds can be found in Chirwa.13 In this 
regard , the standard  applies where the initial ground of inadmissibility has not in substance  been 
overcome. The following definitions of humanitarian and compassionate consider ations were 
given in the XXXXXX  case and states as follows:  
[…] “humanitarian” [is defined] as “regard for the interests of mankind, 
benevolence.”  
 
[…] “compassion” [is defined] as “sorrow or pity excited by the distress or 
misfortunes of another, sympathy ” […] “compassionate considerations” must […] 
be taken to be those facts, established by the evidence, which would execute in a 
reasonable man in a civilized community a desire to relieve the misfortunes of 
another - so long as these misfortunes “warrant th e granting of special relief” from 
the effect of the provisions of the Immigration Act . 
 
[21]  In c onsidering the evidence in this appeal , the Panel recognizes that the appellant’s stated 
reasons for returning to Vietnam was due to his father being diagnosed with colon cancer and his 
mother’s  frantic call to him . The Panel notes in looking at the medical documentation14 provided 
that there is no referen ce to the appellant’s father’s illness of colorectal cancer in and around April 
2013. The medical evidence provides for a CT Scan report dated March 2, 2016 and a Diagnostic 
Tumor report dated April 29, 2016.  
[22]  Therefore, the Panel has not been convinced th at the appellant’s father was ill with 
colorectal cancer in and around April 2013 or even August 2012 for that matter and as a 
consequence the appellant had to return to Vietnam to assist in the care of his father as well as 
assisting in the operation of a  construction business. When corroborating medical evidence could 
have been submitted to show the extent of his father’s illness with colorectal cancer  prom pting the 
appellant’s return to Vietnam and it was not , the Panel is left with giving the appellant’ s remainder 
of his evidence no weight.   
                                                 
13 XXXXXX v. Canada (Minister of Manpower and Immigration)  (1970), 4 I.A.C. 338 (I.A.B.) at 350.  
14 Exhibit A -1, pp. 22 -33.

[23]  Furthermore , the appellant was asked by the Minister to confirm when he learned of his 
father’s illness. He provides it was in April 2013. At this point the appellant was directed to his 
letter15 to the Immigration A ppeal Division  where it describes that in August 2012 he received an 
unexpected phone call from his family back home announcing that his father had stage one 
colorectal cancer. It is also noted in a letter16 the appellant wrote to the Canadian High 
Commissi on that his mother called in August 2012 to announce that his father had colorectal 
cancer. When asked to clarify whether he learned of his father’s illness in August 2012 or April 
2013, his response was , “I don’t remember exactly because it was a long tim e. The accurate date is 
August 2012.”  
[24]  In considering the appellant’s response, it does not remotely inspire any confidence that the 
appellant’s father was sick as described. The Panel is also not sufficiently satisfied as to when the 
appellant  learned of his father’s stage one colorectal cancer diagnosis. There is no credible reason 
whatsoever why the appellant’s oral evidence would not have been the same as his written 
evidence describing when he learned of his father’s diagnosis, given this is the time i t ought to 
have been committed to memory because he seeks a return to Canada as a permanent resident.  
[25]  The Panel also learned from the appellant that his father had surgery in June or July 2015 to 
remove the tumor to avoid it spreading. If this is so, it makes no credible sense why in his letter17 
he indicates that his father received his first operation in April 2016. The  evidence is 
contradictory in this regard  with no credible reason why this is so . Furthermore , this contradiction 
could have been avoided  had the appellant provided credible corroborating evidence of su ch a 
surgery that could possibly  assist the Panel in its deliberation of the appeal. The Panel therefore 
assigns no weight to the appellant’s evidence in this regard.  
[26]  The appellant was asked  by his counsel  to explain  what happened when he returned to 
Vietnam on April 10, 2013. He indicates that his father was in receipt of medical treatment, was 
using a wheelchair  and that he needed someone to care for him and the business. The appellant 
desc ribed that after he returned to Vietnam he worked 12 hour days in the family business seven

days a week. The year after he worked between eight to ten  hours a day. At present he works eight  
hours a day five  days per week.  
[27]  If it is true that the appellant returned to Vietnam to assist his father due to the colorectal 
cancer  diagnosis, whenever it was, with the amount of time the appellant has worked and continues 
to w ork in the business, there is a lack of credible evidence  showing what he managed to do to 
assist  his father back to better health  given the amount of time spent in the family business . 
Clearly, the reason for his  return to Vietnam was to help save the business from possible collapse , 
which in considering all the  evidence had very little to do in assisting his father due to whenever 
the appellant learned of his father’s colorectal diagnosis. A negative credibility finding is made in 
this regard.  
[28]  Even if the Panel believed that the appellant did return to Vietnam w ith a view of assisting 
in nursing his father back to health, which it does not, the appellant failed to credibly show, with  
the production of credible medical documentation as to the determination of the cancer, treatment 
and prognosis thereafter. There a re many more questions than answers. The Panel therefore makes 
a negative inference as a consequence.  
[29]  The appellant  was also asked why he did not return to Canada after the surgery in June or 
July 2015. In response, he provides that he wanted to return but  failed to consult with his sister as 
he had heard that residents must be in Canada for six months.  
[30]  The appellant indicated that he has good communication with his sister. If this is accurate, 
he should have ensured that he asked his sister or make contact with immigration officials about 
the residency obligations for the purpose of  compliance.  This is n ot the case however. T he 
appellant  has  clearly made a life for himself in Vietnam, married, has children and works in the 
family construction business. His life is in Vietnam with little active thought of re -establishing 
himself in Canada.  
[31]  When the appell ant was asked why he had not returned to Canada when his father’s 
condition stabilized, he indicated that his father was not completely stable and that he had to return 
to the doctor for follow up. Whatever medical condition the appellant’s father was in, the evidence 
does not credibly present itself showing a justifiable reason for the appellant’s continued  lengthy

residence from Canada , particularly when he has family, inclusive of his older sister in Vietnam 
who could be available to assist . In addition to that, t he appellant did not even consider hiring a 
medical professional in Vietnam to assist his father in his day -to-day activities which may have 
been limited due to his illness. The Panel makes a negative inference as a result.  
[32]  The appellant states t hat he is now ready to return to Canada as everything is stable in his 
life, business and family. He also indicated that if there is a problem with the business he can sell 
it. Again, if in fact the appellant had wanted to live in Canada as a permanent res ident, he could 
have assisted his father to the best of his ability while trying to assist in saving his father’s business 
with a short -term plan and return to Canada after a few months. The appellant returned to Vietnam, 
whether or not due to his fa ther b eing  ill as described . He  re-established himself there and for all 
intense and purposes, abandoned Canada as his place of permanent residence. Thus, the appellant’s 
actions or lack thereof negatively affects the evidence as presented.  
[33]  It is recognized that  permanent residents may have to return to their countries of citizenship 
to address personal matters, such as ill relatives. However, such matters cannot be expected to be 
used  at infinitum or in other words as a catchall to overcome the legal obligations . If so, then there 
would be little or no reason to have the residency obligations and its objectives.  
Establishment  
[34]  The appellant lived and worked part -time in Canada after obtaining permanent residence 
until leaving  for Vietnam on April 10, 2013. He has no property, assets or savings in Canada. 
When he was in Canada he lived with his sister.  
[35]  In terms  of family in Canada , the appellant has his sister, brother -in-law, one nephew who 
is 17 years  of age and one niece who  is 15 years of age .  
[36]  The appellant’s family in Vietnam consists of his wife, children who are 2 and 4 years of 
age, parents, one older sister and her family who lives 45 minutes away from the appellant and 
their parents. His wife is a pharmacist at a hosp ital in Vietnam who also assists in looking after 
the appellant’s father as they all live in the same home.

[37]  The appellant has a family business, part of which is expanded through his efforts in the 
construction industry, transporting gravel, sand and the l ike.  The business earns $250,000USD 
per year. His income from his full -time employment in the business is $18,000USD per year. 
There is no indication  that the appellant transferred portions of his income to Canada or bough 
property that would indicate some  possible commitment or connection to Canada other  than his 
sister and her family.  
[38]  The  appellant’s  establishment  in Canada is very low and even when factoring in his 
Canadian family, it does not rise to the level that would excit e the Panel to allow the a ppeal on 
humanitarian and compassi onate grounds as he is far more established in Vietnam than in Canada.   
Hardship  
[39]  As far as any hardship t hat would come to the appellant if the appeal were to be dismissed, 
it is noted that  there was a lack of evidence hea rd with respect to this issue. It cannot be said that 
due to the appellant’s seven  years in Canada from when permanent residence was granted on May 
4, 2006 until his departure from Canada on April 10, 2013 when he enrolled in English as a Second 
Language program, attended college and worked, that he was committed to Canada and therefore 
the loss of permanent residence would be tantamount to hardship. If so, that would be a stretch in 
the consideration of hardship.  
[40]  The  appellant’s life , employment and family is, for the most part, in Vietnam.  Insufficient 
evidence was presented to address hardship if the  appellant was not allowed to retain his  status as  a 
permanent  resident .  
Best interests of the child  
[41]  The  appellant has  two  children  who live with XXXm and his wife and family in Vietnam. The 
children should remain living with their parents.  
[42]  The appellant has a niece and a nephew who reside with his sister and brother -in-law. They 
are 15 and 17 years of age. Quite frankly, there has not been a case ma de out that would suggest 
that the appeal should be allowed in the best interests of the children referenced.

CONCLUSION  
[43]  Permanent  resident status is granted by the government in the exercise of its authority to 
regulate  the admission of non -citizens int o Canada and may be lost as a result of the actions of the 
appellant.18 It is incumbent on newcomers to Canada to know their obligations and their rights and 
when they do not satisfy the residency requirements, they have the burden to establish that there a re 
exceptional circumstances to overcome those requirements.19  
[44]  The Panel is not convinced that the appellant would now live in Canada as a permanent 
resident  as no action has been taken to do so, not even the transfer of personal property . If the 
appeal were to be  allowed, the Panel is of the view that the  appellant would continue living his 
life as he has been in Vietnam  with little establishment in Canada , notwithstanding the apparent 
reasons for leaving Canada.  
[45]  The government of Canada’s requirement o n permanent residents to have 730 days of 
physical presence in Canada in any five years under review is not onerous . It recognizes that 
permanent residents may have to return to where they once lived, prior to immigrating to 
Canada, for a variety of person al reasons. However, the evidence in this case does not remotely 
establish much of an interest in living in Canada as per the legal requirements based on the 
actions of the appellant. There ought not to be a reward for such actions unless sufficiency of 
evidence has been adduced on humanitarian and compassionate grounds to overcome the serious 
breach in residency. This unfortunately for the appellant is not the case.  
[46]  The appeal is  hereby dismissed pursuant to subsection 69(1) of the IRPA .

1 REASONS FOR DECISIO N 
OVERVIEW  
[1] XXXXXXXXXXXXX  (“the Appellant”) is a 46-year -old permanent resident of Canada 
(“PR”). He  came to Canada with his wife and two young children in September 2012. They  left 
Canada in late 2012 , 45 days after landing. The family  returned to Pakistan  because the 
Appellant wanted to ensure his children were familiar with Pakistani culture and the Urdu 
language. He also  had a good job in Pakistan that he had held for many years.  When t he 
Appellant wanted to come back to Canada in July 2019 , he applied for  a Permanent Resident 
Travel Document (“PRTD”).1  
[2] A PR must  be physically present in Canada for at least 730 days in every five -year 
period.2 The Appellant did not have the 730 days, and he did not fall into any of the exceptions 
to the law. The visa officer also found there were insufficient humanitarian and compassionate 
considerations (“H&C”) in his case to issue the PRTD .3 The Appellant app ealed that finding at a 
hearing before me.4 
[3] The only positive factor I can weigh in the Appellant’s favour is his family tie s to 
Canada. All  the other H&C  factors  are negative and are insufficient to warrant special relief. The 
appeal is dismissed.  
 
ANALY SIS  
In all the circumstances of the case, and taking into account the best interests of any minor 
children directly affected by the decision, are there sufficient humanitarian and 
compassionate considerations to warrant special relief to the Appellants?   
[4] In considering the H&C grounds in a residency obligation appeal, I must consider the 
best interests of any minor children whose interests might be directly affected by the outcome of 
the appeal , along with numerous factors which I discuss in detail below, a nd which are not 
exhaustive.5 Further, the Federal Court tells me there is no rigid algorithm that determines the 
outcome of this type of appeal.6 Finally, the greater the shortfall in the number of days from the

overcome the impediment of not meeting the residency obligation.  
The Appellant has insufficient days of physical presence  
[5] The Appellant spent  43 days  in Canada  in the five -year period being assessed.7 The 
Appellant’s noncompliance with the residency obligation is almost total.  The Appellant needs 
significant  H&C considerations to overcome this shortfall.  
The Appellant’s reasons for not meeting the residency are not compelling and he did not 
return at the fir st opportunity  
[6] The Appellant came to Canada as a skilled worker in September 2012 . He landed in 
Lethbridge , Alberta under the Alberta Nominee program. He brought his wife and two minor 
children with him. They lived with the XXXXXXXXX’s brother and his fami ly. He found Lethbridge 
to be a small town. The Appellant could not find a job and was homesick,  so the family returned 
to Pakistan after two months. He and his wife both testified that they left Canada in 2012 because 
their children were young and they wa nted them to have a good knowledge and understanding of 
their Pakistani culture and religion. The Appellant  was asked about this by the Minister's counsel 
and he said life in Canada was fast and he wanted to have more time to become accustomed to 
Canadian culture. He also wanted to wait until the children were a better age to settle.  The 
Appellant had taken a leave from his job in Pakistan as a cardiology technician prior to leaving 
for Canada and went back to this job upon his return.   
[7] The Appellant cam e back to Canada in 2014 , leaving his wife and two minor sons behind 
in Pakistan. This time, he came to Toronto, lived with a family friend, and obtained a job in a 
candy factory. He made inquir ies to determine if his education would be recognized in Canada 
and was investigating courses he could take if required. However, his mother, who was in 
Pakistan living with the Appellant’s wife, children, and brother, had a serious stroke. The 
Appellant  returned to Pakistan to care for her, given his medical training.  She required a lot of 
care, which the XXXXXXXXX and his wife provided for her.  The Appellant also went back to his 
former job as a cardiology technician.  The Appellant’s mother passed away in July 2017 and he 
did not apply to come back to Canada until July 2019. The Appellant  became depressed after

 (the IRP Regulations ) imposes a two-prong test to disqualify an adopted child from the family class:  first, that the adoption is not genuine; second, that the adoption was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring a status or privilege under the Act.  [8] In Sahota
,1 at paragraph 19, Member XXXXX noted as follows:  Parliament’s concern under section 4 of the Regulations is that the adoption is genuine.  The term “genuine” has not been defined in IRPA or the Regulations.  The fundamental nature of an adoption is a relationship between parent and child.  Parliament specifically included the factor of a genuine parent/child relationship as one element in the determination of the best interests of the child in the context of section 117(3) of the Regulations.  Nevertheless, I find the issue of a genuine parent/child relationship is also of primary relevance in the context of considering the genuineness of an adoption.  While this factor is by no means the only factor that could be used to determine whether or not an adoption is genuine in the context of section 4 of the Regulations, it is a key factor to consider in assessing an adoption, and I find that this factor is sufficient as a determinative factor in assessing the genuineness of an adoption.  ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION ( RAD ) 
[8] The RAD reviews RPD decisions by conducting an independent assessment of the 
refugee claim. If the RAD’s assessment differs from that of the RPD, the RAD may substitute its 
own decision.1 If the RPD has a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral 
testimony, th en the RPD’s finding will normally be respected and accorded deference.2 
Otherwise, the standard of correctness applies.3  
[9] In this case, the RPD did not have a meaningful advantage; the evidence is fully captured 
in the record. Accordingly, I have conducte d an independent assessment of the oral and 
documentary evidence using the correctness standard.  
[10]  The Appellants have not submitted any new evidence and they are not asking for an oral 
hearing.  
ANALYSIS  
[11]  In my independent assessment, I have taken into consi deration  the most up to date 
country condition evidence contained in the NDP for Nigeria and have also considered the 
Chairperson’s Guideline 4 related to women refugee claimants fearing gender related 
persecution.4 
[12]  The determinative issue in this appeal i s if the Appellants have a viable IFA in Abuja,  
Nigeria. Therefore, I will focus on the IFA findings of the RPD. Where the RPD’s credibility 
findings relate to the IFA analysis, I will consider the Appellants’ arguments in my assessment. 
In this case , IFA is determinative of both Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA) 
section s 96 and section 97 concerns.  
[13]  The Principal Appellant argued that they would like notice if the RAD finds IFA in 
another place other than Abuja5 to be determinative in this claim.  From my independent 
assessments of the record and the audio, I find that the RPD did explore the viability of IFA in 
Abuja and that the Principal Appellant was questioned and given an opportunity to make his 
submissions regarding IFA.

was asked about and had an opportunity to make submissions on the viability of Abuja,  
therefore, notice is not required in this case.  
[15]  In assessing an I FA, I must apply a two -pronged test cited in the Federal Court of 
Appeal’s decision in Rasaratnam :6  
1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no    serious 
possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the co untry to which it finds an 
IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of 
cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to 
exist, of torture in the IFA.  
2) Moreover, t he conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be 
such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those 
particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.  
[16]  Both prongs must be satisfied to find  that the Appellant has an IFA. The Appellants bear 
the burden of proof to show that they face a serious possibility or reasonable chance of 
persecution in the entire country and specifically in the potential IFA area. In this case, the 
proposed IFA area i s Abuja, Nigeria.

unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would

ANALYSIS  
[11]  Before October  24, 2017, section  2 of the Regulations stated  the following : 
dependent child , in respect of a parent, means a child who  
 (a) has one of the following relationships with the parent, namely,  
(i) is the biological child of the parent, if the child has not been adopted by a person other 
than the spouse or common -law partner of the parent, or  
(ii) is the adopted child of the parent; and  
 (b) is in o ne of the following situations of dependency, namely,  
(i) is less than 19 years of age and is not a spouse or common -law partner, or  
(ii) is 19 years of age or older and has depended substantially on the financial support of 
the parent since before the age  of 19 and is unable to be financially self -supporting due to 
a physical or mental condition.   
 
[12]  On October  24, 2017, an amendment to this definition came into force, and the section 
now states  as follows : 
dependent child , in respect of a parent, means a ch ild who

than the spouse or common -law partner of the parent, or  
(ii) is the adopted child of the parent; and  
 (b) is in one of the following situations of dependency, namely,  
(i) is less than 22 years of age and is not a spouse or common -law partner, or  
(ii) is 22 years of age or older and has depended substantially on the financial support of 
the parent since before attaining the age of 22 years and is unable to be financially

[26]  After examining the application for reinstatement and the file as a whole, I do not find

Introduction and Issue  
 
[1] The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXX, appeal s pursuant to section 63(1) of the Immigration and 
Refugee Protection  Act1 (IRPA ) from a decision of the visa officer not to issue a permanent 
resident visa to his spouse, AnXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the applicant), on the basis the 
marriage is not genuine and  that it was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any 
status or privilege under the IRPA , thereby rendering the applicant not a family member in 
relations to the appellant, pursuant to section 4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection 
Regulations2 (Regulations) . 
 
[2] Section 4(1) of the Regulations  deals with “bad faith” marriages, common -law 
partnerships and conjugal partnerships, and reads as follows:  
 
4.(1) For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse, a 
common -law partner, or a conjugal partner if the marriage, common -law partnership, conjugal 
partnership  
 
(a) was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the 
Act; or  
(b) is not genuine.3 
 
[3] Under section 4(1) of t he Regulations , to succeed on appeal the appellant has to prove 
that the marriage was not entered into primarily for the purpose of the applicant gaining any 
status or privilege under the IRPA  and  that it is genuine.  To dismiss the appeal the panel must 
find that the marriage was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or 
privilege under the IRPA  or that it is not genuine.

was entered into primarily for immigration purposes.  The applicant is ther efore not a member of 
the family class in relations to the appellant and cannot be sponsored on that basis.  
 
[5] The appeal is dismissed.

1996.5  During the hearing, the appli cant testified that she entered in a customary marriage with a 
man in Ghana who is the father of her two children born in 1995 and 1996.

Credibility of the Witnesses  
 
[15]  In considering the reliability and credibility of witnesses in the case of inconsistencies 
and an absence of supporting evidence, “.. .The trial judge should not consider the plaintiff’s 
evidence in isolation, but must look at the totality of the evidence to assess the impact of the 
inconsistencies in that evidence on questions of credibility and reliability pertaining to the core 
issue in the case.”10 
 
[16]  The words of the Supreme Court of Canada from the head notes in F.H. v. McDougall11 
are also appropriate at this point:  
 
There is only one standard of proof in a civil case and that is proof on a balance of 
probabilities…One legal rule appli es in all cases and that is that the evidence must be scrutinized 
with care by the trial judge in deciding whether it is more likely than not that an alleged event has 
occurred.  Further, the evidence must always be clear, convincing and cogent  in order to  satisfy 
the balance of probabilities test. [Emphasis added]  
 
[17]  The panel has had the benefit of observing the appellant and hearing the applicant testify 
under affirmation.  In this case, there were multiple inconsistencies and implausibility and the 
panel considers the evidence to be far from “clear, cogent and convincing”.  The witnesses’ 
evidence contradicted each other on many key points, and the panel finds their evidence  vague, 
evasive, contradictory, and in some aspects, defy common sense and logic.   The panel therefore 
does not find the witnesses’ evidence credible, trustworthy or reliable.

Genuineness of Marriage  
 
[30]  The genuineness of a marriage can be affected by a number of different indicia .18  These 
are not  identical in every appeal as the genuineness of the marriage can be affected by any 
number of different factors in each appeal.  
 
[31]  These can include, but are not limited to, such factors as how the relationship developed; 
the intent of the parties to the ma rriage; the length of the relationship; the amount of time spent 
together; conduct at the time of meeting, at the time of an engagement and/or the wedding; 
behaviour subsequent to a wedding; the level of knowledge of each other’s relationship histories; 
levels of continuing contact and communication; the provision of financial support; the 
knowledge of and sharing of responsibility for the care of children brought into the marriage; the 
knowledge of and contact with extended families of the parties; as well  as the level of knowledge 
about each other’s daily lives.  All of these factors can be considered in determining the 
genuineness of a marriage.

Primary Purpose of Acquiring Status under IRPA  
 
[61]  The importance of membership in the family class by marriage is that the applicant is 
largely exempt from other requirements.  The adva ntage sought in spousal appeals is generally 
entry to Canada and the granting of permanent resident status to the applicant as a member of the 
family class.  Whether the relationship was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring 
any status or pri vilege under IRPA  is self -evident and self -explanatory.  
 
[62]  As the Federal Court had stated in XXXX  and XXXXXX , the lack of genuineness in a 
marriage can lead to a presumption that it was entered into for the purpose of gaining status.33 
 
[63]  Although the applican t testified that she has the financial means to support herself in 
Ghana and does not need to come to Canada for economic reasons, there is no credible

unable to leave Israel because of her lack of status there. That means she fears losing her job 
there and she likely does not have the financial means she testifie d to. The economic 
opportunities in Canada and available health and social care can certainly be a strong incentive

Overview  
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX , the Appellant, alleges to be a  citizen of Eritrea. He appeals the 
decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He 
submits new evidence as part of his appeal and requests a hearing before the Refugee Appeal 
Division (RAD). He asks the RAD t o allow his appeal and either accept him as a Convention 
refugee or remit his claim back to the RPD for redetermination.  
Determination  
[2] The appeal is dismissed.  
Background  
[3] The Appellant fears returning to Eritrea because he fled Eritrea illegally and fears 
punishment and persecution. He also fears returning to Eritrea because he will be forced into 
military/national service. The Appellant is a follower of the Pentecostal religion and fears 
persecution because of his religion. Finally, the Appellant submits t hat he has been active in 
opposing the Eritrean government outside Eritrea.  
[4] The Appellant’s claim was heard by the RPD September 11 and October 25, 2018.  It was 
denied in a written decision , signed December 4, 2018. The determinative issues for the RPD 
were identity and credibility.  
Appellant’s Arguments on Appeal  
[5] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its identity analysis. The Appellant submits 
that he provided sufficient evidence with respect to his identity. The Appellant also argues that 
the RPD e rred by coming to the conclusion that the Appellant has status in an unnamed or

[20]  The RPD found the Appellant’s National ID card was in pristine condition, despite being 
over 12 years old when the RPD hearing took place. In my review of the RPD hearing, there 
were several questions and concerns raised by the RPD regarding the provenance and content of

National Documentation Package (NDP), he testified that the security feature is not visible 
because  he re -laminated it. When asked why he re -laminated, it he explained that he did so in the 
United States to protect it, as it was getting old.  
[21]  The RPD compared the Appellant’s National ID card to the description in the Response 
to Information Request (RIR)  and found that aspects of it did not conform to the description. 
When I review the XXXXXXXXX’s testimony, he provided a confusing and evolving account. He 
initially did not say that he re -laminated it, when asked why it was in pristine condition, he 
initi ally said he kept it at home. When asked about missing lettering that is indicative of one of 
the security features, he then stated he got it re -laminated while in the United States to protect it 
and it is covering the missing feature. Then later, when ask ed by his counsel about the security 
lettering being cut off, he explained that the feature was cut off when he got it re -laminated. I 
find he is account of the ID card inconsistent and evolving. I agree with the RPD analysis of the 
credibility of the card .  
[22]  The Appellant challenges this analysis by the RPD member stating that she applied a 
western standard to her approach to analysing the ID card. I do not agree. While a missing letter

Analysis of the new evidence  
[37]  The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA) limits the ability of Appellants to 
present new evid ence on appeal to the RAD. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA states that, on 
appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the 
rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person co uld not 
reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the claim’s 
rejection. If the new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the 
RAD must then consider factors the credibility, relevance, and newness of the evidence.7 
[38]  The Appellant submits evidence from two new witnesses whom he encountered after the 
RPD rejected his claim for refugee protection8. He argues that both pieces of new evidence were 
not reasonably available prior to the rejectio n of his claim, He only encountered these two 
witnesses after the December 2018 decision of the RPD.

 [39]  In my view , the Appellant’s evidence does meet the statutory requirements , as it is clear 
these two witnesses were only encountered after the RPD rejecte d his claim. However , when I 
apply the jurisprudential factors, I do not find the new evidence admissible for a number of 
reasons. The two new witnesses have similar profiles to other witnesses presented to the RPD, 
and already discounted for credibility a nd sufficiency reasons. I find the new witness evidence 
raises similar concerns , such as the long period of time that they have not had contact, and the 
tenuous nature of the relationships, as they were schoolmates and soccer friends. Furthermore, 
when I c onsider the timing of the new evidence in relation to the Appellant’s personal history , I 
find their chance meetings to be lacking in credibility.  
[40]  XXXX defines credibility, in relation to the admissibility of new evidence, as “Is the 
evidence credible, con sidering its sources and the circumstances in which it came into existence? 
If not the evidence need not be considered.”9 
[41]  In this case I find that the circumstances of the Appellant meeting his two new witnesses 
in the days after the rejection of his RPD claim to be too fortuitous. The Appellant has been in 
Canada since XXXX  2017. His RPD hearing was held in September and October 2018, over a 
year and a half after his ar rival in Canada. He encountered two friends whom he knew in Eritrea 
and who attended his RPD hearing in October 2018.  His claim was rejected on December 4, 
2018 and, on January 7 and 20, 2019 respectively, he met two other friends/a distant relative 
whom he knew in Eritrea and with whom he played soccer. I find these two encounters in the 
days after his RPD rejection and days before his RAD appeal is due to be improbable in my 
view. I find the circumstances of this new evidence to be lacking in credibility  and therefore 
inadmissible.  
[42]  It has been held that the RAD appeal is not a second chance to submit evidence to answer 
weaknesses identified by the RPD and supplement a deficient record. Refugee claimants are 
expected to put their best foot forward at the R PD stage.10 In this case I find the new evidence is 
an attempt to rectify problems the RPD found with the witness evidence when the Appellant was 
afforded a second hearing in order to bring witness evidence.  I am also guided by the Federal 
Court in Idugboe11, where the FC upheld similar reasoning regarding the timing of new 
evidence;

[44]  In my review of the appeal , I find the Appellant was not a credible witness. His evidence

15 and confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in Chieu,16 albeit modified to reflect the case of a failure to comply with the residency obligation, provide some guidance as to what should be considered  when looking at “all the circumstances of the case”.  These factors include but are not limited to:  • the nature, extent and degree of non-comp liance with the residency obligation;   • the reasons for continued, or lengthy stay abroad, and the appellant’s intentions in relation to residency in Canada;  • whether the appellant made reasonable attempts to return to Canada at the first opportunity;  • the length of time the appellant has spent in Canada and the degree to which the appellant is established in Canada;   • the continuing connections the appellant has to Canada, including connections to family members here and the hardship and disloca tion to family members in Canada if the appellant ultimately ceases to be a perman ent resident as a result of his or her non compliance;   • the degree of establishment of the appellant outside of Canada;  • the best interests of any child directly affected by the decision; and  • the degree of hardship that would be caused to the appellant by a loss of status in Canada, including the conditions in the likely country of removal;  • whether or not there are unique or special circ umstances present in the case such as meet the Chirwa

more particularly that the appellants had not complied with the residency obligation for at least 
730 days in the five -year period before June 1, 2016.  
 
[2] The appellants did not challenge the legal validity of the determinations and r equested 
that the IAD exercise its discretionary jurisdiction. The appellants conceded that they were 
physically present in Canada for 278 days in the applicable five -year period between June 1, 
2011 and May 31, 2016. The relevant paragraphs of Section 28 of the Act read as follows:

respect to every five -year period.

subsection ( 1): 
(a) a permanent resident complies wit h the residency obligation with 
respect to a five -year period if, on each of a total of at least 730 days 
in that five -year period, they are  
(i) physically present in Canada … 
 
[3] I have considered the contents of the Record prepared by the Minister of Citizen ship and 
Immigration (the “respondent”), additional documents provided by the appellant,2 the testimony 
of the appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and the oral submissions of counsel for the appellants and 
the respondent. The respondent asked that I dismiss the appeal.

ANALYSIS  
 
[6] As noted in other IAD decisions in this area,  the IAD may, in its deliberations, examine 
objective factors suggesting ongoing and continuing ties to Canada, reasons for an appellant’s 
departure from Canada and extended absence from Canada, visits to Canada, family and other 
ties to Canada, whether or  not reasonable attempts to return to Canada were made at the first 
opportunity, issues of dislocation and hardship to family members in Canada, their establishment 
in Canada, the appellants’ situation in Romania and their ongoing intention vis a vis long -term 
residency in Canada even during a period of absence and, generally, whether or not there are 
unique or special circumstances present in the case such as meet the Chirwa3 standard for

REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons and decision of the Imm igration Appeal Division ( IAD) in the 
appeal by XXXXXXXXXX ndre DXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (Appellant ), from a determination made by 
an immigration officer on November 11, 2017 .1 The immigration officer determined that the 
Appellant  failed, as  a permanent resident, to comply with the residency obligation requirements 
in section 28 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA ).2 This determinatio n was 
made at a Port of Entry.  
 
[2] Mr. XXXXXX does not challenge the finding that he did not comp ly with the residency 
obligations. However, he argues that the appeal should be allowed on the basis that sufficient 
humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special relief in light of all the 
circumstances of the case, taking into account the  best interests of any child directly affected by 
the decision.  
 
[3] The Appellant  testified in person and was not represented by counsel.  
 
DECISION  
 
[4] I find that the determination made by the immigration officer  is valid in law and that 
there are not suffici ent humanitarian and compassionate considerations to warrant the exercise of 
special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case. The appeal  is therefore dismissed .  
 
BACKGROUND  
 
[5] The Appellant  is a citizen  of Portugal and is 47 years old. He becam e a permanent 
resident  as a dependent child  of his parents in June 1973. He was two years of age at that time. 
Mr. XXXXXX grew up in Canada and moved to the USA when he was 26 years old. He lived in the 
USA for about 19 years but was deported to Portugal d ue to criminality in 2016. In 
November  2017, he returned to Canada and upon entry was issued a departure order for failure to 
comply with his residency obligations.

 ANALYSIS  
 
[6] Mr. XXXXXX travelled to Canada on November 10, 2017. During the examination upo n 
entry, a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officer spoke to Mr. XXXXXX about his residency 
status in Canada. Mr. XXXXXX explained that he became a permanent resident in 1973 and that he 
lived in Canada for about 24 years. He then moved to the USA wher e he lived until he was 
deported to Portugal in 2016. He stated that he had not returned to Canada between 1997 and 
2017. At the IAD hearing, Mr. XXXXXX confirmed that this information was correct. Based  on the 
evidence before me, Mr. XXXXXX has not met th e residency obliga tion requirements under 
section  28 of the IRPA  and the determination is therefore valid in law and fact.  
 
[7] I ha ve the discretion to allow the Appellant ’s appeal on humanitarian and compassionate 
grounds, taking into account the best intere sts of a child directly affected by the decision. The 
following factors are considered in the exercise of discretionary jurisdiction in the context of 
appeals by permanent residents who failed to m eet their residency obligations: t he extent of the 
non -comp lianc e with the residency obligation; w hen and  why the Appellant  left Canada; t he 
circumstances surrounding the breach of the residency obligation, including the reasons for and 
extent of the absence(s) from Canada;  the length of time the Appellant  have sp ent in Canada and 
the degree to which the Appellant  is established in Canada;  whether the Appellant  made 
reasonable attempts to return to Canada at the first opportunity;  the best interests of any child 
directly affected by the decision;  the Appellant ’s fa mily in Canada and the impact to the family 
that loss of status would cause; and the degree of hardship that would be caused to the Appellant  
by loss of status in Canada, including the conditions in the likely country of removal.  These 
factors are not exha ustive and the weight assigned to each factor will vary depending on the 
circumstances of each case.

 [8] The Appellant  did not identify a child whose best interests would be directl y affected by

relevant five -year period, meaning that he had zero days of physical presence in Canada between 
November 2012 and November 2017. The Appellant  will be required to demonstrate a high 
degree of humanitarian and compassionate considerations in order to overcome the extent of 
non -compliance. It is established that the greater the extent of a party’s non -compliance with the 
residency obligation, the greater the humanitarian and compassionate considerations must be in 
the party’s case to overcome that non -compliance.  
 
[10]  The Appellant  testified about his childhood and early adulthood in Canada. He lived with 
his family, attended school, and worked in the construction industry. Mr. XXXXXX’s establishment 
in Canada be tween 1973 and 1997 is a favourable factor in this appeal.  
 
[11]  However, in 1997, when he was around 26 years old, Mr. XXXXXX left Canada. He 
travelled to the USA to spend some time with his sister, after the sudden death of his step -father 
with whom he had a  close relationship. While he was in the USA, Mr. XXXXXX fell in love with an 
American woman and married in 1998. He obtained permanent resident status (a green card) in 
the USA and built his life there. He worked as a roofer and owned his own business. In  essence, 
he immigrated to the USA and left behind his life in Canada. While his father remained in 
Canada, his mother moved back to Portugal about 15 years ago. During the 19 years that Mr. 
XXXXXX lived in the USA, he would periodically visit Portugal but  he never visited Canada.   
 
[12]  I find that the Appellant  did not make reasonable attempts to return to Canada at the first 
opportunity.  After he obtained status in the USA and established himself, he did not contemplate 
moving back to Canada. He remained in the USA after he divorced in 2009. He did not leave the

[14]  Mr. XXXXXX’s loss of permanent resident status in Canada has caused him some hardship. 
When he was deported from the USA, he was deported to Portugal where he had not live d since

Fortunately, the Appellant ’s mother lives in Portugal and she was able to assist her son when he

 [1] These are the reasons in regard to the s ponsorship appeal made by XXXXXXXXXXX, the appellant, who appeals from a refusal to approv e the permanent resident visa application made by XXXXXXXXXXXX, the applicant, from I ndia who was sponsored by the appellant.  [2] The reasons for refusal were contained in  a letter dated August 30, 2006 from the High Commission of Canada in New Delhi, India.  The basis for the rejection was the position taken by the visa post that the applicant was not a memb er of the family class by virtue of section 117(9)(d) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the Regulations) in that at the time of the application the foreign national, i. e. the applicant was a non-accompanying family member of the sponsor and was not examined.  [3] At the beginning of the hearing held on Ja nuary 22, 2008 counsel for the Minister rose on a point of information to indicate to the panel that he was prepared to consent to the allowing of this appeal based on his position that according to  the face of the Record, section 117(10) of the Regulations would apply.  Namely that the applicant was not examined because an officer determined that the applicant was not required by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  to be examined.  Not surprisingly, counsel for the app licant indicated that it was his position that he would acquiesce to the position taken by Minister’s counsel.  [4] After hearing from both counsel, the Immigra tion Appeal Division indicated that it was not prepared to make a decision to allow the app eal solely on the position taken by both counsel and asked that certain evidence be adduced as to  what happened at the port of entry at Toronto Pearson Airport so that the panel could make a determination whether the said section 117(10) of the Regulations applied.  [5] Evidence was then adduced by counsel for the applicant from the applicant as to what happened in India just before he left and what happened at Toronto Pearson Airport when he arrived in Canada.  Subsequently the panel as ked for written submissions and counsel for the applicant sent his written submissions in on Januar y 22, 2008.  Minister’s counsel then sent in his

[6] After a careful analysis of the submissions  and examining the Record and taking into account the sworn testimony of the appellant the pane l is prepared to allow this appeal for the following reasons.  [7] The evidence does establish that on Septembe r 9, 2005 the applicant did send a letter to the visa post advising them that he had recently been  married.  It should be noted that at the time of granting the appellant’s visa he was classified  as being single.  According to page 46 of the Record this letter was received by the visa post on September 15, 2005.  The permanent resident visa application issued to the appellant was dated on June 6, 2005 and was valid up to January 20, 2006.  [8] The evidence establishes that on September 14, 2005, that is five days after sending the letter to the Canadian High Commission but before it was even received by them, the appellant left for Canada.  At the hearing there was testimo ny from the appellant as to why he only sent the notification to the visa post of his change of matrimonial stat us a few days before he left for Canada.  [9] It is not necessary to go into the details of this testimony as, in the panel’s opinion, it is not fully relevant to the decision except to stat e that the evidence was credible.  This does not excuse, in the panel’s opinion, the fact that the appellant should not have left India without confirming that the Canadian High Commission was aware of his change of matrimonial status and should not have left India without first returning his permanent resident visa as he was required to do so by the instructions given to the appellant when he was issued the visa.  Clearly when the appellant left for Canada on Septembe r 14, 2005 he was in breach of his obligations to inform the visa post since they had not even recei ved his change of status.  Notwithstanding this it is obvious from the appellant’s evidence that he was acting in good faith and did not send the letter at the late stage in order to circumvent the law.

[10] The panel found the appellant’s demeanour to be credible and this is important because of what happened at Toronto Pearson Airport goes to the heart of this appeal.  The appellant gave evidence under oath regarding what happened at Toronto Pearson Airport and the panel has no valid reason to doubt the credibility of this key evidence.  [11] According to the evidence of the appellant he testified that he notified the immigration officer that he had married between the time he was issued his resident visa and the time he arrived in Canada.  He testified that he also told  the officer that he had sent a letter to the High Commission of Canada advising the High Commission of the change.  According to the appellant’s evidence the officer went to her comput er, made some entries, and then indicated to the appellant that the visa post may not have received the letter (presumably not finding any indication on the computer of receipt of such a letter).  The appellant then testified that the officer crossed out the marital status indication on the landing document which showed “single” and then hand wrote “married” at the bottom of the Record of landing.  He also testified that the visa that the immigration officer told him th at because he had been honest with her in volunteering the information that he was now married; he would be able to sponsor his wife, i.e. the applicant, without any difficulty with the changes made to the Record of Landing.  [12] Page 42 of the Record does show a Record of Landing that is consistent with the appellant’s testimony.  One can see that there is a cross out under the “marital status” line on the top of the document and there is some writing at the bottom of the document to indicate a marital status change which according to the panel’s un derstanding means that it was shown that the appellant was married.  [13] There is nothing further from the immigration officer in the Record.  Thus there is no explanation as to why the officer would have told the appellant that he would have no trouble in sponsoring his wife and there is no indication in the Record as to why she believed changing the document the way she did would smooth the way for the applicant to be admitted as a member of the family class simply by this notation.

[14] It seems clear that the immigration officer made errors in law in doing what she did. [15] The immigration officer did not do anything of the sort.  This of course is not the fault of the appellant. The Appellant’s risk under section 97 of the IRPA  
[46]  The Appellant submits the RPD’s failure to conduct a separate section 97 analysis is a 
“reviewable error,”54 and that whether or not she was found credible it was incumbent on the 
RPD to “make a proper Section 97 analysis.”55 In the Appellant’s submission, the RPD’s failure 
to conduct a separate section 97 analysis is a violation of her right to procedural fairness that 
justifies quashing the decision.56 
[47]  I reject the Appellant’s submission. It is trite law that the RPD need not conduct a 
separate section 97 analysis where there is no evidence that could credibly support a finding that 
the Appellant is a person in need of protection,  irrespective of any findings the RPD might make 
about the credibility of the fear they allege under section 96.  
[48]  In this case, the RPD did not make an explicit finding that the evidence before it could 
not support a claim under section 97. However, in my i ndependent assessment no such evidence 
is before me. I particularly note the RPD’s finding that the Appellant submitted a fraudulent 
document to support her allegation that she was abducted and assaulted on the evening of July 
14, 2016.  
[49]  The Appellant has not contested this RPD finding. Based on my independent assessment 
of the letter57 against the Appellant’s testimony about the letter,58 I am satisfied the RPD did not 
err in drawing a negative inference about the credibility of the Appellant’s allegation th at she 
was abducted and assaulted from inconsistencies between the date of the letter and the 
Appellant’s account of when she was discharged from the clinic.

 [22]  In assessing the issue of state protection, I am guided by a number of cases.  The 
principles were applied to this case.  There is a presump tion, except in situations where the state is 
in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens.  A claimant who alleges that 
state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the 
evidence esta blishes that the state protection is inadequate.9   A claimant can rebut the presumption 
by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state’s inability to protect.  For example, a 
claimant might advance testimony of similarly situated individuals let down by the state protection 
arrangement or the claimant’s testimony of past personal incidents in which state protection did not 
materialize.  While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration10, recent Federal 
Court decisions have held  that the test for a finding  of state protection is whether the protection is 
adequate, rather than the effectiveness per se.11 12 13 14 15 16 17   The protection need not be perf ect.18  
One accepted measure of assessment is whether the state is making “serious ef forts” to protect its 
citizens.19 This standard continues to be applied in many Federal Court decisions.20 21 22 23 
[23]  As stated above , no government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its 
citizens at all times, and the fact that a state, is not  always successful in protecting its citizens, is

 INTRODUCTIO N  
[1] The claimant , XXXX XXXX XXXX , alleges  citizen ship  of China who seeks refugee 
protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act 
(IRPA).1  
ALLEGATIONS  
[2] The complete story alleging the basis of the claimant’s fear  is captured in the Personal 
Information Form (PIF).2 The claimant was unhappy as he was experiencing marital problems 
which led to a divorce on XXXX XXXX , 2010. The claimant alleges that he was introduced to the 
underground Catholic Christian movement by a friend in XXXX  2010. On XXXX XXXX XXXX  
2011 , the Public Security Bureau, P.S.B raided the house church. The claimant and some other 
members managed to make good their  escape  from a back door and the claimant was able to hire a 
taxi which took him to his cousin’s place. The P.S.B is looking for the claimant and with the 
assistance of his cousin was able to leave China on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  2011 via Hong 
Kong and arrived in Canada illegally on the same date. The claimant made a claim to refugee 
protection i n Canada on April 6, 2011 .  
DECISION  
[3] The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of 
protection. The panel also finds that should the claimant return to China he would not be subjected 
personally to a risk to his l ife or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Further, on 
substantial grounds there is no danger of torture.  
IDENTITY  
[4] The panel has concerns regarding the claimant’s identity, notwithstanding  Exhibit C -2 
which contains personal documents. The perso nal documents do not adequately confirm the 
claimant’s identity and that he is a Chinese national. Consequently, the claimant’s identity and that 
of a Chinese national has no t been sufficiently established.

 [5] On the issue of identity, section 106 of the Act  and Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection 
Division Rules states the following:  
The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the 
credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation 
establishing identity,  and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation 
for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain such 
documentation.  
Rule 7:  The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and 
other elements of the claim.  A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents 
must explain why they were not provided and what steps were taken to obtain them.    
[6] In the absence of credible and trustworthy documentation that could reasonably show that 
the claimant is in  fact a citizen of China, the panel therefore is not satisfied that the claimant is a 
citizen of China  as alleged . The panel is of this view  particularly when the claimant was asked to  
and failed to  provide satisfactory identity documents, such as the Chin ese Resident Identity Card 
and the like as contained in the file screening form which was disclosed to the claimant prior to the 
hearing .  
[7] The claimant’s identity continued to be an issue at the end of the first hearing into the merits 
of the claim held on  June 24,  2013 and remained so at the conclusion of the hearing last held on 
September 30,  2013 . The fact that the claimant provided a copy of his Resident Identity Card due to 
the original identity card was not received by the claimant when mailed to him does not off -set the 
panel’s concerns as to the claimant’s identity as a Chinese national. There is no indication that the 
claimant made efforts to obtain a replacement card issued by the competent authorities in China. 
The copy of the said card cannot be assessed as to its authenticity.  The lack of credible identity 
documents from the claimant brings his identity into disrepute.  
[8] Even if the claimant had satisfied the panel as to his identity and that he is a citizen of 
China, the claim would still fail on the issue of the credibility of the evidence submitted.

be scrutinized with care by the trial judge in deciding whether it is more likely 
than not that an alleged event has occurred.   Further, the evidence must always be 
clear, convincing and cogent  in order to satisfy the balance of probabilities test.

[9] As noted above, the appellant brings his appeal under section 67(1)(c) of IRPA  and seeks

circumstances surrounding it;  
 the remorsefulness of the appellant;  
 the le ngth of time spent in Canada and the degree to which the appellant is 
established in Canada;  
 the appellant's family in Canada and the impact on the family that removal would 
cause;  and  
 the degree of hardship that would be caused to the appellant by removal  from Canada, 
including the conditions in the likely country of removal.  
 
The panel also considers the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision.  The panel 
considers any exceptional circumstances.

 ANALYSIS  
 
[15]  In Maldonado ,9 the Federal Court of Appeal held that when an applicant swears  to the 
truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there is 
reason to doubt their truthfulness. In this case the RPD accepted the Appellant as credible but has 
not explained why it rejected the Appellant’s  evidence in regard to future risk. I find that the 
RPD erred in this finding.  
 
[16]  I have reviewed  the analysis of the Federal Court which clearly sets out that in this case, 
neither the RPD nor the first RAD Panel clearly explained why the Appellant’s alleg ation that he 
would be persecuted  in the future  by Georgian authorities who threatened and harmed him 
during the 2014 elections when he was an activist for the opposition pol itical party was not 
accepted. Both t he RPD  and RAD  found the XXXXXXXXX to be a cr edible witness but then went on, 
without further analysis, to either disbelieve or doubt his response to the RPD’s questions about 
future persecution.  
 
[17]  While the RPD has not used the word “plausibility” in its reasons for decision,  I find this 
was indeed an issue of implausibility, even if the RPD attempted to frame it as one of insufficient 
evidence. In essence, the RPD found it implausible that those who threatened and attacked the 
Appellant would continue to do so if he returned to Georgia and continued  his political activism 
against the governing political party. The RPD went on to find that it would be implausible for a 
lower level political activist to be targeted in the future even though the RPD accepted as 
credible that this is exactly what occurre d to the XXXXXXXXX in the 2014 elections. The RPD then 
faulted the Appellant for failing to establish his allegation of future persecution.

SCOPE OF APPEAL  
[13]  Sub section  110(1) of the IRPA states the following : 
110(1) Subject to subsections  (1.1) and (2), a person or the Minister may appeal, in 
accordance with the rules of the Board, on a question of law, of fact or of mixed law 
and fact, to the Refugee Appeal Division against a decision of the Refugee Protection 
Division to allow or reject the person’s claim for refugee protection.  
 
[14]  Sub section  111(1) of the IRPA provides  that the  RAD  may confirm the determination, set i t 
aside and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made , or refer the matter 
to the RPD for re -determination, giving the directions to the RPD that it considers appropriate.  
[15]  The IRPA does not set out the standard of intervention that the  RAD  should  apply whe n it 
reviews RPD decisions.  
[16]  In light of the Federal Court of Appeal ’s decision in  Huruglica ,1 I find that the  RAD  must 
really act as an appellate tribunal and conduct  its own analysis of the case in order to determine 
whether the RPD actually committed the alleged error. This involves conduct ing, in substa nce, a  
reasoned, thorough , comp rehensive and  ind epend ent review.2  
[17]  The RAD  must apply the correctness standard in reviewing RPD  decisions concerning 
findings of  law, fact or mixed law and fact  where they do not raise the issue of the credibility of 
oral evidence . 
[18]  In each case, i t must  determine the level of deference it owe s to t he findings of fact or 
mixed fact  and law  that are based on the credibility of oral evidence , while determining  whether the 
RPD benefited from  an advantage ous position . 
[19]  In this case, I will  show a measure of deference to the RPD’s findings if I am of the view 
that it truly benefited from  an advantage ous position  in assessing the appellant’s testimony.

Confrontation with the I mam at the mosque

controlled by  the Taliban  during the Friday pray er. It did not find his explanation credible, that is,

[4] On June 21, 2018 the IAD received the appellant’s response to the IAD letter. No response 
was received from the Minister.  
ANALYSIS

[6] Section 117(1)(h) of the Regulations  sets out that a foreign national is a member of the

the sponsor does not have a mother or father  who is a Canadian citizen, Indian or permanent

[7] The appellant submits that given her mother’s advanced age and health condition, her 
mother would “likely be found inadmissible on health grounds”.  While the appellant 
acknowledges that her mother can be sponsored as a parent, her mother’s con dition makes this 
“practically impossible”.  The appellant requests that the IAD consider the circumstances of the 
appellant as well as humanitarian and compassionate grounds.   
[8] The guidance from the Federal Court of Appeal indicates that the visa officer is not

OVERVIEW  
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX  (Principal Appellant) , XXXX XXXX XXXX  (Associate

(Minor Female Appellant)  are citizen s of Nigeria . They appealed a decision of the Refugee

The Appellants allege they face persecution and a risk to their lives at the hands of their family 
because of their refusal t o have the Minor Female Appellant  undergo female genital 
mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) . The determinative issue for the RPD was credibility.  
[2] I agree with the RPD that the Appellant s have not credibly established their allegations. 
For the reasons that follow,  the appeal is dismissed.  
BACKGROUND  
[3] The Principal Appellant and  the Associate Appellant  are married,  and the Minor Male 
Appellant  and the Minor Female Appellant  are their children. The Appellant s allege that the 
Associate Appellant ’s family is insisting that the Minor Female Appellant should undergo 
FGM/C.  The Appellants allege that they are in opposition to this practice and therefore have 
refused to allow it.  The Principal Appellant alleges that as a result of her refusal  to compl y with 
her  in-law s’ demands, she has been assaulted and threatened. The Appellants allege that they 
face a forward -looking risk at the hands of the Associate Appellant ’s family.  
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION  
[4] The Refugee Appeal Division ( RAD ) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of 
correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception 
to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of 
oral testimony hear d, which in particular cases, attracts deference. Unless specifically stated 
below, I have applied a correctness standard.1

 1 REASONS AND DECISION  
 
[1] These are my reasons and decision in the appeal of XXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the “appellant ”) who 
appeals the refusal to approve the p ermanent resident visa application of his wife  XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX(the “applicant ”) who applied to immi grate to Canada as a member of the family class.   
 
[2] This couple married in China on October 18, 2010 and the appellant subsequently filed an 
application to spo nsor his wife for immigration to Canada. The applicant was interviewed by a 
visa officer in Hong Kong on September 21, 2011 . It was following that interview that the visa 
officer refused her application to immigrate to Canada pursuant to section 4(1) of th e 
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (the “Regulations” )1 on the grounds that the 
visa officer concluded the marriage was not genuine and had been entered into by the applicant 
primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege unde r the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Act (the “Act ”).2 The visa officer also refused the application because he concluded 
that the applicant was unable to support herself and had not provided evidence that adequate 
arrangement for care and support had been made pursuant to section 39 of the Act . 
 
[3] Section 4(1) of the Regulations provides as follows:  
4.(1)  Bad Faith  – For the purposes of these R egulations, a foreign national 
shall not be considered a spouse, a common -law partner or a conjugal partner 
of a person if the marriage, common -law partnership or conjugal partnership  
(a) was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or 
privilege under the Act; or,  
(b) is not genuine.3 
 
Section 39 of the Act  provides as follows:  
 
39. Financial reasons – A foreign national is inadmissible for financial 
reasons if they are or will be unable or unwilling to support themselves or any 
other person who is dependent on them, and have not satisfied an officer that 
adequate arrangements for care and support, oth er than those that involve 
social assistance, have been made.

INTRODUCTION  
[1] The claimant,  XXXXX XXXX , is a citizen of Nigeria. He seeks refugee protection pursuant 
to sections 96 and 97( 1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA ). 1 
ALLEGATIONS  
[2] The claimant alleges as follows:  
[3] In 2004 the claimant was hired, on a contractual basis, by the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX , to  collect information on former Delta State 
Governor , XXXXXXXXXX , who was being investigated by the Commission with respect to alleged 
money laundering and embezzlement of public funds.  
[4] The claimant then proceeded to collect incriminating inform ation on XXXXX XXXX , 
which he subsequently submitted to XXXX  Director , XXXXXXXXXX , through XXXXX XXXX , 
an XXX X employee, who was directly supervising the work of the claimant. After  XXXXX XXXX  
was removed from his position, the claimant started getting strange calls and death threats from one 
XXXXX XXXX , an agent of XXXXX XXXX . XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX to kill the claimant for his 
role in bringing charges of corruption against  XXXXXXXXXX . 
[5] In XXXXX  2008, the claimant was shot at while in a friend’s car, but managed to escape. 
Believing his identity had been compromised, and having received no support from the police in his 
home town of XXXX , the claimant went into hiding in XXXX . While in XXXX , the claimant was 
once again discovered, and XXXXXXXXXX , his supervisor at XXXX , was killed , while both were 
out together for the evening. Believ ing that his life was in danger, the claimant fled to Lagos where 
arrangements were the n made for his flight to Canada.  
DETERMINATION  
[6] The P anel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor is he a person in need 
of protection in accordance w ith section 97(1)(a) and (b) of the IRPA .

Identity   
[7] The claimant produced a number of documents corroborating his identity .2 The Panel is
