[8] The claimant indicated in his Personal Information Form (PIF)3 that he had begun work as 
an administrative assistant in his uncle’s private investigation business, but quickly learned the 
business, working primarily “for clients who sought to fi nd out about their partner’s infidelity ...and 
for clients who sought to know if their employees were stealing from them.”4 He was then , 
allegedly , offered a job by the Director of the EFCC to gather incriminating information on the then 
Governor of Delta S tate, XXXXX XXXX . The Panel finds it implausible that the Director of a high 
profile national agency would hire a 25 year old inexperienced private investigator, whose 
experience essentially was made up of s pying on cheating spouses and dishonest employees, to 
investigate a senior government official suspected of committing major fraud and misuse of public 
funds.  
[9] The claimant produced a letter from the XXXX  signed by XXXXXXXXXXXX , Head of the 
Forensic Unit, who was killed shortly afterwards. The letter indicated that the claimant was 
authorized to conduct inquiries with respect to Chief XXXXX XXXX  and Agencies of t he Federal 
Government of Nigeria.5 The letter, however, does not provide any dates as to when the claimant 
actually performed these duties on behalf of the XXXX  or the period he was employed by the 
XXXX . The letter itself does not appear to be authentic. T he XXXX  logo on the letter appears to be 
cut off at the top , and is visibly different from the logo as it appears both in an article in one of the 
claimant’s exhibits,6 as well as, on XXXX  official website.7 The address line in the letterhead has

 Section 97:  Risk of Harm  
[14]  The claimant has not demonstrated that, it is more likely than not, that he would face a risk 
to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture if he were to 
return Nigeria. There was no persuasive evidence,  that the attack in XXXX  was anything other than, 
as the police concluded, an act of criminality .  
[15]  Further, no  evidence was presented to allow the Panel to conclude that the subsequent 
shooting of XXXXX XXXX  in XXXXX , in anyway , involved the claimant,  or that he was also 
targeted. When XXXXX XXXX  was shot and killed, the claimant was in the washroom at the time. 
One would have expected assassins to have struck either before or after the claimant left to go to the 
washroom if in fact he was also being targeted. The Panel must then conclude that if the claimant 
were to return to Nigeria, he would not be subjected to an individualized risk of harm under section 
97( 1). Therefore, the claimant has not demonstrated, on a balance of probabilities, that he would 
face harm under section 97(1) of IRPA  if he were to return to Nigeria.  
CONCLUSION  
[16]  The Panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of 
protection.

sister’s family if M s. E were to lose h er status. Lastly, the Appellant  did not identify hardship, 
other than her concern about her student loan, that she would face by the loss of her status in

CONCLUSION  
 
[18]  Overall, I find that there are few considerations that wo uld warrant special relief . I find

BACKGROUND  
[1] This decision concerns three appellants. They are XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the principal 
appellant) , his spouse XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and their daughter XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX . All three 
emigrated from Iran and became permanent residents of Canada on September 20, 2010. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the appellants’ son and brother respectively, also became a permanent resident of 
Canada on the same date. On January 21, 2016 , the appellants a pplied for travel documents to 
Canada. They were refused entry to Canada and advised by a visa officer that they had not 
complied with the residency obligation set out in section 28 of the Immigration and Refugee

days with respect to a five -year period. During the five -year period , from January 21, 2011 to 
January 21, 2016 , the principal appellant had spent 148 days in Canada, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX had 
spent 345 days, and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX had spent 106 days. The appellants do not dispute that 
they had not complied with the residency obligation. However, they plead special relief on 
humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds under section 67(1)( c) of the Act. 
DECISION  
[3] For the reasons that follow , after considering the document evidence and submissions of 
the parties and hearing from the appellants and XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, I find sufficient  H&C grounds 
to allow XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  appeal. I find insufficient H&C  grounds to allow the principal 
appellant’s  and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX appeals .

ISSUE AND LAW  
[4] Section 67(1)( c) of  the Act allows the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD) to grant 
special relief in cases where sufficient H&C  considerations warrant such relief.  
[5] Prior decision -makers of the  IAD have considered  the following factors in the 
determination of whether there are sufficient H&C  considerations to grant special relief in 
residency obligation appeals: (i) the extent of t he non -compliance with the residency obligation; 
(ii) the reasons for the departure and extended stay abroad; (iii) the degree of establishment in 
Canada, initially and at the time of hearing; (iv) family ties in Canada; (v) whether attempts to 
return to C anada were made at the first opportunity; (vi) hardship and dislocation to the 
Appellant and family members if she loses her permanent resident status; and, (vii) whether there 
are other unique or special circumstances that merit special relief . These fact ors are not 
exhaustive and can vary from case to case. The weight assigned to each factor varies according 
to the circumstances of the case.2  
[6] The issue in this appeal is whether , having regard to all the circumstances of the case, 
there are sufficient H&C  grounds to justify  the appellants ’ retain ing  their  permanent resident 
status . 
[7] I will address each appellant’s facts in turn. For clarity and simplicity, I will refer to the 
appellants by their first names.

[1] These are the reasons for decision in the appeal of LXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the appellant) from a removal (exclusion) order,  dated January 14, 2009, issued against him by Member XXXXXXXXXXXXX of the Immigration Divi sion (“ID”), who found him to be inadmissible pursuant to section 40(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (“IRPA”). [2] Subsection 40(1)(a) of the IRPA reads as follows: 
Misrepresentation 40. (1) A permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible for misrepresentation  (a) for directly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of the Act. 
[3] The appellant, who came to Canada from Ni geria, was ordered removed from Canada on the basis that he had failed to disclose the fact  that he was a full-time employee of GS Telecom (Nigeria) (“GS”) at the time of his landing and accordingly did not meet the definition of dependent child under the IRPA and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (“Regulations”), and therefore engaged in a direct misrepresentation of a material fact. [4] The appellant, who is fluent in English, testif ied without the assistance of an interpreter. Documentary evidence was filed on his behalf.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons and decis ion of the Immigration Appeal Division ( the “IAD”) in 
the appeal of MarXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the “appellant”) from the refusal to approve the 
application for a permanent resident visa for her husband XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the 
“applicant”), who was sponsored  by the appellant. The application for a visa was refused because 
the visa officer found that the applicant is not a member of the family class. The applicant was 
not declared or examined at the time of the appellant’s own application for permanent residen ce.  
 
 
ISSUE  
 
[2] At issue in this  appeal is whether paragraph  117(9)(d) of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Regulations (the “ Regulations ”)1 applies, thereby excluding the applicant from 
consideration as a member of the family class.   
 
 
DECISION  
 
[3] I find  that the appellant has not es tablished that paragraph  117(9)(d) of the Regulations 
does not apply. The appeal is dismissed.  
 
 
BACKGROUND  
 
[4] The appellant is a national of the Philippines aged 34. She has been in a relationship with 
the applicant since 2008.  The appellant came to Canada as a temporary worker in 2009. She

The document indicates that the appellant is single, and the appellant also signed the document

[7] The appellant submitted her application to sponsor the applicant in January 2018. On

[8] The a pplication was then refused by an officer at the Embassy in Manila on 
October  1, 2018 on the basis that the applicant is excluded from the family class by operation of 
paragraph 117(9)(d)  of the Regulations . The refusal letter reverses the dates of marriag e and 
landing, and makes no reference to assessing whether the applicant’s application could be 
allowed on humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds.

together with the Record in making my decision. It is unnecessary to convene an oral hearing. I

ANALYSIS  
 
[11]  The appellant submits in essence that she did not declare the applicant as her husb and 
prior to becoming a permanent residence, and he was consequently not examined prior to the 
appellant’s admission to Canada as a permanent resident, as the result of her previous counsel’s 
negligence. I find that her submissions have no merit. The appel lant herself, in her letter of 
August 30, 2018, indicated that she relied on her consultant and “forgot to inform them that I 
have plans of getting married as well.”7 
 
[12]  I find that the appellant has provided sufficient communication records to establish tha t 
she did mention her plans to marry the applicant in the months leading up to the issuance of her 
permanent residence visa to both her consultant and his assistant. When this  plan was first 
mentioned to  her consultant, he advised her “You should include y our hubby to be in the 
application…will slow down the process but be much cheaper in the long run.” I do not find any 
evidence put forth by the appellant establishes that the appellant disclosed or sought advice on 
whether she should marry her husband befo re becoming landed as a permanent resident, and

 what steps she should then take with respect to being landed herself and sponsoring him. Finally, 
it appears that the appellant only registered a complaint a gainst  the consultant in April 2019 after 
Minister’ s counsel’s submissions advising that the appellant could not credibly allege negligence 
of counsel without at least registering a letter of complaint.  
 
[13]  The appellant had her PR visa prior to leaving for the Philippines  in February 2012 . The 
facts indicat e that while the appellant’s former consultant had been advised that the appellant 
intended to get married in the Philippines in March  2012 , the appellant decided to get married 
before being landed as a matter of choice, and there is no indication that the  consultant or anyone 
in his office knew she w ould get married before getting landed. Furthermore, the appellant 
concedes that she did not advise the officer who examined her when landing as a permanent 
resident that she had been  married.  
 
[14]  Even taking a s ympathetic view of the appellant’s actions and failure to advise the officer 
who landed her of her change in marital status, her  reasons for not disclosing the applicant prior 
to her admission to Canada are not relevant to whether paragraph 117(9)(d) of th e Regulations is 
applicable to this appeal . The jurisprudence is well -settled that even a lack of subjective 
knowledge of the non -disclosure of a dependent is not material. In Adjani,8 the Federal Court 
(FC) found:  
 
[31]  In my view the impugned provision d oes not allow for such an 
interpretation. The language is clear and unambiguous, subjective knowledge of 
the misrepresentation or non -disclosure is not contemplated in the regulation. The 
Court of Appeal in Azizi , above, at paragraph 28 of its reasons, int erpreted the 
provision as follows: “It simply provides that non -accompanying family members 
who have not been examined for a reason other than a decision by a visa officer  
will not be admitted as members of the family class.” (My emphasis) This 
interpretat ion is consistent with decisions of the Federal Court. As stated above, in 
XXXX  at paragraph 11, the motive is unimportant, a failure to disclose which 
prevents examination of the dependent precludes future sponsorship of that person 
as a member of the fam ily class. See also Jean -Jacques v. M.C.I ., 2005 FC 104 at 
paragraph 9.

[32]  In my view, the meaning, scope, purpose and application of the impugned 
regulation have been comprehensively dealt with in the jurisprudence.  The scope 
of the regulation is not limited to deliberate or fraudulent non -disclosure but to 
any non -disclosure which may prevent examination of a dependent. Non -
disclosed, non -accompanying family members cannot be admitted as members of 
the family class.  
 
 
[15]  I am bound by the decision of the FC in  XXXXXX . The appellant was landed as a permanent 
resident without the applicant having been examined. I find that the officer who admitted the 
appellant as a permanent resident believed her to be single. I find that her former consultant 
neither knew  she was married, nor advised her not to disclose her spouse. The appellant had an 
opportunity to declare that she was married prior to being landed but she did not. The  appellant’s 
explanation does not overcome the requirement for examination in paragraph  117(9)(d) of the 
Regulations . Therefore, the applicant  cannot be admitted as a member  of the family class.  
 
[16]  While I do not have the jurisdiction to consider H&C factors in determining this appeal, a 
subsequent application would have to be assessed by  an immigration officer in accordance with 
current policies and their discretion to  grant H&C relief pursuant to section  25 of the 
Immigration and Refugee Protection Act .9  
 
 
CONCLUSION  
 
[17]  The applicant was not examined when the appellant became a perma nent resident of 
Canada . I find that the applicant is a person described in paragraph 117(9)(d) of the Regulations 
and is therefore excluded from the family class. As the applicant is not a member of the family 
class, the IAD has no jurisdiction to conside r humanitar ian and compassionate factors.

REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
INTRODUCTION  
 
[1] The appellant, GuXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, appeals from the refusal of an application for a 
permanent resident visa made by the applicant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX . The appellant married the 
applicant and sponsored the applicant  as a member of the family class.   The application was 
refused because a visa officer determined that the marriage is not genuine and was entered into 
primarily for the purpose of acquiring  status under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 
(the “ IRPA”). 
 
ISSUE AND DECISION  
 
 
[2] Effective September 30, 2010 section 4 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection 
Regulations2 (the “Regulations” ) dealing with “bad faith” marriages, common -law partnerships 
and conjugal partnerships was amended to read as follow s: 
 
4. (1) For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be 
considered a spouse, a common -law partner, or a conjugal partner if the 
marriage, common -law partnership, conjugal partnership  
(a) was entered into primarily for the purpose  of acquiring any status or 
privilege under the Act; or  
(b) is not genuine.3 
 
 
[3] Thus, to succeed on appeal the appellant has to prove that the marriage was not entered 
into primarily for the purpose of the applicant gaining any status or privilege under the IRPA  and 
that it is genuine. To dismiss the appeal, I must find that the marri age was entered into primarily

CONCLUSION   
 
[72]   I am aware the appellant has made five trips to India since the marriage  and the appellant 
made the applicant the beneficiary of her life insurance policy effective July 3, 2012.  On the 
whole of the ev idence before me, I cannot discount the numerous contradictions between the 
forms and the testimony of the appellant and the applicant nor do I find credible the attempts to 
explain away the too numerous internal and external inconsistencies in the testimo ny that relate 
to the genesis of the relationship which is crucial to determining the genuineness of the marriage 
and whether the marriage was entered into primarily for immigration purposes.  
 
[73]  I have concluded that the evidence of the appellant and the applicant is not accurate, 
honest, reliable, and credible generally. Consequently, I place little weight on the post -refusal 
evidence which I view, in the circumstances of this case, as submitted only to advance the 
appeal, and not as an indication of the genuineness of the relationship between the appellant and 
the applicant.  
 
[74]  Accordingly, I find based on the totality of the evidence and on a balance of probabilities 
that the applicant’s marriage  to the appellant is not genuine and that the primary reason for the 
applicant marrying the appellant was for the purpose of acquiring status in Canada under the 
IRPA . 
 
[75]  The appeal is dismissed.

DECISION   
[5] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 The 
RPD was correct to find that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  is neither a Convention refugee 
nor a person in need of protection. I do not agree with any of the arguments that XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX counsel makes on appeal for why he believe s that the RPD erred in this 
case. In my view, the RPD was correct to fi nd that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  failed 
to rebut the presumption that he would have access to adequate state protection in Chile. The RPD 
also correctly found that the instances of discrimination alleged by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 
XXXX  did not amount to persec ution, even when considered cumulatively.

ANALYSIS OF MERITS  
RPD did not err in relation to state protection finding  
[11]  XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  seeks to rely on various court decisions to submit 
that the RPD rendered a perverse and selective finding on the issue of state protection. His Counsel 
argues that the RPD failed to consider the operational reality of state protection in Chile, that i t 
ignored relevant evidence, and that it failed to consider XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  
particular circumstances as a victim of organized crime. I do not take issue with any of the 
jurisprudence quoted by Counsel in the appeal memorandum. However, I disagree with him that 
the RPD erred in the ways alleged.  
[12]  First, I find that the RPD’s state protection analysis was very detailed and thorough. The 
RPD did not limit itself to considering the existence of laws on the books; instead, it took care to 
examine the doc umentary evidence in relation to the operational effectiveness of state protection 
in Chile.  
[13]  Second, I disagree with Counsel that the proper question for the RPD to have asked was 
whether there was clear and convincing evidence that the state could protect  XXXX XXXX XXXX 
XXXX XXXX  given his particular circumstances. While I do agree with Counsel that the RPD 
had to take into account XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  particular circumstances, it was 
his onus to present clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presu mption of state protection in 
this case. I agree with the RPD that he failed to do so.  
[14]  As noted by the RPD, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  submitted articles from 2012 
to 2014 about drug arrests and organized crime in Chile. In my view, the RPD did not err in 
preferring the more recent country conditions evidence contained in the National Documentation 
Package for Chile , given that the articles submitted by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  dated 
from more than four years before the RPD hearing. In addition, the RPD was correct to find that 
the mere existence of organized crime in a particular country does not rebut the presumption of 
state protection. Finally, the RPD was correct to note that even some of XXXX XXXX XXXX

OVERVIEW  
[1] The principal appellant , XXXXXXXXX , and his son , XXXXXXXXX , the associate 
appellant, are citizens of Haiti. In his claim for refugee protection,1 the principal appellant state d 
that if they were to return to Haiti, he and his son would be killed by the same people who killed 
his father on XXXX XXXX , 2004, in the f amily home in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX . 
A short time after this event , the appellant went to the Dominican Republic  to escape the killers, 
fearing that they would try to kill him because he could  identify them. Indeed, a few days later, 
they returned and r ansacked the house . Sensing that his family needed him, the appellant decided 
to return to Haiti , but took care to keep away from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX . He 
lived in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  for almost two years before settling in Venezuela 
on XXXX XXXX , 2005. His son was born there . 
[2] Eleven years later, on XXXX XXXX , 2016, the appellant s left V enezuela and went to the

they were excluded from protection under the IRPA , pursuant to section  98 of the IRPA.  In 
support of this conclusion , the RPD noted that the principal appellant had stated in his claim for

RPD, the principal appellant still had this status at the time of the hearing , despite the fact that 
his permanent residence card had expired.3 The associate a ppellant has Venezuelan citizenship.

Venezuela based on  one of the five Convention grounds and that the evidence did not establish,

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the  reasons and decision  in a n appeal by XXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the “appellant”) from 
the refusal of the sponsored application for a permanent residence visa for hi s spouse, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the “applicant”).  
 
 
BACKGROUND  
 
[2] The refusal was pursuant to 4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  
(the “Regulations” ). 1 The visa officer found the marriage between the appellant and the 
applicant is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of the applicant acquiring 
status under the Immigr ation and Refugee Protection Act  (the “Act” ).2 
 
[3] The appellant is a 48 -year -old citizen of Canada who emigrated from Vietnam in 1998 . 
The applicant is 27  years old . She was  born and still resides in Vietnam .  
 
[4] The appellant and applicant met in Hue, Vietnam , when the appellant hired the 
applicant’s taxi for two short trips on March 8, 2013.  Thereafter, they met a few times before the 
appellant returned to Canada in April 2013. Subsequently, the appellant and applicant kept in 
touch by  electronic means. The a ppellant next visited the applicant,  in Vietnam,  in June 2013 
when he stayed for an entire year. The couple married in February 2014, and the appellant has 
returned to Vietnam for long periods of time frequently since that time .

 ISSUES AND HEARING PROCES S 
 
[5] The issue in this appeal is whether 4(1) of the Regulations  applies . The onus is on the 
appellant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that his spouse is a member of his family 
class.  
 
[6] Regulation  4(1) provides that a spouse is disqualified as fa mily class member if the 
marriage : 
(a) was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the 
Act; or  
 
(b) is not genuine.  
 
For this appeal to succeed, the appellant must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that his 
spouse is  not disqualified. Therefore, if the evidence establishes that either one of the above tests 
is met, then the applicant is disqualified because she is not a member of the  family class.  
 
[7] After interviewing both the applicant and appellant in person, the vis a officer concluded 
their marriage is not genuine and that Regulation  4(1) disqualified the applicant to enter Canada 
as a family class member . As a result of his appeal, the hearing before me was the appellant’s 
opportunity to provide evidence to  address the visa officer’ s concerns and establish the 
applicant’s membership in the family class . 
 
[8] In addition to the Appeal Record, the appellant provided documents  marked as Exhibits 
A-1 to A -3. Both the appellant and the applicant testified using an interpreter  present in the 
hearing room , as did the appellant’ s sister. Both c ounsel provided oral submissions on the second 
hearing date noted above.

 DECISION  
 
[9] Considering all of the evi dence, I  find it is sufficient to satisfy the appellant’s onus to 
prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the marriage is genuine and not entered into primarily 
for the purpose of acquiring a status or privilege under the Act. As a result, the applicant is a 
member of the family class and t he appeal is  allowed . 
 
 
ANALYSIS  
 
[10]  In ord er for an appeal of this kind to succeed, the evidence must demonstrate it is more 
probable than not that a marriage is genuine and not entered into for the primary purpose of 
immigration . As a result , reliability of the witnesses’ descriptions of events, circumstances , and 
their intentions must be analyzed . In this case, I did not form the im pression any witness was 
deliberately trying to deceive me . Nevertheless, some inconsistencies compromise d the 
reliability of each witnesses’  testimony, which was acce ntuated when compared to documents 
(such as application forms) presum ed to accurately reflect the facts . Further, circumstances upon 
which a reasonable inference may be drawn regarding the applicant’s motivation for marrying 
the appellant figured prominent ly in my deliberations.  
 
[11]  The visa officer listed five concerns: the significant age disparity between the spouses, 
the applicant’ s previous unsuccessful application  to leave Vietnam as a student, two 
inconsistencies relating to the appellant’s business in Canada, and a lack of specificity regarding 
the couple’s future plans in Canada. While certain evidence presented at the hearing addressed 
and answered some of these concerns, other inconsistencies and questions  surfaced  during the 
testimonies of all three  witnesses  and some of these questions arose in areas not canvassed by the 
visa officer.  
 
[12]  Dealing first with the visa officer’s concerns which were relatively easily resolved by the 
appellant’s evidence, I find the differences between the appellant’s and a pplicant’s knowledge of 
his business financing or principle objectives in becoming self -employed insignificant  and

 understandable , in light of the overall context of the relationship. Further, I accept the applicant’s 
explanation that there was either an e rror in form completion or lapse in her memory regarding 
her application for an American student visa in 2009.  
 
[13]  The two remaining concerns (i .e.) the significant age difference between the spouses and 
the applicant’s inability to provide details about her  expected life in Canada , are intertwined and 
accentuated by other related concerns arising from gaps and inadequacies in the evidence . These 
concerns, which were also emphasized by the Minister’s counsel, require more extensive 
analysis, which follows bel ow.  
 
[14]  While the appellant testified that he and his wife live with his sister, XXXX, in Dalat when 
he is in Vietnam , XXXX’s testimony did not fully corroborate this. Initially,  XXXX said  she lives 
“close” to the applicant and when her brother (the appellant ) comes to visit Vietnam he stays 
mostly in her  house with no one else. Later, XXXX testified that both the applicant and her brother 
stay with her , when he is in Vietnam,  but that they  “sometimes visit her family  in Hue or go on 
other outings.”  XXXX did n ot say the applicant lives with her  when her brother is not in Vietnam , 
although the applicant inferred this during her testimony , as did the appellant’s counsel during 
final submiss ions . The Record reflects that the applicant noted her residence with her mother and 
siblings in Hue in her October 2015 application form.  Given the variations in the testimonies 
between the appellant, the applicant and XXXX, it is not possible to be certain which is the most 
accurate.  Nevertheless, the preponderance of evidenc e leads to my conclusion that  the applicant 
lives with XXXX only when the appellant is in Vietnam and, when he is not present, the applicant 
lives with her own family in Hue.   
 
[15]  Documents purporting to illustrate electronic communication  between the appella nt and 
applicant  were untranslated,  and there was  inconsistent evidence around how the parties 
communicate with each other when apart (i .e.) by  phone and/or wi -fi. Having said this, the most 
compelling evidence which tends to  demonstrate a genuine and abid ing commitme nt to the 
marriage is the approximately  49 months out o f the past 63  months that the appellant has spent in 
Vietnam.

Significantly, the appellant said no one  from his family attended the wed ding or reception but he

testified he met the applicant’s mother during the same trip to Vietnam during which he met the 
applicant (ie. March -April 2013), however the applicant said the meeting did not occur until after

For  the purposes of this decision, it is not necessary to recite more or all the inconsistencies 
between the appellant and applicant’s testimonies regarding certain eve nts or internal 
inconsistencies between their application forms and viva voce evidence. Suffice it to say I find 
the inconsistencies relatively minor when placed within the broader context of the evidence 
which demonstrates the genuineness of the marriage . While these inconsistenci es were carefully 
explored by the Minister’s counsel, they were also explained to my satisfaction  by the appellant 
and the applicant .  
 
[22]  Beyond the inconsistencies, the Minister’s counsel emphasized that the significant age 
gap bet ween the couple and  the appellant’s rather hasty proposal are the biggest obstacles the 
appellant must overcome in this appeal. I agree, and, after considering the totality of the evidence 
and weighing it carefully, I am satisfied the evidence is sufficien t to  prove the marriage is 
genuine on a balance of probabilities.  
 
[23]  Turning next to consideration of the primary purpose of the marriage, it is notable that t he 
appellant’s daughter in Canada is 21 and has never met or spoken with the applicant. His 4  olde r 
siblings in Canada all disagreed with  the marriage and did not travel to Vietnam to attend the 
ceremony. Perhaps even more significantly, neither of his 2 sisters in Vie tnam attended the 
wedding ; expressing their disapproval  of the union due to the age d ifference between their 
brother and his young bride.  With the exception of his daughter, whom the appellant said just 
wants him to be happy, all of the appellant’s close family members (siblings)  have expressed 
concern that the applicant was probably  using  him to immigrate to Canada and would leave him 
upon gaining status. They reminded him of his first marriage which ended in divorce after his 
wife’s decision to move on to a new relationship  in Canada . 
 
[24]  Both the applicant and the appellant spoke about his worry that the applicant would 
abandon the marriage after she was permitted to come to Canada . The a pplicant acknowledged

 this concern  and that she and her husband have had conversations about it. Although she  did not 
elaborate, she  testified  that “we love  each  other truly.”  The appella nt, on the other hand, admitted  
in cross -examination that one of the reasons he took a considerable period  to apply to sponsor his 
wife to come to Canada was to give her time to “prove her love” for him and for his family to 
observe her developin g devotion. He wanted time to establish  a deeper trust in his wife’s motives 
and, by the time he testified at the hearing, he was confident in h er love which he said was 
proven largely by their sexual connection . Like the applicant, th e appellant did not provide much 
detail about how or why he knows his wife is committed to the marriage, except to say that their 
sex life provides proof of her love. The appellant’s candid acknowledgement that he had 
concerns about the applicant’s primary  motivation for marrying him , which continued well after 
their wedding date , enhances his credi bility . 
 
[25]  The essential question regarding the applicant’s motivation for marriage is not whether 
she had some desire to acquire status in Canada; it is whether i mmigration was her primary 
reason for marrying the appellant. One circumstance that gives rise to a concern that the 
appellant’s status might have been a significant reason for the applicant’s  interest in him  is that 
the applicant said she knew he was Cana dian during the first days of their acquaintance.  A 
second concerning circumstance is the applicant’s willingness to entertain the appellant’s  
“proposal” to move their friendly relationship toward a potential marriage during a telephone 
conversation, afte r spending a fairly limited period of time with him in Vietnam. Notably, this 
couple met through a purely commercial transaction when the applicant drove the appellant in 
her taxi and there was nothing remarkable about their first contacts that would lead one to predict 
a romantic attachment would follow. It is somewhat implausible that the applicant would become 
familiar or fond enough of the appellant during a few other social encounters during that March 
to April 2013 period to explain her willingness to  “take the relationship further” and  accept an 
engagement ring in June.  
 
[26]  These considerations lead to a reasonable inference that immigration to Canada was one  
of the motivating factors behind the applicant’s decision to marry as she did. Having said this , 
her continued devotion to the marriage demonstrates not only its genuineness, but also that her 
primary purpose was to be married, and not to immigrate. The  appellant considered his wife’s

 motivation carefully, and was undoubtedly influenced by the conce rns of his family members 
and prior divorce. He and the applicant spoke abo ut these concerns, which  reflects positively on 
the depth and maturity of their communication. The evidence also establishes that the appellant 
has an  earnest desire to have a succe ssful marriage with the applicant and enjoy a full life with 
her in Canada . The applicant has obtained training to work in the appellant’s  nail business in 
Canada, and expressed interest in ha ving children with him . The totality of the evidence 
demonstrate s a genuine and ongoing commitment to the marriage beyond immigration benefits. 
Further, if th is was a marriage of convenience for the applicant, it is unlikely she would have 
been willing to wait the years she did while her husband gained sufficient trust  to commence the 
sponsorship process. Therefore, I find it is more probable than not that the applicant was 
interested in gaining status in Canada arising from her marriage,  but the evidence  does not 
demonstrate gaining such status was her primary motivati on.  The enduring nature of this 
relationship  is a significant consideration, and together with the other circumstances noted above,  
establishes  on balance of probabilities that the applicant’s primary purpose was not immigration.  
 
[27]  The  totality of the evid ence leads me to conclude it is more probable than not that the 
marriage is genuine and was not entered into for the primary purpose of facilitating the 
applicant’s immigration  to Canada. Therefore, this appeal is allowed.

REASONS FOR DECISION  
[1] This is an Application pursu ant to Rule  43(1) of the Immigration Appeal Division (the 
“IAD”) Rules  for an order extending the time to file the Notice of Appeal. Counsel for the 
respondent opposes the application.  
The Facts  
[2] XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the applicant) received a refusal of he r sponsored permanent 
residence application as a member of the Family Class dated 15 July 2013 received by the 
appellant on 25 July 2013. The appellant’s Notice of Appeal was received at the Immigration and 
Refugee Board on 25 October 2013, beyond the thir ty-day deadline for the submission of 
documents at this appeal.  
[3] The appellant has submitted an application to extend time for filing a Notice of Appeal. 
The respondent opposes this application.  
DECISION  
[4] The application to extend the time for filing the No tice of Appeal is dismissed.  
The appellant’s position  
[5] The appellant submits that he relied on a friend who works as an immigration consultant 
to file the Notice of Appeal on his behalf. This individual failed to file the Notice of Appeal in 
the requisite t ime. The appellant fo llowed up with this individual i n October 2013, at which time 
he discovered the Notice of Appeal had not been filed. The appellant requests that the application 
to extend time for filing the Notice of Appeal be allowed.  
The Minister’s position  
[6] Counsel for the Minister submits that the ap pellant has failed to identify  the friend who 
offered to file the Notice of Appeal on his behalf, that the Notice of Appeal is late; and that, had 
the appellant been concerned about the filing of this ap peal, he would have followed up with his

[8] The panel has considered the submissions of the  appellant and respondent within the 
context of an application to extend the time limit for filing an appeal.  
[9] Hennelly1 stands for the proposition that an application to extend time must meet the 
following four preconditions:  
1. The applicant must demonstr ate a continuing intention to pursue the 
application.  
2. The application must have some merit.  
3. No prejudice to the respondent arises from the delay.  
4. A reasonable explanation for the delay exists.  
[10]  These factors must be read with the earlier decision o f the Federal Court of Appeal in 
XXXXXX v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) , [1985] 2 FC 263, 63 NR 106, which 
makes it clear that the underlying consideration when weighing these four factors is that justice be 
done between the parties, and  that an extension  of time may still be granted if one of the criteria is

[11]  The onus lies on the appellant to establish his case on a balance of probabilities. As 
confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in F.H. v. McDougall ,3 the evidence must always be 
clear, convincing and cogent i n order to satisfy the balance of probabilities test.  
[12]  With respect to the first precondition, the appellant’s actions and the explanations for his 
delay are not consistent with a continuing, and therefore, a continuous, intention to pursue this 
appeal. The  appellant failed to confirm, with his friend, whether the Notice of Appeal was duly 
filed within the according timelines until October 2013, approximately two months after the 
deadline for filing th e Notice of Appeal had expired.  
[13]  The appellant’s affidavit  indicates that he relied on his friend, who works as an 
immigration consultant, to help him appeal the decision and to file the Notice of Appeal on his 
behalf. In as much as this person acted on the appellant’s behalf as a representative, the appellant 
is held to his choice of adviser and his allegations of any incompetence on the part of that adviser 
must be accompanied by corroborating evidence .4 The appellant presents no such corroborating 
evidence. The appellant has therefore not presented cogent evide nce  to establish a reasonable 
explanation for the delay in filing a Notice of Appeal. It is the responsibility of the appellant to 
ensure the Notice of Appeal is received. In the case at hand, the appellant did not ensure the 
Notice of Appeal was filed in a timely fashion  nor, at a minimum, did he contact his friend, who 
was representing him, or the IAD, to ensure his compliance with this requirement.  
[14]  With respect to the question of prejudice to the respondent, the panel cannot find that the 
delay inordinat ely prejudices the respondent. It is true that should the application be granted, the 
respondent would be required to prepare this case, however, given the respondent’s expertise, 
prejudice would not be significant. Considering potential prejudice to the r espondent, there is 
moreover no evidence of any significant concerns arising due to the passage of time. In this vein,

The importance of that public interest is reflected in the relatively short time 
limits for the commencement of challenges to administrative decisi ons - within 30 
days from the date on which the decision is communicated, or such further time as 
the Court may allow on a motion for an extension of time. That time limit is not 
whimsical. It exists in the public interest, in order to bring finality to 
administrative decisions so as to ensure their effective implementation without 
delay and to provide security to those who comply with the decision or enforce 
compliance with it, often at considerable expense.  
[15]  The above finding also applies with respect to the appellant’s failure to file his Notice of 
Appeal with the IAD in a timely fashion. Interests in bringing about the conclusion of 
administrative proceedings within a reasonable time and adequately implementing Canadian 
immigration laws must be considere d in conjunction with all other factors in this case.  
[16]  The panel has also considered the merit of the appellant’s application and finds that this 
application has merit, this being the reunification of families in Canada. This obj ective is 
outlined in secti on 3 (d) of the IRPA. This factor, however, is insufficient to outweigh the 
considerations outlined above, which, when placed in the balance, do not weigh in the 
appellant’s favo ur. 
[17]  Accordingly, for all of the above reasons, the application to extend the ti me to file the 
Notice of Appeal is dismissed.  
CONCLUSION  
[18]  The appellant has not met his onus of demonstrating in a clear, convincing and cogent 
manner that a reasonable explanation for his delay in filing a Notice of Appeal exists. Having 
weighed the appeal ’s relative merit against the appellant’s conduct and the necessity of bringing 
finality to administrative decisions and effectively implementing Canada’s immigration laws 
within the context of these specific facts of this case, the panel finds that the in terests of justice 
as between the parties do not justify excusing the appellant from compliance with the IAD Rules . 
[19]  The application for an extension of time is dismiss ed.

ISSUES  
 
[8] The appellant’s representative did not challenge the legal validity of the appellant’s 
exclusion order, nor, however, did she expressly concede that the exclusion order was legally 
valid. Accordingly, the first issue before me is the legal va lidity of the exclusion order. The 
appellant expressly asks the IAD to use its discretionary jurisdiction to grant special relief and 
the second issue before me is whether, taking into account the best interests of a child directly  
affected by the decision, sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant 
special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case.

 EVIDENCE  
 
[9] In addition to hearing the oral testimony of the appellant, the Panel was also provided 
documentary evidence by the appellant3 and the Minister .4 I have taken into consideration the 
contents of the Appeal Record (the “Record”) and the oral submissions of the parties.  
 
DECISION  
 
[10]  I find the exclusion order made on November 3, 2014 to be legally  valid with respect to 
the appellant. Based on the evidence before me, taking into account the  best interests of a child 
directly affected by the decision, I find there are not sufficient humanitarian and compassionate 
considerations to warrant special rel ief in light of all the circumstances of the case. The appeal is 
dismissed.  
 
ANALYSIS  
 
[11]  In Bellido ,5 the Federal  Court found that two factors must be present for a finding of 
inadmissibility under s.  40(1) of the Act . There must be misrepresentations made a nd those

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, appeals pursuant to section 63(1) of the Immigration and 
Refugee Protection  Act1 (the Act) from a decision of the visa officer not to issue a permanent 
resident visa to her spouse, Carlos OrlanXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the applicant), on the basis that the 
marriage is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or 
privilege under the Act, thereby rendering the applicant not a member of the family class 
pursuant to section 4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protecti on Regulations2 (Regulations) . 
 
[2] The appellant bears the burden of proof. At the hearing of this appeal the appellant 
testified in person and the applicant by telephone conference call, with the assistance of a 
Spanish interpreter. The appellant was not represented by counsel. She filed t wo exhibits of 
documents, marked as exhibits A -1 and A -2. The Respondent is the Minister of Citizenship and 
Immigration and was represented by Minister’s counsel. The Minister’s document is the Record.  
 
DECISION  
 
[3] Having considered the evidence and submiss ions of the parties, I find that, on a balance 
of probabilities, the marriage was not entered into primarily for immigration purposes and is 
genuine.  
 
[4] The appeal is allowed.  
 
ISSUE  
 
[5] Under  section 4(1) of the  Regulations  the issue is whether, on a balance o f probabilities, 
this marriage is genuine and one that was not entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring 
status or privilege under the  Act . I can dismiss the appeal if either prong of the test in  section 4(1)

one or both of the spouses at the time of entering into the marriage. The marriage will be caught 
by the first prong if, for one or both of the spouses, the primary  purpose of entering into the 
marriage is to gain an ad vantage in immigration. The temporal element of the test is at the time 
of entering into the marriage and the immigration purpose must be the primary purpose.

ANALYSIS  
 
[11]  In considering whether the marriage is genuine for the purposes of the Regulations,  I 
examined a number o f factors6 and took into account additional evidence that was not before the 
visa officer.7 I am cognizant of the immigration objectives, especially “to see that families are 
reunited in Canada.”8 
 
Credibility of the witnesses  
 
[12]  I had the benefit of seeing and hearing the appellant testify in person and hearing the 
applicant testify by teleconference, both under affirmation in this hearing de novo . In general, 
there is a presumption of truth in sworn evidence, unless there is some  reason to doubt that 
truthfulness.9 I found the appellant’s and applicant’s evidence to be mostly consistent and 
credible.  
 
Genuineness of marriage  
 
[13]  The genuineness of a marriage can be affected by a number of different indicia .10 These 
are not identical i n every appeal as the genuineness of the marriage can be affected by any 
number of different factors in each appeal.  
 
[14]  These can include, but are not limited to, such factors as how the relationship developed; 
the intent of the parties to the marriage; the length of the relationship; the amount of time spent 
together; conduct at the time of meeting, at the time of an engagement and/or the wedding; 
behaviour subsequent to a wedding; the level of knowledge of each other’s relationship histories; 
level of conti nuing contact and communication; the provision of financial support; the 
knowledge of and sharing of responsibility for the care of children brought into the marriage; the

Attempts to conceive  
 
[21]  The appellant was treated  in a fertility clinic in Toronto. She had artificial insemination 
twice in Colombia to increase her chances of conceiving. I find that this attempt to have a child, 
though not determinative, is further evidence of the genuineness of the couple’s marriage . 
 
Future plans  
 
[22]  Both the appellant and the applicant have discussed their plans if this appeal is allowed 
and if it is refused. If the appeal is allowed the applicant will find a job in Canada. If this appeal 
is not successful the appellant and the applica nt both testified that the applicant  will settle things 
in Canada and return to Colombia , or they would go to some other country in order  to live 
together. I believe that the priority of the couple is to live together.  
 
Appellant’s and applicant’s immigration history  
 
[23]  I agree with the visa officer that the immigration history of the couple raises questions of 
credibility and calls into question the motivation for the marriage. The appellant married her first 
husband three months after she came to Canada and was sponsore d by him, although she was 
separated from him at the time. The applicant’s previous attempts to come to Canada also raise 
concerns that his intention in marrying the appellant was to gain entry to Canada. As noted 
above, the applicant met a woman from Cana da on line and married her in Colombia. His first 
wife sponsored him, but the sponsorship was refused and they divorced. The applicant also 
attempted to obtain a visitor’s visa to Canada by providing false information on his visa 
application form that he w as in a common -law relationship, when he was not. However, although 
these concerns are serious, I find that this particular marriage was genuine ab initio  and the 
primary purpose of the marriage was not to gain entry into Canada.

CONCLUSION  
 
[24]  The onus is  on the appellant to satisfy me, on a balance of probabilities, that this marriage 
is not caught by section 4(1) of the Regulations . In considering the totality of evidence, I find 
that the appellant has met that burden in this case.  
 
[25]  I have considered the  evidence and submissions in this case, including the documentary 
evidence, the photographic evidence, the telephone invoices, the evidence of the appellant’s 
visits to Colombia and the testimony at the hearing.  
 
[26]  This case rests largely on the credibility of the parties. As stated, I find both the 
appellant’s and the applicant’s evidence credible in regard to the foundation of their marriage. 
The logical inference is that the relationship and hence the marriage is genuine and was not 
entered into primarily for gaining status or privilege under the Act . 
 
[27]  The appeal is allowed.

REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1]      XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the appellant), a permanent resident and a citizen of the Kingdom of 
Morocco by birth, appeals pursuant to ss. 63(3) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  
(the Act ) from a removal order made against him on December 1, 2016 by the Immigration 
Division at Montreal, Quebec, for reasons of misrepresentation.  
 
[2]      I received the oral evidence of the appellant at a hearing on November 29, 2018.  At a 
subsequent hearing on February 21, 2019, I received the oral evidence of the appellant’s cur rent 
common -law partner and mother of his two children, his wife and sponsor and the sponsor’s son.  
A sworn interpreter in the Moroccan dialect of Arabic was present on a standby basis throughout 
both sittings and at no time was any difficulty in communic ation apparent or alleged.  
 
[3]      At the conclusion of oral testimony, the appellant disputed the legal validity of the 
removal order.  In the alternative , he argued that sufficient humanitarian considerations were 
present to justify granting special relief.  Th e Minister held the position that the removal order 
was valid in law.  The Minister further held that there were insufficient humanitarian 
considerations present to justify granting special relief.  In the alternative, particularly with 
regard to the best interest of a child directly affected, the Minister suggested a stay of removal of 
three  years would be appropriate.  The appellant endorsed the Minister’s proposal of a stay.  
 
[4]      After considering the evidence before me, the oral testimony and the positions of the 
parties, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the removal order made against the 
appellant is valid in law.  I further determine, taking into account the best interest of a child 
directly affected, that sufficient humanitarian and compa ssionate considerations do not exist, in 
all the circumstances of the case, to justify granting special relief.  I , therefore , dismiss the 
present appeal for the reasons set out below.

Legal Validity  
 
[5]      The appellant was granted permanent residen ce on the basis of his sponsorship by his 
wife.  That application was initially dismissed by an immigration officer.  The sponsor appealed 
that decision to the Immigration Appeal Division, which set aside that decision by order dated 
December 13, 2010.1 The matter was referred back to an immigration officer in accordance with 
ss. 70(1) of the Act , and the appellant’s permanent resident visa was eventually issued.  
 
[6]      Subsequent to his marriage, the appellant learned that his wife had engaged in a romantic 
exch ange of emails with another man.  Although he said he forgave her, he testified that he 
entered into an online relationship of his own with another woman living in Ottawa on the 
‘Badoo’ dating site.  The appellant testified that his online profile identifi ed himself as single, 
when, in fact, he was married to his wife. The relationship reached a point that the woman in 
Canada began sending the appellant money in Morocco.  
 
[7]      When the permanent resident visa was issued to the appellant, he testified that his wi fe 
did not have the funds to pay for his ticket to Canada.  The appellant’s wife, however, testified 
that the appellant never told him the visa was issued.  She also testified, contrary to his testimony 
that she never told the appellant he would need to bu y his own ticket.  I prefer the testimony of 
his wife over that over the appellant.  Despite the extensive financial support from the other 
woman, the appellant did not have the funds to pay for his own airline ticket.  Instead, he 
persuaded the woman in O ttawa to pay for his ticket as far as Montreal.  He testified that the plan 
was for that woman to receive him at Montreal airport. The woman gave him the money for his 
ticket to Ottawa.  He did not tell his wife and sponsor that another woman had paid for his ticket 
to Canada.  He did not inform his wife and sponsor when he was coming to Canada. He arrived 
in Canada at Pierre Elliot Trudeau Airport in Montreal on April 17, 2011.2 
 
[8]      The appellant’s problems began when, upon completing the customs declaration form 
required of arriving passengers, he provided the address of the woman in Ottawa, and not that of 
his wife as provided in the immigration documents he presented.  The officer examining him

The Seriousness of the misrepresentation leading to the Removal Order and the 
circumstances surrounding it  
 
[17]      Obtaining permanent residence through misrepresentation is serious in and of itself.  I 
find that the appellant’s pattern of persistent, deceitful behaviour aggravates the seriousness 
considerably.  He was not a credible or trustworthy witness before me.  The appellant’s pattern 
of deceitful behaviour has affected the lives of two women in Canada, including the wife who 
sponsored him. In th e circumstances of the present appeal, I find that the seriousness of the 
misrepresentation is an aggravating factor in my consideration.  
 
The Remorsefulness of the Appellant  
 
[18]      The appellant testified that he was sorry for what happened between him and his wife and 
sponsor.  I do not find his expressions of remorsefulness to be sincere or credible, because I 
found his testimony before me not to be wholly credible.  I find rather that his remorsefulness

The Length of Time spent in Canada and the Degree to which the Appellant is established

[19]      The appellant has been eight years in Canada since his ob taining permanent residence in 
April 2019. He has held a number of jobs in Edmonton, Ottawa and the Greater Toronto Area.  
The appellant did not disclose any Notices of Assessment or paystubs to substantiate his income.  
He testified at the time of the fir st sitting of the hearing he had been laid off and he was drawing 
Employment Insurance.  He did disclose an offer of employment for a position beginning 
December 18, 2018.7 His annual salary was set to be $24,000.   
 
[20]      The Federal Court has provided divergent guidance on how the IAD is to consider 
establishment in the context of removal order for misrepresentation. I am guided by the decision 
of the Federal Court in XXX , wherein Mr. Justice XXXX declared in part:  
‘I agre e with the Minister’s submission that the decision is unreasonable because 
the IAD, in considering the issue of establishment did not feel [Ms. XXX’s] 
misrepresentation was a relevant factor.”   In my view, it is a relevant factor 
when considering a person’ s degree of establishment.  To do otherwise is to 
place the immigration cheat on an equal footing with the person who has 
complied with the law.   Whether the impact of the fraud is to reduce the 
establishment to zero or to something more is a question for the discretion of the 
decision -maker based on the particular facts before him or her.   But it must be 
considered.’8 
 
[21]      In light of my analysis of the extent of the appellant’s misrepresentation and his lack of 
genuine, credible remorse, I give little weight to the length and degree of the appellant’s 
establishment in Canada.  
 
The Appellant’s Family in Canada  
 
[22]      The appellant is with a common -law partner since 2013 and the couple has two children 
together.  The appellant has no other family in Canada, other than  his estranged wife and 
sponsor.  The presence of his children in Canada particularly is a mitigating factor in my 
consideration.

[27]      The appellant was raised and schooled in Morocco.  He previously worked in Morocco.  
He has parents, his ma rried sister and other close family who reside in that country.  There was 
no oral or written evidence that would substantiate hardship for the appellant, beyond the

Best Inter est of a Child  
 
[28]      The appellant’s two young children are directly affected by the disposition of the appeal.  
The appellant’s partner testified that he is a good father to their children. They are not yet 
schooling but the appellant disclosed objective count ry condition documentation9 which supports 
the suggestion that the children’s best interest do not lie in joining the appellant upon his removal 
to Morocco. Neither child speaks French or Moroccan Arabic, the main languages prevailing in

[29]      The  appellant would be exclude d from Canada for a period of five  years upon his 
removal from Canada.  The children would potentially be separated from their father for a

[30]      On the whole , I find that the best interest of the appellant’s children favours allowing the 
appeal to permit the appellant’s children to continue to grow up with both parents.  
Stay of Removal  
 
[31]      The Minister proposed in the event the appeal were to be allowed that speci al relief 
should be in the form of  a stay of removal under s. 68 of the Act .  If I understand the Minister’s 
rationale, it lies in the continued presence in Canada being beneficial to his children. While I 
sympathize with that approach, I find that consid eration is already addressed by my assessment 
of the best interest of the child.  
 
[32]      My understanding of stays of removal is that they are intended to afford the appellant an 
opportunity to demonstrate rehabilitation and avoid recidivism, leading to a reinteg ration as a

CONCLUSION  
 
[33]      The removal order before me is valid in law.  Upon considering the humanitarian and 
compassionate co nsiderations present in this matter, I find that the seriousness of the 
misrepresentation, lack of genuine, credible remorse and the lack of hardship for the appellant 
outweigh the appellant’s relatively low degree of establishment,  the impact of the remo val on 
the family and the best interest of his two children.  I acknowledge that the best interest of a child 
is an important consideration, but in the circumstances of the appellant’s case, I find they are not 
a determinative factor.  
 
[34]      I conclude that the a ppellant has failed to establish , on a balance of probabilities, taking 
into account the best interest of a child directly affected, that sufficient humanitarian and 
compassionate considerations exist, in all the circumstances of the case, to justify grant ing 
special relief.  
 
[35]      The appeal is dismissed.

Protection Act (the “ Act ”).1 The appellant appeals pursuant to s ection  63(5) of the Act . 
 
[2] On April 2, 2003, the appellant prepared a section  44(1) admissi bility report alleging that

 BACKGROUND  
 
[5] The respondent is an Iranian national aged 58. He has been living in Canada since he 
came here in 1992 at the age of 31 and has been a protected person since 1993. He is married to a 
Canadian citizen and has two children born in Canada who are now in their teens.  
 
[6] The respondent left Iran in 1979 for studies and spent most of the following 13 years in 
India before coming to Canada and making a claim for refugee  protection against Iran in 
May  1992. His claim was based on the risk that he would face as a supporter of the People’s 
Mujahi deen Organization (PMO ).2  
 
[7] His refugee claim was granted in June 1993 and he applied for permanent residence in 
June 1994. That application has never been decided due to the concerns of Canadian Security 
Intelligence Service ( CSIS ) and immigration enforcem ent entities about his possible 
inadmissibility to Canada on security grounds.  
 
[8] The respondent was interviewed by CSIS on two occasions in 1994 and 1995, following 
which CSIS concluded in February 1997 that it had no intention to initiate fu rther steps to 
investigate the r espondent’s admissibility under the Immigration Act .3  
 
[9] However, the respondent was then interviewed by a Canada Border Services Agency

has not yet made a decision on this application. It was until June 2016 tha t the appellant

parties then agreed to a timeline for written submission on the issue. The ID issued its decision

ISSUES  
 
[12]  Does the ID have the jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceedings of an admissibility 
hearing where it finds that the Minister has committed an abuse of process? If so, is a stay of 
proceedings an appropriate remedy in the circumstances of this cas e? 
 
DECISION  
 
[13]  The ID has the jurisdiction to grant an appropriate remedy where it finds that any party 
before it commits an abuse of process. I find that the Minister did commit an abuse of process in 
delaying referral of the admissibility hearing of the r espondent  to the ID 13 years after the 
section  44(2) referral to a hearing had been signed. I also find that the ability of the respondent to 
make full answer to the allegations against him has been prejudiced to such an extent that a stay 
of proceedings i s the only suitable remedy. The appeal is therefore dismissed.

Jurisdiction  
 
[14]  The appellant submits that the ID does not have jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceedings, 
relying on the decision of the Federal Court in Torre .4  In Torre,  Justice XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX was 
asked to review a decision in which the ID found  that it lacked the jurisdiction to grant a stay of 
proceedings to a permanent resident who was ultimately convoked to an admissibility hearing in 
2013 based on criminal conviction s in Canada in 1996. The Court found that the ID did not err in 
refusing to hear a motion for a stay of proceedings because it lacked jurisdiction, and additionally 
opined that “it is unlikely” that the ID has the jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceeding s.  
 
[15]  XXXXX  was upheld by the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) and leave to appeal the FCA 
decision to the Supreme Court of Canada was denied. Torre  has become a leading case on the 
issues that are under consideration in this appeal  and  has been relied upon by  the Federal Court 
to uphold several subsequent decisions where the ID has held that it lacks jurisdiction to consider 
whether the Minister has committed an abuse of process in unreasonably  and unjustifiably 
delaying referral to an admissibility hearing.  
 
[16]  While I respect the Court’s finding in XXXXX , I do not find that Justice XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  
opinion on whether the ID has the jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceedings for unreasonable 
and inordinate delay was dispositive of that case. Indeed, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed 
the appeal on the basis that the jurisdictional question was no t dispositive of the appeal and 
should never have been certified .5 The jurisdictional question was somewhat secondary in the 
Court’s analysis since the Court went ahead and assessed whether to grant a stay of proceedings 
for abuse of process itself. I find  that the question of whether the ID has the jurisdiction to grant 
a stay of proceedings for abuse of process is contextual. It may indeed be unlikely that the ID 
will have the jurisdiction to grant this extraordinary remedy except in the rarest and graves t of

 The analysis of administrative delay in a particular case is factual and contextual. As 
Just XXXXXXXXXXXXXX explained at par . 122 of Blencoe :9  
[T]he determination of whether a delay has become inordinate dep ends on the 
nature of the case and its complexity, the facts and issues, the purpose and nature 
of the proceedings, whether the respondent contributed to the delay or waived the 
delay, and ot her circumstances of the case. As previously mentioned, the 
deter mination of whether a delay is inordinate is not based on the length of the 
delay alone, but on contextual factors, including the nature of the various rights at 
stake in the proceedings, in the attempt to determine whether the community’s 
sense of fairnes s would be offended by the delay.  
 
[20]  Neither the IAD nor the Federal Court is so well -positioned to assess whether the 13 -year 
delay in initiating an  admissibility hearing once a section  44(2) referral to a hearing had been 
signed is unreasonable and inordin ate than the ID itself as the decision -making body to which all 
such referrals must be made. The ID is also ideally positioned to make a preliminary assessment 
of whether in light of the allegations made and the complexity of the matter, the delay had 
prej udiced the ability of the respondent to meet the case against him. In other words, the legal 
test set out in Blencoe  for assessing whether a delay is inordinate is squarely within the ID’s 
expertise and experience.  
 
[21]  In this case, the ID found that the respondent had been prejudiced to such a degree that 
the proceedings would be unfair and that a stay of proceedings was the only appropriate remedy. 
With respect to the Court, I find that it undermines the principle that the tribunal is master of its 
own h ouse to strip it of its ability to apply an appropriate remedy where the Minister is 
responsible for an unreasonable and inordinate delay that had so prejudiced the person concerned 
that it was unfair to proceed.  
 
[22]  In Torre , Justice XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX acknowled ges that the ID has the jurisdiction to 
dispose of questions of law, including the jurisdiction to examine and apply the Charter. 
However, she opines that it is unlikely that the ID can grant a stay of proceedings in light of the 
statutor y framework which requires the Immigration and Refugee B oard to hold an admissibility

[25]  In my view, XXXXXXX  leaves little doubt that a tribunal such as the ID has the jurisdiction 
to grant a remedy wher e the fairness of a hearing is impacted by inordinate delay:11  
There is no doubt that the principles of natural justice and the duty of fairness are part of 
every administrative proceeding.   Where delay impairs a party’s ability to answer the 
complaint against him or her, because, for example, memories have faded, ess ential 
witnesses have died or are unavailable, or evidence has been lost, then administrative 
delay may be invoked to impugn the validity of the administrative proceedings and 
provide a remedy (XXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXX, Judicial Review of Administrat ive 
Action in Canada  (loose -leaf), at p. 9 -67; XXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXX, Administrative Law  
(7th ed. 1994), at pp. 435 -36).   It is thus accepted that the principles of natural justice and 
the duty of fairness include the right to a fair hearing and that undu e delay in the 
processing of an administrative proceeding that impairs the fairness of the hearing can be 
remedied (see, for example, XXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXX, Administrative 
Law:   Cases, Text, and Materials  (4th ed. 1995), at p. 256; Wa de and Forsyth, supra , at 
pp. 435 -36;  XXXXXXX , supra , at p. 756; Canadian Airlines , supra ; Ford Motor Co. of 
Canada v. Ontario (Human Rights Commission)  (1995), 24 C.H.R.R. D/464 (Ont. Div. 
Ct.); XXXXXXXX v. College of Physicians & Surgeons (New Brunswick)  (1996), 1996 
CanLII 4828 (NB QB) , 41 Admin. L.R. (2d) 196 (N.B.Q.B.) ). 
 
[26]  Given the foregoing, I find that the ID had jurisdiction to grant the remedy sought. In t he 
face of a 13 year delay in referring the admissibility report to the ID, the ID was compelled to 
hear the  respondent ’s motion that the proceedings should be stayed due to inordinate delay.

 REMEDY  
 
[27]  I find that the ID has set out the relevant considerations and correctly applied the law in 
determining that the Minister committed an abuse of process in failing to refer the respondent’s 
admissibility report to the ID for 13 years. I also agree with the ID that in the circumstances of 
the case, the respondent is prejudiced in his ability to rebut the Minister’s allegation to such an 
extent that the only appropriate remedy is a stay of proceedings.  
 
[28]  As set out in XXXXXXX , undue delay in the processing of an administrative proceeding that 
impairs the fairness of the hearing can be remedied. Even so, it is only in the clearest of cases 
where the proceedings would “unfair to the point that they are contrary to the interests of justice” 
that an undue delay can  be found to be an abuse of process.  
 
[29]  I find that even in comparison to other cases where abuse of process was argued for 
delays in referring individuals to immigration enforcement proceedings including XXXXXXX ,12 a 
case which in which the Federal Court gr anted a stay of proceedings for abuse of process in 
circumstances very similar to those in this appeal, a 13 -year delay in referring an admissibilit y 
hearing to the ID after the section  44(2) referral has been signed is a uniquely inordinate, 
egregious and  inexcusable delay.  
 
[30]  The Minister’s reliance on its previous policy on holding referrals in abeyance where a 
Ministerial relief application has been made and appears to have some merit, and a subsequent 
change in its own policies in 2013 , does not adequat ely explain or excuse the delay in question. 
The Minister was not barred from bringing the matter forward, and no decision has been made 
on the ministerial relief application after 15 years.  
 
[31]  As far as the impact of the delay on the fairness of the procee dings, I find that it is 
reasonable that the respondent ’s memory has faded and that his ability to call witnesses that

call into question the respondent’s swor n statement on this issue .13 I find that assessing whether 
the respondent was a member of a terrorist organization for his involvement with the MISS from 
1979 to 1992 is a complex fact -driven assessment, and that his ability to call evidence that could 
rebut the Minister’s case has b een prejudiced by the inordinate delay in referring the 
inadmissibility report to the ID to such an extent that it would be unfair to proceed.  
 
[32]  The  respondent has had the possibility of removal to Ir an hanging over his head for 
26 years despite being found to be a protected person . I do not doubt that he has suffered a 
substantial amount of emotional stress  as a result of this uncertainty but  I do not find that the 
appellant  has adduced sufficient evidence to establish that the delay has had such a pro found 
negative psychological impact that a stay of proceedings would be appropriate on that ground.  
 
[33]  However, I find that the delay in referring the admissibility report to the ID for 13 years 
has had a profound negative impact on the  respondent , the dela y is unexplained, unfair and 
inordinate, and the respondent’s ability to rebut the allegations against him have been 
significantly compromised. I find that it would be contrary to the interests of justice for an 
admissibility hearing to proceed. In the cir cumstances, I find that the only appropriate re medy is 
a stay of proceedings.  
 
CONCLUSION  
 
[34]  I find that the ID has jurisdiction to consider whether a party before it commits an abuse 
of process and to apply an appropriate remedy. I find that the ID was cor rect in finding that the 
delay in referring the respondent to an admissibility hearing was inordinate and amounted to an 
abuse of process. I find that it was within the ID’s jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceedings to 
remedy the Minister’s abuse of proc ess, and that it was an appropriate remedy in this case.

Failure to Claim Elsewhere  
[11]  The claimant said he left Colombia because the FARC extorted money from him and 
threatened if he did not take over his uncle’s payment he would have to leave the country or they 
would kill him . He bought a plane ticket and left his country on XXXX XXXX XXXX  2011. He 
remained in the US until XXXX XXXX XXXX  2011 when he illegally crossed over the Canadian -
US border in Montreal and filed for refugee status the same day. The claimant testified that  he did 
not file for asylum in the US. Asked why he did not file for asylum, he said because XXXX , who 
had enquired about asylum in the US, told him that if he applied for asylum he would not be 
successful. Asked if he had sought a second opinion, he repli ed “no”. Asked why not, he replied 
because he believed XXXX  because he is family.  
[12]  The panel finds his explanation unsatisfactory and rejects it. He stated that he was 
threatened with death by a dangerous criminal guerrilla group, he fled his country to the  US; thus he 
has a responsibility to claim asylum in that country. F ailure to claim refugee protection from a 
country within which the claimant resided or even sojourned or travelled before coming to Canada, 
when that country is a signatory to the Conventi on Relating to the Status of Refugees, can be seen to 
negate the claimant’s fear.  
[13]  Counsel in her submissions4 said that it was reasonable for the claimant to rely on XXXX ’ 
advice given their family connection. The panel respectfully disagrees; there is no evidence before 
this panel that XXXX  had any legal training. While the claimant testified that XXXX  told him that 
he contacted an organization that advised him on the asylum process in the US, the name of this 
organization just happens to remain nameless. The claimant testified that he didn’t remember the 
name of the organization. Even counsel refers to it as “an organization” in written submissions.5 
[14]  The claimant had opportunity to seek asylum in the US, or at least to seek information from 
official govern ment sources regarding the process, but he did not do so. The panel finds that the 
claimant did not offer a reasonable explanation for why he did not apply for refugee protection in 
the US. It is reasonable to assume a person with a well -founded fear of pe rsecution will attempt to

PRINCIPLES AND JURISPRUDENCE APPLIED  
[49]  In the case at hand, the panel has applied the following principles and jurisprudence.  
[50]  The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by the jurisprudence from  the 
Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The courts have established a number of 
principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.  
[51]  There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state i s in complete breakdown, 
the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its 
citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee 
claimant has no other r ecourse available. Having canvassed the country conditions documents,38 I 
find that Colombia is a democracy in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning 
security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country.  
[52]  To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide “clear and 
convincing” confirmation of the state’s inability to protect its citizens.39 A claimant who alleges that 
state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes  that the state 
protection is in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be 
reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state 
protection is inadequate.40 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police 
and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the

[2] The parties relied on the test imony of the Respondent at the ID hearing.  XXXXXXXXXXXXX, the 
Director of Active Security provided oral testimony at the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD)

[3] The Respondent is a 49-year -old  citizen of India. The following is the undisputed timeline  
of events. All of these events occurred in 2019:

2320610 Ontario Inc. operating as Active Security Enterprises (“Active Security”)

Canada for the period August 14 to 28, for the purpose of visiting his daughter.

[4] The Minister’s position is that when th e Respondent applied for a visitor visa and when he

under section 40 o f the Act.
