not intend to work. He was unaware that the  LMIA had been approved. He did not bring with him

with Active Security and acceptance of a position from immigration authorities  does not amount to

[6] There is little dispute regarding the facts in this case. The issue is this appeal is whether the 
Respondent is inadmissible for misrepresentation. To determine this issue, the following questions 
need to be answered:

DECISION  
[7] The Minister’s appeal is allowed.   I find the Respondent’s failure to disclose the 
acceptance of a job offer in Canada amounts to misrepresentation. He is therefore inadmissible to

THE LAW  
[8] Section 40(1)(a) of the Act states:  
40 (1) A permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible for misrepresentation  
(a) for dire ctly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts 
relating to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the 
administration of this Act;  
ANALYSIS  
The Respondent withheld a fact   
[9] In this appeal, there is no question that the Respondent did not tell immigration authorities, 
either in his TRV application or upon his entry to Canada , that he was in the process of pursuing 
employment in Canada. The issue then becomes whether that fact was material to a relevant matter 
and whether that matter could have induced an error in the administration of the Act.  
The withheld fact was material to a relevant matter  
[10]  The Respondent’s counsel argues that when the Respondent entered Canada , he had no 
intention of engaging in employment. In suppor t of this, counsel points to the fact that the 
Respondent did not have the necessary documents with him to apply for a work permit and that he 
did not know that the LMIA had been approved. When he learned that the LMIA had been 
approved, he asked his assis tant to courier the results of his English proficiency test and medical 
results to him in Canada.

XXXX , citizens of Venezuela, appeal a decision of the Refugee Pr otection Division (RPD)

Central Allegations of Claim  
[2] The Appellants alleged before the RPD that they have been threatened by co -workers of 
the principal Appellant because of their political opinion and consequently the Appellants fear for

Procedural Events  
[3] The Appellants’ claims  for refugee protection was heard on August 9, 2016.  In a written 
decision of August 24, 2016 , the RPD rej ected the Appellants’ claim s finding that the Appellants’

granted the Appellants an Extension of Time to tender an amended Appellant s’ Record.

Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the RPD to find that the Appellants are Convention

Subsection 110(4) of the I RPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may 
present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably 
available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to h ave 
presented, at the time of the rejection.

 [9] The RAD’s analysis of the admissibility of the proposed new evidence must begin first 
with the test set out in s. 110(4). In assessing whether the proposed new evidence meets the 
statutory provisions of s. 110(4), the RAD considered the following:  
a) First, did the evidence arise after the rejection of the Appellant’s refugee claim? Here , 
the RAD may consider whether the evidence is capable of proving the current state of 
affairs in the country of feared persecution, or an event that occurred, or a 
circumstance that arose after the rejection of the refugee claim.  
i) The RAD will consider not  only the date on which the document came into 
existence but the timing of the event or circumstance which the document 
seeks to prove.6 For example, an affidavit or newspaper article may have 
been created after the rejection of the Appellant’s refugee cla im, but the 
information in the document may be several years old, and the RAD may 
therefore find that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim, 
despite the date of the document.  
 
ii) It is important to note here that s. 110(4) does not cont emplate whether the 
evidence arose after the RPD’s hearing, but rather after the rejection of the 
Appellant’s claim. Where a document arose after the hearing but before the 
rejection of the refugee claim, it is necessary for the RAD to consider 
whether the  Appellant could have presented the document to the RPD by way 
of a post -hearing submission.  
 
iii) If the evidence is capable of proving an event that occurred or circumstances 
that arose after the RPD hearing, then the evidence must be considered, and 
the RAD will proceed to assess the probative value of the evidence.  
b) Second, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the 
Appellant’s refugee claim, it must consider the next factor in s. 110(4). If the evidence 
is capable of proving only an event that occurred or circumstances that arose prior to the 
rejection, has the Appellant established that the evidence was not reasonably available

 ROLE OF THE RAD  
[18]  The RAD finds that the Federal Court of Appeal’s decision, in Huruglica ,7 provides the 
RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized 
tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first -level administrative tribunal.  
[19]  The RAD concludes from its s tatutory analysis that, with respect to findings of fact (and 
mixed fact and law), the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. 
Thus, after carefully considering the RPD’s decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the 
recor d to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred.  
[20]  The standard of intervention to be applied by the RAD in considering decisions has been 
further clarified with the decision of a three member panel . 8  The RAD notes that the decision of  
a three -member panel is binding on a single -member panel such as in the present case.9   
[21]  In accordance with that three -member panel the following standard of review will be 
applied:  
a. The RAD will normally apply a standard of correctness to all findings of the RPD.  
b. Where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making a particular finding, the 
RAD may assess that finding using a standard of reasonableness, modified to apply to 
the RAD context.  
c. Where the RAD finds that deference is warranted, it is obligated to explain how the 
RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage with respect to the finding in question.  
d. Where the RAD shows deference to a finding, it will nevertheless consider both the 
process and the outcome. The finding must be the result of a comprehensible 
reasoning process - the RAD must be able to read the RPD’s decision and understand 
how the RPD’s conclusion was reached. In considering the outcome, the RAD must 
assess whether the finding is based on the evidence in the record; in order to do so, the

Appellants ’ Issues on Re -Opening  
[22]  On the re -opening of this appeal, t he Appellants  raise two issues in their Memorandum of 
Argument : 
1) The Appellant s submit that the RPD ’s finding with regard to the credibility of the 
principal Appellant was both unreasonable on the fact before it and unfair in light of 
previous counsel’s incompetence; and,  
2) The Appellants have met their burden of demonstrating that they are Convention 
Refugee s and should be granted protection in Canada.   
Natural Justice and Procedural Fairness  
[23]  The Appellants have submitted that they were inadequately represented at their RPD 
hearing.  The RAD fin ds that the Appellants have established that they were not adequately 
prepared for their hearing by their counsel, that their counsel did not review and assist them in the 
preparation of their claim documents including the preparation of their narrative, and that their 
counsel failed to tender documents available to him which may have supported the Appellants’ 
claim s.  The RAD finds that these deficiencies on the part of counsel resulted in denial of  the 
Appellants’  right to a fair hearing.  The RAD finds that the failures of counsel impaired the 
Appellants’ right to be heard.  
[24]    The RAD notes that the Appellants rely on both their new evidence and submissions as 
well as the evidence that was before the RPD.  While it is difficult to determine to what extent the 
RPD’s findings were influence d by the deficiencies in their representation before the RPD , the 
RAD finds that there is ample evidence to establish that the representation  at the Appellant’s RPD 
hearing was flawed to the extent that, on a balance of probabilities, it impeded the Appellants ’

 right to be heard.  Accordingly , the RAD finds that there was a denial of natural justice and a 
breach of procedural fairness which renders the RPD’s determination unstainable.   
CONCLUSION  
[25]  The RAD finds that, after its own review and assessment of the evidence, the RPD’s 
determination cannot be sustained. The RAD finds that, while there was reason to question the 
credibility of the Appellant s, the RPD’s findings were influenced by the failures of counsel.   
Disposition and Remedy  
[26]  Subsection 111(1) of the IRPA allows the RAD to: 
(a)  confirm the determination of the Refugee Protection Division;  
(b)  set aside a decision of the RPD and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, 
should have been made;  
(c)  refer the matter back to the RPD, giving the directions to the RPD.

 [27]  The RAD can make the referral described in 111(1)(c) only if it was of the opinion that the 
decision of the RPD was wrong in law, in fact, or in mixed law and fact, and the RAD cannot 
make a decision to confirm or substitute the RPD’s decision without h earing evidence that was 
presented to the RPD.10  
[28]  Once the RPD’s unreasonable credibility conclusions are removed, there is insufficient 
evidence left on the record for the RAD to confirm the determination of the RPD without re -
hearing the evidence presente d to the RPD in conjunction with the new evidence tendered by the 
Appellants. The RAD finds that there are a number of credibility concerns which still must be 
addressed, and the RAD is not able to substitute its own determination. The RAD finds that it 
would have to re -hear evidence that the RPD already heard. For these reasons, the RAD cannot 
substitute its own determination for that of the RPD, and it cannot find the Appellant s to be 
Convention refugee s or person s in need of protection.  
[29]  This appeal is al lowed. Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Act , the Refugee Appeal Division refers the matter to the Refugee Protection Division 
for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.

 Reasons for Decision 
[1] These are the reasons in the appeal filed before the Immigration Appeal Division by XXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the appellant) in respect of the deni al of the sponsored permanent resident application of her brother MouXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the applicant). The appeal is filed pursuant to subsection 63(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
1 (the Act). [2] The sponsored application was denied by a visa  officer in a letter dated 12 June 2008 at Abidjan further to the officer finding that the applicant was not eligible to Canada as a member of the family class as he was not an orphan within the meaning of paragraph 117(1) (f) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations
2 (the Regulations). Issue [3] The appellant asserts that her parents, being those of the applicant as well, are still living, except they are of an age that they are infirm and incapable of taki ng care of the applicant in Senegal.  [4] The question before the panel is whether or not in  light of the declaration by the appellant that her parent’s are not deceased, there is discretion under the Act or Regulations to regard the applicant as a member of the family class and thereby eligible for admissibility as a sponsored person. Decision [5] The panel finds that there is no discretion available to it in this case in terms of humanitarian and compassionate relief that can overcome the fact that the applicant is not an orphan. The appeal is therefore dismissed for the following reasons.

 Background [6] The appellant is a permanent resident of Ca nada who obtained landing on June 10, 2005. She was born in Senegal on January 26, 1974 and presently resides in Montreal, Quebec. She is married to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX who also is a permanent resident of Canada in addition to being a citizen of France. [7] Both are employed full time in the Montreal area. [8] The applicant was born in Senegal on October 2 5, 1994 and at the time of the appeal hearing he is 14 years of age. He is a full time student. Th ere is one other sibling identified in the appeal record, a sister, however, she is not part of this sponsorship application. [9] The appellant completed her application for th e sponsorship of her brother on April 17, 2008. The visa officer subsequently examined the a pplication and supporting documents and concluded, without any interview of the applicant, that he was not a member of the family class. Therefore, he was found not to be eligible for admissibility as a permanent resident.  Analysis [10] Paragraph 117(1)(f) of the Regulations provides, in part, that a foreign national is a member of the family class and thereby eligible for sponsorship  if they are: “ ... a person whose parents are deceased, who is under 18 years of age, who is not a spouse or common-law partner and who is (i) a child of the sponsor’s mother or father ...”.  [11] In her appeal submission the appellant concedes that her parents are not deceased. Yet, she infers that there are extenuating circumstances as she states:  [12] « Je suis à la charge de ma famille car mon Père Ousseynou KE BE a 82 ans retraite né le 2 décembre 1927 à Saint Louis du Sénégal. Ma  mère XXXXXXXXXXXXXX est ménagère née en 1950 et elle n’a pas les moyens de s’occuper de mon frère et de ma sœur. Car sur la lettre que vous m’avez demandé si mon frère est orpheli n. Non mais vu l’âge de mon père et de l’inactivité de ma mère j’ai la charge totale de  ma famille et ça sera plus simple pour moi si j’amène mon frère ici pour prendre soin de son éducation scolaire ... »

 [13] There is no discretion under the Act which permits the panel on an appeal such as this to pre- empt the application of section 117 of Regulations in terms of who is eligible for sponsorship as a member of the family class. Parliament has made this clear in enacting section 65 of the Act which prevents a panel from using a discretion that it mi ght otherwise have in other cases on account of humanitarian and compassionate considerations. That  is, section 65 states that such discretion is not
 available unless the foreign national is a me mber of the family class, as defined. [14] In the present appeal the facts are not in disput e. The applicant is not an orphan. Even though the appellant appears to be his primary caregiver and support person this does not obviate the fact that his parents are not deceased. As long as this is th e case he is not an orphan and cannot be considered a member of the family class within the meaning of paragraph 117(1) (f) of the Regulations.  
NOTICE OF DECISION 
[15] The appeal is dismissed.    XXXXXXXXXXXXX  XXXXXXXXXXXXX

INTRODUCTION  
[1] Mr.  XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  (the appel lant), his wife Mrs. XXXXXXXXXXXXXX ,

and which ha d exposed him to certain risks, this is not sufficient to find the I FA  unreasonable. The 
evidence shows that he will not be deprived of his general ability to earn a living. 46  
[72]  The Federal court of appeal has set a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. 
According to the Court:  
It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the 
life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily  relocating to a safe area. 
… This is in sharp contrast with undue hardship resulting from loss of employment, 
loss of status, reduction in quality of life, loss of aspirations, loss of beloved ones 
and frustration of one ’s wishes and expectations.47 
[73]  The ap pellants have not established that it would be unreasonable for them to move to 
Lahore and for the appellant  to maintain a livelihood by being a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX , 
instead of XXXX XXXX .  
[74]  I therefore conclude that the appellant and his family have a viable I FA  in Lahore.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX  (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection 
Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has not submitted new evidence and 
has not requested an oral hearing. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to 
send the  matter back to the RPD for a redetermination by a different member.  
DETERMINATION  
[2] Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA ), the 
RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refug ee nor a 
person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.  
Background  
[3] The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he fears returning to India with his wife 
because his wife was a Muslim before she converted to Hinduism and because she is much 
younger than him. He further alleged that he fears returning to India with his son because his ex -
wife and her family members believe that his son will inherit his property instead of them.  
[4] The Appellant’s claim for refugee protection was heard on June 17, 2014, O ctober 7, 2014 
and March 24, 2015. By a decision of April 29, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD found 
that the risk the Appellant faces in returning to India does not reach the level of more than a mere 
possibility  of persecution . It concluded , on a balance of probabilities , that the Appellant failed to 
provide testimony and central documentation that gives him a nexus to a Convention ground or is 
consistent with an individual whom is at risk of persecution upon return to their home country.  
[5] The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in law by failing to consider him as a member 
of a particular social group, namely his family, and the persecution that he would suffer if he is 
returned to India, if that is indeed found to be his country of nation ality which was not properly 
determined.  
[6] The joined claims of the Appellant’s spouse and son, citizens of Uzbekistan, were heard 
on the same dates as the Appellant’s claim. By the decision of April 29, 2015, the RPD accepted

of protection.  
ANALYSIS  
Role of the RAD  
[7] What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD? 
Although the Appellant makes no arguments with respect to the  role of the RAD in his 
Memorandum of Argument, the RAD notes, i n Huruglica, the Court considered the appropriate 
relationship between the RAD and the RPD.1 It found that the RAD had erred in simply reviewing 
the RPD’s decision on a standard of reasonablen ess, rather than conducting its own independent 
assessment of the Appellants’ refugee claims. The Court held that the RAD’s application of a 
reasonableness standard curtailed the tribunal’s appellate role, contrary to the purpose of the RAD 
and the provisi ons of the IRPA . In the Court’s view, the RAD should not even engage in a 
standard of review analysis; rather, it should consider the purpose of the appellate tribunal, the 
statutory provisions, comparable expertise, and comparative appellate regimes.2  
[8] Justice XXXXXX stated the following in Huruglica : 
Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD’s decision on the 
standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the 
RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It  must review all aspects of the 
RPD’s decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is 
a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment 
departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decis ion.3  
In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the 
RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular 
advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate 
court is, t o intervening on facts only where there is an “overriding and palpable 
error.”4

The RPD’s Findings and Appellant’s Argument  
Risk in India  
[10]  The RPD found that the risk for the Appellant in returning to India does not reach the level 
of more than a mere possibility. It noted that, during his time in Uzbekistan, the XXXXXXXXX  
returned to India on an almost monthly basis to deal with issues for his business. It also noted that 
his travel to India continued even after threats from his ex -wife and his extended family and he 
even settled his family in India for approximately one y ear despite the threats. The RPD noted 
that the allegations of risk all relate to the XXXXXXXXX’s wife and child and concluded that the 
Appellant does not have a nexus to a Convention ground and is not at risk of persecution in India.  
[11]    The Appellant subm its that it is impossible to be satisfied that the RPD considered the 
evidence properly before it. He further submits that his fear of persecution is well -founded 
subjectively and objectively. The Appellant submits that India’s human rights record with res pect 
to mixed marriages is poor and this would indicate that he had a genuine need for protection. He 
argues that he and his wife and son are a close -knit unit and, even though the claims of his wife 
and son were accepted, if he were to be returned to Indi a they would return with him. He goes on 
to indicate that they would be perceived as a mixed Hindu and Muslim family and would be 
subject to persecution.  
[12]  The Appellant submits that the RPD erred by failing to consider the evidence that he may 
have been de prived of his Indian citizenship. He further submits that the RPD erred in law by 
failing to consider him as a member of a particular social group, namely his family, and the 
persecution that he would suffer if he is returned to India, if that is indeed fo und to be his country 
of nationality which was not properly determined.

 [13]  The RAD notes that there is no indication in the Appellant’s Basis of Claim Form (BoC) 
narrative that he faces a risk of persecution or harm in India if he were to return alone. He 
indicated at his hearing that he did not face a risk of persecution or harm in India if he were to 
return alone. When asked by the RPD if he believed he was at any risk in India if he returned 
without his family, the Appellant said that the only danger was t hat he would die without his kid.  
When asked what danger he would suffer in Mumbai, the appellant indicated that he would not 
face any danger if he went alone but his family would leave him. When asked if he would face 
any danger in Delhi, the Appellant sa id he would not if he was living alone but he was living for 
his son.  
[14]  The RPD was not wrong in indicating in the reasons for its decision that it was not obliged 
to consider the risk the Appellant may face in India if he were to return with his wife and s on. The 
Appellant’s wife and son were determined to be persons in need of protection and their claims for 
refugee protection were accepted by the RPD. Even though the Appellant indicates that he would 
not like to return to India without his wife and son, t he Federal Court has been clear in indicating 
that family unity is not a concept that exists in Canadian refugee law and the  family as a social 
group for making a claim is based on the evidence of persecution of the family as a social group 
and not on the principle of family unity. The following are excerpts and notes from various 
Federal Court decisions on the matter:  
[15]  Family unity is not a concept that exists in Canadian refugee law. It was clearly an error of 
law to rely on the concept of family unity and on paragraphs 181 to 185 of the UNHCR  Handbook 
to support the claims of the respondents under IRPA , ss. 96 and 97.5 
[16]  The RPD did not err in failing to analyse the issue of the separation of the family unit. 
Family unity is not a concept recognized by Canadian refugee law. The family as a “social group” 
basis for seeking Convention refugee status is based on the evidence  of persecution of the family 
as a social group and not on the principle of family unity.6

 [17]  The Court reiterated that the concept of family unity in refugee matters has been rejected. 
It also indicated that the documentary evidence on the general situation is not by itself sufficient 
to establish the well -foundedness of a claim; a real fear of persecution must be demonstrated.7 
[18]  In XXXXX , the Court had indicated that the concept of family unity did not appear in the

[19]  Persecution of one family memb er does not automatically entitle all other family members 
to Convention refugee status.9  
[20]  Considering the evidence in this case and the jurisprudence the RAD finds that the 
Appellant has not established that he has a nexus to one of the Convention grounds  or that he 
personally has a well -founded fear of persecution in India.   
Consideration of the evidence  
[21]  As noted above, the Appellant submits that it is impossible to be satisfied that the RPD 
considered the evidence properly before it. He argues that the  RPD’s reasons do not show that it 
considered the documentary evidence regarding the situation in India and its effect on persons in 
his particular social group as a result of his mixed marriage.   
[22]  The RPD is presumed to have considered all of the evidence  before it, and there is no 
requirement for the panel to refer to each document in the record.10 However, where there is 
evidence which is contrary to its decision, the RPD must analyze that evidence and provide 
reasons why it does not consider it relevant or trustworthy, or why it chose to disregard it.11 
[23]  In this case the Appellant testified that he would not face a risk of persecution or harm in 
India if he returned alone. It is not for the RPD or the RAD to impose on the Appellant a contrary 
view of the ri sk he believes he faces. The Appellant was born and raised in India. He resided in

DISPOSITION  
[28]  The Appellant has alleged that the RPD erred by failing to properly determine his country 
of citizenship, failed to consider him as a member of a particular social group and fa iled to 
consider the persecution that he would suffer if he returns to India. However, upon review of the 
evidence, the RAD has reached the same conclusion as the RPD. The RAD finds that the 
Appellant is a citizen of India and he does not have a well -found ed fear of persecution if he were 
to return to India. The RAD finds that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of 
persecution in India and also finds that his removal to India would not subject him personally to a 
risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial 
grounds to exist, of torture.  
CONCLUSION  
[29]  Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the 
Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person i n need of protection. This appeal is 
dismissed.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons and decision of the Immigration Appeal Division (  IAD ) in the 
appeal of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the appellant ) from the refusal to approve the sponsored 
application for a per manent resident visa of his adopted son, KXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the 
applicant ), from India.  
 
[2] The application was refused on a number of grounds. The  immigration officer  was of the 
opinion that  the adoption was not genuine and was ent ered into primarily for the purpose of 
acquiring permanent resident status in Canada , within the meaning of  section 4 of the 
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the Regul ations ).1 In addition, the officer also 
mad e the refus al under  paragraphs  117(3)( c) and ( d) of the  Regulations , finding that  the adoption 
was not in the best interests of the child as it did not create a genuine parent -child relationship 
and was not in accordance with the laws of India. The details of the refusal are set out in a letter 
and the Computer Assiste d Immigration Processing System ( CAIPS ) notes.2 
 
BACKGROUND  
 
[3] The appellant is 64  years old. He is married and had three biological children, that is, one 
son and two daughter s. The appellant, his wife, son and younger daughter immigrated to Canada 
on September 8, 1999, having been sponsored by their elder daughter.3 The appellant’s son died 
September 20, 2003.4  
 
[4] The applicant is the appellant’s nephew’s son and was born April  13, 1994.5 The date of 
the adoption as set out in the adoption deed was March 21, 2004.6

 [5] Section 4 of the  Regulations  was amended on September 30, 2010.7 The wording of the 
test for adoptions in subsection 4(2) of the Regulations  is quite similar  to the previous version;  
however, the amendments affect  whether one or two prongs of the test  must be applied in order 
to disqualify an adopted child . There is also  an additional provision to the effect that 
subsection  4(2) of the  Regulations  does not apply to adoptions referred to in paragraph  117(1)( g) 
and subsections 117(2) and (4) of the Regulations . Both c ounsel agreed at the outset that the 
amended Regulations  apply to this appeal. The amendments to the  Regulations  do not change the

ANALYSIS  
Subsection 4(2) of the  Regulations  
 
[5] I will deal first with the refusal under  subsection 4(2) of the  Regulations . Two tests can 
be applied in order to exclude  an adopted child under subsection 4(2) of the Regulations .  Only 
one test needs to be satisfied for an adopted child to be excluded . The tests are: that the adoption 
did not create a genuine parent -child relationship and that the adoption was entered into 
primarily for the purpose of acquir ing any status or privilege under the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Act  (the Act ).8 The onus of proof is on the appellant to show, on a balance of 
probabilities, that the applicant is not excluded  as an adopted child under subsection  4(2) of the 
Regulations . 
 
[6] The term “genuine” has not been defined in the Act  or the  Regulations . The fundamental 
nature of an adoption is a relationship between parent and child. Parliament also specifically 
included the factor of a genuine parent -child r elationship as one element in the determination of 
the best interests of the child within the meaning  of subsection 117(3) of the Regulations .  
 
[7] In the case  of an adoption , the status or privilege that can be acquired under the Act is 
that the adopted child is granted permanent resident status in Canada through membership in the 
family class , if the adopted child meets the conditions required  to be sponsored to Canada.9

 Genuine parent -child relationship  
 
[8] First I will deal with the issue of whether or not the adoption created a genuine parent -
child relationship. I am of the opinion  that the existence of a genuine parent -child relationship is 
a question of fact and it rests on a ll of the factors relating to  the past, current and future state of 
the relationship.10 In d etermining the issue of a genuine parent -child relationship, I have considered 
the following factors:  
 
 the motivation for the adoption;  
 
 the extent to w hich the adoptive parents have maintained care and control over the child 
since the adoption;  
 
 the nature and extent of contact between the adoptive parents and the child;  
 
 the extent of knowledge of each other; and  
 
 the plans and arrangements for the ap plicant’s future.  
 
These factors are not exhaustive and the weight assigned to each factor will vary depending on the 
circumstances of each case.  
 
 
 
[9] The appellant and the applicant testified at the hearing and additional documentary 
evidence was submitted.11 I find the evidence to be generally credible and trustworthy and , given 
the circumstances of this case, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence is  indicative 
of a genuine parent -child relationship.  
 
Motivation  for the adoption

were completely shattered  and felt alone , given that  their daughters were married , and so they 
decided to adopt. They ch ose the appellant’s nephew’s son because they had previously lived

CONCLUSION  
 
[17]  Given the timing of and motivatio n for the adoption, the extent of care and control over 
the child since the adoption, the contact between the adoptive parent and the child, the extent of 
knowledge of each other and evidence of future plans for the applicant , I find, on a b alance of 
proba bilities, the evidence demonstrates a genuine parent -child relationship.   
 
Purpose of Acquiring a Status or Privilege under the Act  
 
[18]  The question of whether or not the adoption was entered into primarily for the purpose of 
acquiring any status or privilege  under the Act  is also determined from the evidence on the issues 
already discussed. It is not necessary for me to reiterate the evidence as clear inferences and 
findings can be made from the evidence already set out that the adoption was not arranged 
prim arily for the applicant to acquire permanent resident status in Canada. Moreover, there was 
credible evidence to rebut the immigration officer’s initial assessment, the Minister’s counsel’s 
concerns and to show the adoption was not entered primarily for th e purpose of the applicant 
acquiring permanent resident status in Canada.  
 
[19]  The appellant has demonstrated that he has developed a parental bond with the applicant 
and was able to demonstrate knowledge of his circumstances and has made arrangements for the  
applicant’s future. In addition, based on the evidence before me, there was satisfactory 
explanation as to why the applicant’s biological parents would give up their child for adoption to 
the appellant given their previous living arrangements and relation ship and the death of their

Other Grounds of Refusal  
 
[20]  Subsection 117(3) of the Regulations  sets out condit ions under which an adoption will be 
considered in the best interests of a child. This application was specifically refused on the basis 
of paragraphs 117(3)(c) and (d) of the Regulations . 
 
[21]  Paragraph 117(3)(c) of the Regulations  requires that the adoption created a genuine 
parent -child relationship. Based on the reasons provided above in relation to subsection 4(2) of 
the Regulations , I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the adoption has created a genuine 
parent -child relationship.  
 
[22]  Paragraph 117(3)( d) of the Regulations  requires that the adoption be in accordance with 
the laws of the place where the adoption took place. Specifically, the immigration officer’s 
concern was in relation to the intent to transfer as required under subsection 11(vi) of the  Hindu 
Adoptions and Maintenance Act , 1956 ( HAMA ).19 A finding of intent to transfer does not 
preclude some ongoing contact with the biological family of the adopted child. Based on the 
credible testimony and documentary evidence submitted and the rea sons set out above in relation 
to subsection 4(2) of the  Regulations , regarding the timing and reasons for the adoption, the 
physical location of the child over the years after the adoption and the ongoing contact, 
maintenance and support provided by the a ppellant for the applicant, on a balance of 
probabilities, I find the applicant was given in adoption with the intent to transfer him from the 
family of his birth to the family of his adoption.

 DECISION  
 
[23]  Based on the evidence before me, I conclude that th e appellant has met the burden of 
proof.   
 
[24]  I find, on a balance of probabilities, the adoption did create a genuine parent -child 
relationship and was not entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or 
privilege under the  Act . The applic ant is an adopted child and not caught by subsection 4(2) of 
the Regulations .  
 
[25]  Moreover , on a balance of probabilities , I find the adoption was in accordance with the 
laws of India, specifically subsections 5(1), 5(2) and 11(vi) of the HAMA  and the adopti on can 
be considered to be in the best interests of the child as it took place under ci rcumstances 
consistent with par agraphs 117(3)(c) and (d) of the Regulations .  
 
[26]  Therefore, the appeal is allowed.   
 
NOTICE OF DECISION  
 
 The appeal is allowed. The offic er’s decision to refuse a permanent resident visa is set 
aside, and an officer must continue to process the application in accordance with the reasons of 
the Immigration Appeal Division .

 [1] These are the reasons and decision of the Im migration Appeal Division (the “IAD”) in the appeal by XXXXXXXXXXX (the “appellant”) , from a determination made against her on September 3, 2010.  The appellant was found to ha ve failed to comply with the residency obligation requirements under section 28 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

The appellant agreed that she had been in Canada 140 days in the relevant five-year period, being August 18, 2005 to August 17, 2010.  Therefore, based on the evidence before me, the determination is valid in law.  [3] The IAD has discretionary jurisdiction to perm it an appellant to retain their permanent resident status despite a breach of the residency ob ligation.  The test to be applied in the exercise of the IAD’s discretionary jurisdiction is that the IAD must be satisfied at the time that the appeal is disposed of, which would be today, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, whether there are sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations that warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case.  [4] The appellant testified at the hearing and a dditional documentary evidence was submitted and the appellant’s husband attended the heari ng for support. [19]  The Federal Court of Appeal , in Huruglica , stated the following regarding the role of the

[103]       I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and

[21]  It is generally accepted that a psychological report presente d by a refugee claimant does 
not serve to prove the alleged persecution suffered by that individual. Such a report may establish 
that the Appellant suffers from a condition or exhibits symptoms that are consistent with the 
alleged trauma. Moreover, a psych iatric  report might assist the RPD in conducting the hearing in 
an appropriately sensitive manner or to consider whether apparent credibility problems are 
explained by a psychological condition. In this case the evidence now includes a report by a 
psychiat rist outlining the Appellant ’s mental health issues that need to be taken into consideration 
by the RPD.  
[22]  The RAD also acknowledges that the Federal Court has commented on this issue and 
stated:  
Just because a patient is suffering from psychological proble ms and manifests symptoms 
associated with those problems does not mean that the patient’s account of past 
persecution as the cause of those problems can be believed.10 
[23]  It is the RPD’s responsibility to determine whether the Appellant is credible, and the RP D 
is not required to defer to a psychologist’s report when making findings of fact with  respect to 
alleged past persecution. However, the RPD has to provide clear reasons why it rejects the report 
and , in particular , how it eroded the Appellant ’s credibili ty further.  
[24]  Based on the foregoing, the RAD finds that the RPD breached procedural fairness in this 
case.   
[25]  The RAD finds that it does not have sufficient credible evidence on which to make a 
finding whether the RPD’s findings are supportable, and whether  the Appellant is a Convention 
refugee or a person in need of protection. In this case, the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot 
provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the 
matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination .

SCOPE OF THE APPEAL  
[12]  In his memorandum, the appellant’s lawyer presents no  arguments as to the standard of 
intervention that  the RAD  should apply . 
[13]  I am of the opinion that the scope of the RAD appeal must be reviewed in light of the IRPA 
and the case law on the issue .  
[14]  First, the IRPA does not speci fically set out the standard of intervention that the RAD 
must apply  when reviewing RPD decisions. The introductory wording of subsection  110(1) of the 
IRPA states:  
Subject to subsections  (1.1) and (2), a person or the Minister may appeal, in accordance 
with the rules of the Board, on a question of law, of fact or of mixed law and fact, to the 
Refugee Appeal Division against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division to allow 
or reject the person’s claim for refugee protection . 
[15]  Furthermore, in terms of  RAD decisions, subsection  111(1) of the IRPA states that the 
RAD may confirm the determination of the RPD; set aside the determination and substitute a 
determination that, in its opinion, should have been made; or refer the matter to the RPD, giving 
the dir ections to the RPD that it considers appropriate. In Huruglica , the Federal Court of Appeal 
finds that the role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in fact and 
law .1 It also concludes that an appeal before the RAD is not, ho wever,  a true de novo 
proceeding.2 Moreover, i t clearly states  the approach that  the RAD  should use :

 [103]  I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and 
mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no i ssue of credibility 
of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. 
Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis 
of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the app ellant, the RPD erred. 
Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the 
RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of 
the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opi nion that it cannot provide such 
a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the 
matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of 
the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable.  
[16]  As for the degree of restraint or deference that  the RAD must show  toward  the RPD’s 
findings concerning the credibility or weight of testimony, the Federal Court of Appeal also notes 
the following in Huruglica : 
[70]  This also recognizes that there may be ca ses where the RPD enjoys a 
meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, 
because they require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral 
evidence it hears. It further indicates that although the  RAD should sometimes exercise 
a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the 
circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case -by-case basis. In 
each case, the RAD ought to determine whether th e RPD truly benefited from an 
advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final 
decision in respect of the refugee claim.  
[71]  One can imagine many possible scenarios. For example, when the RPD finds a 
witness straightforward  and credible, there is no issue of credibility per se . This will also 
be the case when the RAD is able to reach a conclusion on the claim, relying on the 
RPD’s findings of fact regarding the relative weight of testimonies and their credibility 
or lack the reof.  
[72]  Problems will occur when the credibility findings themselves are disputed on 
appeal, and the RAD has no way to reach a conclusion without endorsing or rejecting 
those findings. If the RAD can identify an error in situations where, for example, a  
claimant was not found credible because his story was not plausible based on common 
sense, the RPD may have no real advantage over the RAD.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
INTRODUCTION  
[1] These are the reasons in the  residency obligation a ppeal by Cesar XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  
(the appellant).  It was determined the appellant did not meet his residency obligation set out in 
section 28 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA ), which requires a permanent 
resident to be physically present in Canada for at least 730 days with respect to a 5 -year period.  
This 5 -year period in his case started on July 7, 2011 and  ended on July 7, 2016.  
[2] The appellant did not contest the legal validity of the decision and recognized he spent less 
than 730 days in Canada for the reference period. Therefore, I find the decision to be legally 
valid.  
[3] The appellant is requesting special relief from his residency obligation because of 
humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds.  The issue here is whether, taking into account 
the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, there are sufficient H&C 
considerations to warran t special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case.  
DECISION  
[4] The appeal is dismissed.  I find insufficient H&C consideration to grant special relief for 
the reasons that follow.  
BACKGROUND  
[5] The appellant was born in Mexico in 1980. When he was a  month old, his parents returned 
to Canada with the appellant and his older sister where they had permanent resident status. The 
appellant grew up as a child in Canada and left in 1986 and never returned to this country. The 
appellant continued to live in Mexico until 2003 when he decided to move to the United States. 
The appellant has been residing in that country since 2003 with no status. He is now married and 
has been living with his wife who is also a native of Mexico but living in the United States

[6] Given the uncertainty of his future in the United States , the  appellant applied for a new

ANALYSIS  
[7] In terms of H&C analysis, prior decision -makers of the Immigration Appeal Division  have 
considered  the following factors in the determination of whether there are sufficient H&C 
considerations to grant speci al relief in residency obligation appeals1: Extent of the non -
compliance with the residency obligation; Reasons for the departure and extended stay abroad; 
Degree of establishment in Canada, initially and at the time of hearing; Family ties in Canada; 
Whet her attempts to return to Canada were made at the first opportunity; Hardship and 
dislocation to the appellant and family members if he/she loses his/ her permanent resident status; 
and, Best interest of the children affected by this appeal.  
[8] These factors a re not exhaustive and can vary from case to case. The weight assigned to 
each factor varies according to the circumstances of the case. Here is my analysis of the most 
relevant  factors i n this  appeal.  
Extent of non -compliance  
[9] The appellant did not dispute  he spent zero days in Canada within his reference period 
which is the maximal breach. Accordingly, I find the appellant would require a very substantial 
amount of H&C consideration to be granted special relief.  
Reasons for the appell ant’s departure from Canada   
[10]  The appellant left Canada approximately at the age of 6 following his parents’ return to 
Mexico. Given the appellant had no choice at that stage but to leave the country, I find there are

[12]  The issue here is that the appellant had status in Canada but preferred to go to the United 
States.  The appel lant testified he did not know he had resident status in Canada. The appellant 
testified he knew about his landing paper s in Canada since he was approximately 17 or 18 and 
clearly had memories of residing in this country. However, the appellant did not fur ther put 
efforts in evaluating if he had the option to go to Canada instead of the United States. The 
appellant explained he did not have the financial resources to hire an attorney but I don’t accept

[14]  The appellant attended kindergarten as a child in Canada but did not return since 1986 . He 
never worked nor has any assets in Canada. I find the appellant has no establishment in Canada 
which is a negative factor in the appeal.

Hardship for the appellant  
[16]  The appellant explained he could be deported at any time to Mexico which would cause

[18]  I appreciate the appellant’s children changing their env ironment could face difficulties in

deportation of the appellant is still speculative to this point. I finally consider the appellant’s

OVERVIEW   
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX  is a citizen of Venezuela  who has  appeal ed a decision of the 
Refugee Protection Division (RPD)  rejecting his claim for refugee protection.  For the reasons 
that follow,  the appeal is granted.  
[2] Mr. XXXX  fears that he would be killed or seriously harmed by members of the 
Tupa mar os armed collective if he were to return to Venezuela. Mr. XXXX  was eighteen years 
old when he began being personally targeted by the Tupamaros. His two older siblings were 
assaulted and fired upon by members of the Tupa mar os because they were student acti vists in the 
Popular Will Party. The siblings successfully sought refugee protection in Canada . After  
Mr.  XXXX  siblings left Venezuela, members of the Tupamaros started  harassing him and his 
family culminating in an incident where the XXXXXXXXX located Mr.  XXXX  at his friend’s house 
where he had been staying. Mr. XXXX  managed to escape but the XXXXXXXXX killed his friend. 
Mr. XXXX  came to Canada shortly thereafter and claimed refugee protection.  
[3] The RPD found that Mr. XXXX  political opinion in opposition to  the government of 
Venezuela was credible and that the conditions in Venezuela for those who oppose the 
government and wish to express those opinions expose them to a serious possibility of 
persecution. Indeed, that was the case for Mr. XXXX  siblings. However, the RPD member found 
that the determinative issue in this case was whether Mr. XXXX  was entitled to Colombian 
citizenship. The RPD found that Mr. XXXX  did have a right to Colombian citizenship under 
Colombian law  because his mother is a national o f Colombia . It also found that there were no 
significant impediments preventing him from accessing Colombian citizenship and that he had 
failed to make reasonable efforts to obtain Colombian citizenship.  
[4] With the greatest of respect to the RPD member in th is case, I agree with the analysis of 
the member who decided the claims filed by Mr. XXXX  siblings. I find that his case does not 
significantly differ from theirs. In my view, the RPD member in this case erred in finding that 
the Appellant did not face sig nificant impediments to accessing Colombian citizenship. In the

[5] The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of 
correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.1 The exception 
to this rule is that the RAD may apply a deferential standard in some circumstances.2 I have 
conducted my own independent assessment of all of the evidence in this case, including the

correctness standard in this case.

Governing legal principles  
[6] As noted by the RPD member, the legal test in cases such as the present is the test set 
out in the XXXXXXXX  and XXXXXXXXXXX  decisions of the Federal Court of Appeal.3 In XXXXXXXX , the 
Court  found that a claim for refugee status will be denied if it was within the control of a 
claimant to acquire citizenship of a country with respect to which they have no well -founded fear 
of p ersecution.  The Court elaborated upon this test in Tretsetsang  where it found that a claimant 
who alleges the existence of an impediment to exercising his or her rights of citizenship in 
another country must establish the following on a balance of probabilities:  
a) The existence of a significant impediment that may reas onably be considered capable of 
preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection 
in that country of nationality; and

[7] As the Federal Court of Appeal noted in XXXXXXXXXXX , the issue of what will constitute 
reasonable efforts to overcome a significant impediment can only be determined  on a case -by-
case basis. As noted by the Court, a claimant will not be required to make any effort to overcome 
such impediment if the claimant establishes that it would not be reasonable to require him or her 
to make any such effort.5 
Significant impedime nts to exercising citizenship rights  
[8] It is not disputed that Mr.  XXXX  has the right to acquire Columbian citizenship under 
the Colombian Constitution because both of his biological parents are Colombian. It is also not 
disputed that, in order to formally a cquire Colombian citizenship, Mr.  XXXX  would have had to 
obtain a Colombian civil birth registration. Finally, it is also not disputed that, in order to acquire 
a Colombian civil birth registration, Mr.  XXXX  would have had to produce various identity 
docum ents  for one or both of his parents .   
[9] The dispute in this case cent res on t hree  issues. The first issue was whether Mr.  XXXX  
would have had to provide identity documents for both of his parents or whether it would have 
been sufficient to provide identity documents showing  that his mother is Colombian. This was an 
issue because , although Mr.  XXXX  father is also Colombian,  Mr.  XXXXX  is estranged from him  
as he has had no communication with him since he was three years old. The second issue in 
dispute in this case is whether the requirement s to obtain identification documents for his mother 
and/or father is a significant impediment to his obtaining Colombian Citizenship. The third issue 
is, if the requirement for identity documents does present a significant impediment for him, 
whether he has made reasonable efforts to overcome that impediment.  
[10]  In my view, the available evidence is e ntirely unclear as to whether a foreign -born 
national, such as Mr.  XXXX , who is the child of a Colombian mother and father, must provide 
the authorities with identity documents for simply one parent or both  parents. The most recent 
Response to Information Request  (RIR)  to address the issue is the 2018 RIR contained in the

separate pages. If one of the parents has a different nationality, they should pre sent a valid

[12]  As such , when reading the information from the  Colombian consulate together with the

[13]  In my view, this uncertainty itself posed a significant impediment to  Mr.  XXXX . The 
fact that the RPD arrived at two different interpretations of the requirements for obtaining 
Colombian citizenship in the cases of Mr.  XXXX  and his siblings provides ample evidence that 
the available information is far from clear. In order t o claim his right to Colombian citizenship, 
Mr.  XXXX  would have had to determine exactly what persons were required to provide in cases 
such as his. This itself was a significant impediment which caused his right to citizenship to 
depend on much more than mere formalities on his part.  
[14]  Even setting aside  this uncertainty , I find that on the facts of this case it would have 
been a significant impediment for Mr.  XXXX  to file Colombian identification documents for his 
mother alone . The obtention of these  documents were not within his control . Instead they were

[16]  With great respect, I find that the RPD erred in its analysis of whether Mr.  XXXX  had

described above. In this respect, I do not agree with the RPD member that the Appell ant’s

[19]  I agree with the RPD’s assessment that Mr.  XXXX  account of his political opinion and

ANALYSIS  
[10]  The respondents acknowledge that they requested and received  Turkish passports in

 [15]  The United Nation s High Commissioner for Refugees Handbook indicates that the 
cessation clause implies three require ments: voluntariness, intention and re availment.7 There is, 
of course, ov erlap among these requirements .  
Voluntariness  
[16]  The respondent s obtained their  passpo rts and returned to Turkey  voluntarily, by choice, 
and under no duress. It is the case that they planned to obtain passports and deliberately chose 
Turkey as the location for fertility treatment among other places in the world. There is no 
evidence that they were  constrained by or required, out of some legal necessity or otherwise, to 
acquire a passport or return to Turkey . They were  not deported, extradited or kidnapped. No 
person or government forced or pressured them to acquire  passport s and return. The couple  
freely  decided to obtain Turkish passports and travel there three times . I therefore find that this 
was voluntary.  
Intention  
[17]  I find that obtaining  Turkish passports and travelling to Turkey on them demonstrates an 
intention to rely on the diploma tic protection of that country as nationals. The respondents argue 
that they had no intention of revailing themselves of the protection of Turkey; they expected 
nothing whatsoever from the authorities given the failure in state protection in their past 
exp erience. In my view , the respondents asserted their citizenship merely by obtaining their 
passports. Travelling to Turkey as nationals  also implies an intention to have her interests 
defended and rights protected by the Turkish  state . The fact that they di splayed their permanent 
resident cards in addition to their passports at borders does not alter this finding. T he UNHCR 
Handbook  supports this conclusion :

the contrary, be presumed that he intends  to avail himself of the protection of 
the country of his nationality . On the other  hand, the acquisition of documents

OVERVIEW   
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX  (Principal  Appellant ) and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 
XXXX  (Associate Appellant s), citizen s of Nigeria , appeal ed the decision of the Refugee 
Protection Division (RPD), dated  October  21, 2019 , rejecting their claim s for refugee protection.  
[2] The Appellant s fear the Ogboni Fraternity and their s tate accomplices that killed the father 
of the Principal  Appellant  in the year  2000 and threatened to kill them 16 years later , as well as 
the state because of political positions that the Principal  Appellan t took on Twitter . 
[3] The RPD rejected their asylum claims , finding them not to be credible rega rding certain 
aspects of their claim, particularly in regard to the degree of influence of the Ogboni Fraternity, 
and because they provided insufficient credible e vidence regarding the political aspect of their 
claim.  
[4] Before the Refugee Appeals Division (RAD) , the Appellant s submit that the RPD erred in 
failing to conduct a full, fair and impartial hearing and properly examine the merits of the claim.  
[5] After examining all of the evidence, considering the Chairperson ’s Guidelines and applying 
a correctness standard, I find that the Appellant s had a full, fair and impartial hearing and that the 
RPD decision is correct. I reject the appeal and confirm the RPD dec ision. The reasons are as 
follows.  
ANALYSIS  
[6] The determinative issues are procedural fairness , whether a faulty standard of proof was 
applied , whether a faulty  legal  test was applied , and credibility.

i. The Appellant s’ submissions  
[7] The Appellant s submit that the RPD demonstrated bias by giving more weight to the 
National Documentation Package (NDP) over the Appellant s’ evidence which was not impugned 
by credibility despite the fact that the NDP states that there is very little concrete information or 
evidence available about the Ogboni Fraternity  or information that is not speculative.  They “cited” 
the RPD for bias at the hearing when it questioned the Appellant s about this documentary evidence . 
They argue that the evaluation must be made from a Nigerian perspective and that the entire 
hearing was conducted in an ill -founded manner without regard to the evidence before i t. 
ii. The NDP evidence in question   
[8] The evidence referred to by the Appellants consists of the Response to Information 
Request  NGA106269.E (the RIR) and the EASO COI Meeting Report found  respectively  at 
Tab s 13.3  and 1.3 of the NDP . The various sources consulted by the research directorate  in the 
RIR essentially state that the Ogboni Fraternity  functions in a few “remote kingdoms” of Nigeria,  
but no  longer has any  significant influence anywhere else  in the country.  
[9] As the RIR cites  numerous sources, it should be noted that they differ as to when the decline 
of the Ogboni Fraternity ’s influence started, and  they  use different language to describe the current 
situation  including : “Yoruba kings only have ceremonial positions ”; the Fraternity  is “waning” ; is 
“defunct” ; that its “membership, presence, and activities are insignificant ”; that it has “no  power 
or influence” ; or that it is “stigmatized as a ‘pagan remnant’ of the past ”. 
[10]  While these various sources referred to in the RIR use different language, they are generally 
consistent as to the absence of significant influence of the Fraternity  today  save for some remote 
locations . This is also consistent with  the EASO COI Meeting Report .

ANAL YSIS  
[9] To succeed on appeal the Appellant must establish that the marriage is genuine and  that it 
was not entered into primarily for the purpose of the Applicant gaining privilege under the Act ; 
i.e., that section 4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the “Regulations”) 
does not apply.  As confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in F.H. v. McDougall , the 
evidence must always be clear, convincing and cogent in order to satisfy the balance of 
probabilities test.5 
[10]  I found the Appel lant to be a credible witness.  There were some inconsistencies between 
his testimony and some of the Applicant’s statements at the visa post interview.  For example, he 
was quite adamant that the Applicant told him about her immigration situation in Canad a before 
they had the Nikka , but she told the visa officer that she had concealed that information from 
him:  
Q:  Did you tell him you had no status at the time?  
 
A:  Not when we first met . 
 
Q:  When did you tell him?  
 
A:  After a while, when we started to get close we did a XXXXX in Aug2014 and I 
definitely  didn’t tell him then because I wanted to gauge I had so many failed 
marriages.6 
 
[11]  That said, the Appellant’s testimony was otherwise internally consistent, forthright and 
responsive.  I accept that, more likely than not, the relationship is genuine from his perspective.  
[12]  For the appeal to succeed, however, the Appellant must establish that the marriage is 
mutually  genuine.  The Applicant did not give viva voce  evidence at the de novo  hearing.  It is 
not cle ar why she was not called to testify and I am not prepared to speculate as to counsel’s 
litigation strategy.  
[13]  That the Applicant did not testify was fatal to the appeal.

[14]  In some cases, it may be possible for an Appellant to meet their evidentiary onus witho ut 
the testimony of their sponsored spouse.  In the Mann7 decision, IAD Member XXXXX agreed that 
sometimes the testimony of an Appellant alone can suffice to persuade the panel of the 
bona  fides  of the intentions of both spouses.  However, she went on to list situations where the 
Applicant’s testimony may be essential:  
This is not to say that there are no cases in which the testimony of the applicant 
will be necessary to successfully discharge th e evidentiary burden.  Appeals in 
which it might be advisable or even necessary to call the applicant as a witness 
include circumstances such as the following:  
 
 Where there are specific and significant inconsistencies in the 
record – as between the appella nt and the applicant or within the 
applicant’s own answers;  
 
 Where the applicant has a questionable immigration history;  
 
 Where there is an obvious reason to question the motivation of the 
applicant, such as where there is persuasive evidence that the 
applicant is using the appellant to acquire status in Canada;  
 
 Where there is minimal or inadequate documentary evidence to 
corroborate the testimony of the appellant.8 
 
[15]  In my view, the situations listed by Member XXXXX exist in this appeal.  We have 
incon sistencies that the applicant should have been called upon to explain , such as  her address 
history and visa post interview.  She has a lengthy immigration history in Canada that could easily 
be characterized as “questionable” and it is apparent that she ha s used marriage in the past as a 
basis to apply for status here.  The genuineness of two of her prior relationships is questionable and 
was not something that the Appellant could address in his testimony.  There was also little 
documentary evidence to show  when and where the Applicant lived in Canada.  
[16]  I also note the Federal Court jurisprudence in this regard.  The Honourable Mr. Justice 
Shore in XX v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration )9 suggested that failing to call an Applicant 
in an IAD marriage appeal can properly lead to an adverse inference being drawn.  The Federal 
Court provided a useful overview of the relevant principles involved:

[1]                 The principles of law on adve rse inference are well -established. The 
leading statement is to be found in Wigmore , “Evidence in Trials at Common 
Law”, 1979 (Chadbourn Rev.) at vol. 2, 285, page 192:  
…The failure to bring before the tribunal some circumstance, documents, 
or witness, whe n either the party himself or his opponent claims that the 
facts would thereby be elucidated, serves to indicate, as the most natural 
inference, that the party fears to do so, and this fear is some evidence that 
the circumstance or document or witness, if brought, would have exposed 
facts unfavourable to the party . These inferences, to be sure, cannot fairly 
be made except upon certain conditions; and they are also open always to 
explanation by circumstances which make some other hypothesis a more 
natural one than the party’s fear of exposure. But the propriety of such an 
inference in general is not doubted . (Emphasis added).  
 
[2]                 Reasonableness dictates that in the case of the Immigration and Refugee 
Board (and all its divisions), although the rules of evidence in its regard are 
relaxed, nevertheless , when evidence is available, or could be made available but 
not produced, or when a person can testify, is given the opportunity to testify, but 
does not testify, then an adverse inference can be drawn.  
  
[3]                 The adverse inference is drawn not merely from the failure to produce, 
“but from non -production when it would be natural for the party to produce” such 
evidence: XXXXXXX , vol. 2 at 199; reference is also made to XXXXXX v. Union 
Steamships Ltd.  (1954), 13 W.W.R. 72, aff’d, 14 W.W.R. 673 (B.C.C.A.), 
adopting and citing XXXXXXX : 
It is certainly a maxim that all evidence is to be weighed according 
to the proof which it was in the power of one side to have 
produced, and in the power of the other to have contradicted.  
  
[4]                 The Supreme Court of Canada has dealt with this issue in the often 
referred to decision of XXXXXXXX v. XXXXXX , [1970] S.C.R. 1010. It was held that a 
court must presume that such evidence would adversely affect the plaintiff’s case, 
as said by Justice LoXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX on behalf of the majority of the court, at 
pp. 1012 -3. 
  
[5]                 In XXXXXXXX v. XXXXXXXXX , [1995] P.E.I.J. No. 23 (QL), 53 A.C.W.S. (3d) 
786, the Prince Edward Island Court of Appeal following XXXXXXXX , above, found 
that the trial judge erred in failing to draw an adverse inference from the fact that 
a key witness to the case was not called to give evidence:  
[36]       ... Generally speaking, where a plaintiff is at best able to 
raise only a possibility a certain condition was the ca use of the 
plaintiff's condition, the plaintiff's failure to produce evidence, 
which may be material to the cause and which is within the power 
of the plaintiff to produce, must result in an adverse inference that 
the evidence which was not produced, would  adversely affect the 
plaintiff's case . The weight which may be given to such an adverse

however, the trial judge's failure to draw an adverse inference, in 
such circumstances, is an error whic h goes to the trial judge's

[6]                Indeed, that is the crux of this matter. It would have been natural for the 
spouse to have testified at the appeal. It is clear that she, as the spouse, was 
particularly and uniquely qualified to give evidence on the material issue in the 
appeal, namely, her credibility. She failed to do so. While the Immigration Appeal

[4] Section 28  of the Act  provides for a number of ways to meet the residency obligation

[5] Subsection 61(3) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the

DISCRETIONARY RELIEF  
 
[11]  Pursuant to paragraph  67(1)(c) of the Act the IAD has been granted authority to consider 
discretionary relief and permit an appellant to retain their permanent resident status despite a 
breach of the residency obligation.  The test to be applied in the exercise of discr etionary 
jurisdiction is that:    
 
The Immigration Appeal Division must be satisfied that, at the time that the 
appeal is disposed of taking into account the best interests of a child directly 
affected by the decision, sufficient humanitarian and compassion ate 
considerations warrant special relief in light of all  the circumstances of the case.  
 
[12]  I regard the following factors to be the appropriate considerations in the exercise of 
discretionary jurisdiction in the context of an appeal based on the appellant’s  failure to meet the 
residency obligation.  These factors are not exhaustive and the weight assigned to each factor will 
vary depending on the circumstances of each case.  
 
 the circumstances surrounding the breach of the residency obligation, including 
the reasons for and extent of the absence(s) from Canada and the appellant’s 
intentions in relation to residency in Canada;  
 
 whether the appellant made reasonable attempts to return to Canada at the first 
opportunity;  
 
 the length of time the appellant has spen t in Canada and the degree to which the 
appellant is established in Canada;  
 
 the appellant's family in Canada and the impact to the family that loss of status 
would cause;  
 
 the best interests of any child directly affected by the decision; and  
 
 the degree of hardship that would be caused to the appellant by loss of status in 
Canada, including the conditions in the likely country of removal.

Analysis  
 
Humanitarian and compassionate grounds  
 
[14]  While the refusal is valid in law, the Panel may allow the appeal if it finds that sufficient 
humanitarian and compassionate grounds warrant  special relief . The guiding analytical 
framework is found in Buffete Arce4 and Kok.5  The non -exhaustive factors considered include:  
 
i) The amount of time that the appellant has spent in Canada;  
ii) The appellant’s initial and continuing degree of establishment  in Canada;  
iii) The appellant’s reasons for departing from Canada, and the appellants reasons 
for continued, or lengthy, stay outside of Canada;  
iv) Ties to Canada in terms of family and their hardship if the appellant is 
removed;  
v) Whether reasonable attempts to re turn to Canada were made at the first 
opportunity;  
vi) The hardship the appellant faces in his home country; and,  
vii) Whether or not there are unique or special circumstances present in the case 
such as the Chirwa6 standard for equitable relief.  
 
[15]  The legislation a lso requires the decision -maker to take into consideration the best 
interests of any child directly affected by the decision.

[16]  The appellant testified that he returned to Pakistan shortly after landing in Canada as he 
wished to be with his grandmother . Prior to coming to Canada the appellant lived with his 
grandmother and was extremely close with her and vice versa. He testified that he wanted to 
return to her and his family agreed that he should return and  live with his grandmother.

[20]  The residency requirements ar e not particularly onerous, and in fact offer a generous 
flexibility to new immigrants by not requiring large time commitments in Canada. The 
requirement of only 730 days in any five year period, which days need not be continuous, 
amounts to less than a tw o year physical presence commitment.  
 
[21]  The panel appreciates that the appellant was a minor at the time that he returned to

grandmother.

[22]  Counsel submits that as the appellant was minor, he could not form an intent to abandon 
his residency. The same can be said that as a minor, he could not have informed an intent to 
immigrate in the first place. The panel does not find that intent of a minor is the only

parents, his testimony was clear that his wish was to be in Pakistan also.  
 
[23]  The panel believes that parents are generally in the best position to assess the best 
interests of their minor children. The fact that the appellant’s pare nts were prepared to separate 
from their son at a young age and have him raised in Pakistan with other family in violation of 
his residency requirements, failing to bring him on physical visits to Canada at all, reflects 
adversely on any intention that the y had to see that he maintained his residency obligations. 
Instead of visiting their son regularly in Pakistan, they could have facilitated his return to Canada 
so that he could have accumulated some residency days.  
 
[24]  The appellant was asked why his parents  did not sponsor him back to Canada when he 
fell into breach, and he testified that they believed it would be faster to appeal. In reality, the 
appellant was not interested in being sponsored back to Canada until his grandmother passed 
away, which is why XXX was outside of Canada continuously for over seven years before applying.  
 
[25]  The appellant’s parents did not appear as witnesses in support of his appeal, nor provide 
any affidavit evidence and, as such there is no way to determine their motivation and thou ght 
process in allowing the residency breach in the first place.  
 
[26]  The benefit of being a permanent resident of Canada also comes with obligations, which 
the appellant fell far short of satisfying . The evidence before the panel is that this residency 
breach  would have continued until the death of the appellant’s grandmother, signifying no ties to

designed to be respected in the moment.

OVERVIEW  
[1] XXXX XXXX  is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated 
February 20, 2017.  
[2] Mr. XXXX  claims to be born in Afghanistan on XXXX XXXX , 1998. He claims to be at 
risk in Afghanistan because his father worked as a XXXX  for the XXXX Army  and was tortured 
and executed by the Taliban in 2010 for this reason. The fam ily was detained by the Taliban but 
escaped with the help of his father’s friend. The family was smuggled out of Afghanistan into 
Iran where they lived with his paternal uncle. Mr. XXXX  lived with his uncle for 10 -11 months 
before travelling to Turkey. His  mother and uncle believed that he was still in danger as the 
eldest son. His mother and siblings stayed in Iran.  
[3] After about a year in Turkey, he travelled to Greece where he stayed 9 -10 months. From 
Greece , he made his way to Canada via XXXX , XXXX , XXXX and XXXX . From XXXX , a 
smuggler provided him with a XXXX  passport and he travelled by air to Canada via XXXX , 
XXXX , using the name “ XXXX XXXX .” He was accompanied on the flights to Canada by the 
smuggler’s friend. He returned the passport to the smuggler u pon arrival in Canada.  
[4] In Canada, the smuggler left him in Downtown Montreal where he reported to a police 
station on July 7, 2015  to claim asylum.  Mr. XXXX  was then detained for reasons of identity. He 
was liberated from detention with conditions on July  13, 2015, in the care of his designated 
representative, though he was still unable to confirm his identity  to the satisfaction of the Canada 
Border Services Agency . 
[5] Mr. XXXX  was a minor, aged 17 years old, at the hearing before the RPD. He was 
accompanied  by a designated representative and counsel.  However, Mr. XXXX  is now an adult, 
therefore the designation is no longer necessary.  
[6] The Minister intervened before the RPD for cause of identity  and was present at the 
hearing . The Minister argued  that it could  find no record of his entry into Canada based on the

birth.1 Tazkira  certificates include the bearer's name, father's name, grandfather's name, the date

“To harass or afflict with repeated acts of cruelty or annoyance; to afflict or punish because of

INTRODUCTION  
 
 
[1] A DNA test is a compelling piece of direct evidence to prove who the biological parents 
of a child are . It can also be a powerful piece of indirect evide nce to prove that a marriage is 
genuine . This is  because parties to a non -genuine marriage normally do not go so far as to have a 
child  in order to p ass off their marriage as genuine . In this appeal a DNA test shows that XXXXXXXXXX (“the appellant”) and XXXXXX (“the applicant”) had a child together and then were 
married.  
 
 
[2] Despite this, a visa officer decided that their marriage was not genuine and refused the 
applicant’s sponsored application to come to Canada as a member of the family class. The 
appellant appealed this decision to the Immigration Appeal Division (“IAD”) . He and the 
applicant gave evidence , but they  both lack credibility in relation to important aspects of this 
case. This leads me to agree with the visa officer’s conclusion. As a result the appeal  is 
dismissed. The reasons below explain why.
