genuine , the v isa officer also decides the marriage was entered into primarily to enable the 
applicant to acquire status under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (the “ Act ”).2

their credibility is important because this is not a case where there is documentary evidence that

credibility of a witness has to be tested against the standard of what “… a practical and informed 
person would readily recognize as reasonable in that place and in those conditions”4. Because of

sponsored by him  and had no other social support  in Toronto . When I consider all of the 
circumstances surrounding the breakdown of his first marriage , I do not believe that the reason 
the appellant went back to Changle in December 2009 was because he was so emotionally 
distressed by a marriage breakdown caused by his first wife.  
 
 
[23]  I appreciate that this appeal is about the appellant’s second marriage a nd not whether his

CONCL USION  
 
 
[37]  There is no single piece of evidence in this appeal which is determinative. When all the 
evidence is considered together, it is more likely than not that this marriage is not genuine. The 
inconsistencies in the evidence of the appellant and the app licant ; the lack of documents to show 
ongoing contact in the period before the visa officer refused the application;  and the absence of 
spontaneous detail in the testimony of the witnesses all suggest that the marriage is not genuine. 
This evidence outweig hs the fact that the appellant and the applicant have had a child together.  
 
 
[38]  Having decided that the marriage is not genuine, I do not need to determine whether it 
was entered into primarily for the purpose of gaining admission to Canada . The appeal is 
dismissed .

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
OVERVIEW  
[1] This decision involves XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  (the Appellant), a citizen of 
Nigeria.  She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim 
for refugee protection.  The Appellant alleges that she is a victim of domestic v iolence at the 
hands of her husband and that he is attempting to force her to convert to Islam from Christianity.  
I find that the determinative issue in her appeal is credibility.  I agree with the RPD that the 
Appellant failed to establish her allegation s on a balance of probabilities, as there were a number 
of significant inconsistencies in the evidence that were detrimental to their credibility.  I also 
agree with the RPD that her other evidence did not overcome these credibility concerns.  
DECISION  
[2] Afte r considering her arguments and all of the evidence, I dismiss the Appellant’s appeal.  
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)( a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I 
confirm the determination of the RPD.  
BACKGROUND  
[3] The Appellant claims that she has been a victim of domestic violence by her husband, 
which escalated after he converted to Islam and demanded that she too convert from Christianity.  
As a result of the abuse and threat of a deadline to convert, she fled he r home and then to the 
United States on XXXX XXXX , 2017, where her son has a green card.  She claims to fear 
domestic violence and a forced conversion to the Teblique Muslim sect should she return to 
Nigeria.  She states that she decided to seek protection  in Canada rather than the United States 
because of President XXXXX’s immigration policies and because of fear of crime there.  She came 
to Canada on XXXX XXXX , 2017.   
[4] The Appellant’s refugee claim was heard by the RPD on June 6 and July 14, 2017.  In its  
reasons dated August 22, 2017, the RPD rejected the Appellant’s claim on the basis of credibility.  
Some of its findings included the following:

 a) inconsistencies in the evidence regarding dates and chronology of when she fled her home 
and where she stayed until she left Nigeria to travel to the United States; and  
b) inconsistencies regarding when she reported the abuse to the police and their response to 
her report.  
[5] As a result, the RPD found that the XXXXXXXXX’s testimony was “riddled” with 
contradictions and  that she completely lacked credibility.  It also found that her additional 
documentary evidence did not overcome these credibility findings, and that ultimately she had not 
established her allegations on a balance of probabilities.   
ISSUES  
[6] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred as follows:  
a) In failing to apply Chairperson’s Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing 
Gender -related Persecution  (Gender Guideline) ;1 
b) In its assessment of the Appellant’s credibility.  
[7] The Appellant has not provided new evide nce or asked for an oral hearing.   
ANALYSIS  
[8] After conducting my own analysis of the record, I dismiss the appeal.  I turn now to 
explain my reasons for reaching this conclusion.  
ROLE OF THE RAD  
[9] As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica,2 the RAD  must review the RPD 
decisions on a correctness standard with respect to questions of law and findings of fact (and 
                                                 
 
1 Guideline issued by the Chairperson pursuant to paragraph 159(1)(h) of the IRPA.  
2 M.C.I.  v. Huruglica, Bujar  (F.C.A., no. A-470 -14), XXXXXXXX, XXXX, XXXX, March 29, 2016, 2016 FCA 93.

 mixed fact and law) which raise no issue of the credibility of oral evidence. Deference may be 
required when the RPD is in an advantageous p osition with respect to the assessment of oral 
evidence.3  In this appeal, the findings are based on the substance and content of the Appellant’s 
evidence, and I do not find that the RPD was in an advantageous position in assessing this 
evidence.   
a) Did the RPD err in failing to apply Chairperson ’s Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants 
Fearing Gender -related Persecution ? 
[10]  The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in failing to take the Gender Guideline into 
account in assessing the Appellant’s case.  She sub mits that the RPD did not expressly state that it 
applied the Gender Guideline, nor did it consider the Guideline in assessing her evidence, lacking 
sensitivity to the gendered nature of her experiences and explanations.   
[11]  I disagree with the Appellant, an d find that the RPD did not err in failing to consider the 
Gender Guideline.  She is correct in her assertion that the RPD did not explicitly mention the 
Gender Guideline in its reasons, but as she notes in her submissions, what is more important is 
whethe r the RPD made its decision in a way that is consistent with the Guidelines.  I find that it 
did so.   
[12]  The Appellant argues that the RPD was insensitive to the difficulty she was having in 
recounting the chronology of her abuse, focusing all of its attenti on on inconsistencies in dates 
regarding when she sought refuge with relatives in March 2017.  I disagree.  As will be discussed 
in further detail below regarding the RPD’s credibility findings, although I do not place as much 
emphasis as does the RPD on t he inconsistencies of these dates, I find it was appropriate for the 
RPD to ask about them, as there were significant inconsistencies in both the dates and the details 
of the Appellant’s narrative.  Further, based on my review of the recording of the heari ng, I find 
that the RPD’s questions were asked in a respectful, sensitive and neutral fashion, and that the 
RPD did not violate the principles set out in the Gender Guideline in the manner that it carried out 
the Appellant’s hearing.

 [13]  The Appellant raises  concerns about questions asked by the RPD, including a question 
about the group with her husband who attended at their home in December 2016.  The Appellant 
argues that the RPD should have considered battered women’s syndrome in relation to why she 
stayed  with and returned to her husband, or why she did not seek protection at an earlier date.  I 
disagree, as the RPD did not make any negative credibility findings in relation to the question of 
why the Appellant stayed with or returned to her husband, or on the basis of any other 
inappropriate stereotypes relating to domestic violence.  As will be discussed in more detail 
below, the RPD made credibility findings on the basis of inconsistencies in the evidence that are 
not related to inappropriate assumptions about violence against women; for example, it found that 
her narrative regarding where she went when she left her family home as a result of threats by her 
husband to be inconsistent.  This does not relate to any assumptions or stereotypes about women 
surv ivors of violence.  
[14]  Further, I find that it was appropriate for the RPD to canvass the issue of delay and why 
the Appellant did not claim asylum at an earlier date when she had visited the United States in 
2016, as she claimed that her husband had been viol ent since 2011.  It is important to note, 
however, that the RPD did not make any findings based on these questions or on the issue of 
delay; and I find that this suggests that the RPD did in fact consider the Gender Guidelines, and 
took the context of the Appellant’s claims of domestic violence into account into its findings.   
[15]  The Appellant also argues that based on the Gender Guideline, the RPD should have put 
more weight on her sister -in-law ’s and son’s letters, as the Guidelines instruct that claimants who 
are victims of violence often cannot rely on the more standard or typical forms of evidence of 
their allegations.  In the XXXXXXXXX’s case, however, she did provide a standard form of evidence, a 
police report, which was inconsistent with her other evi dence in a number of ways.  These 
inconsistencies contributed to the RPD’s negative credibility findings.  I find that this is not a case 
where I would put more  weight on non -standard types of evidence than on the police report.  The 
RPD did not err in pla cing limited weight on the letters, which further did not overcome its other 
credibility findings.

 b) Did the RPD err in its assessment of the XXXXXXXXX ’s credibility?  
[16]  The Appellant argues that the RPD also erred in its assessment of her credibility.  Based 
on my review of the RPD reasons and evidence, I disagree, and find that the RPD did not err.  
Focus on inconsistencies  
[17]  The Appellant argues that the RPD did not analyze the credibility of her testimony 
regarding the violence that she experienced, whic h is central to her claim, but rather focused on 
inconsistencies in the dates of assaults and when she went into hiding.  She asserts that any 
inconsistencies were minor and not central to her claim, and that the RPD erred in being 
microscopic in its appro ach.   I disagree, as will be explained below.  
Inconsistencies in when and where she fled  
[18]  The RPD found that the evidence regarding when and where the Appellant fled after 
leaving her home was inconsistent.  In her Basis of Claim ( BOC ), the Appellant states  that after 
learning of the plan to force her to convert on March 3, 2017, she fled to her family home on 
March 1, 2017 and after discussions within the family, she returned to her own home with her 
husband on March 20, 2017.  She was allegedly beaten then  by her husband, after which she 
escaped to her niece’s home on March 22, 2017.   
[19]  During her oral testimony, the Appellant stated that she left her home and sought refuge at 
her niece’s home on XXXX  1, 2017, instead of her family’s home, and that she shutt led back and 
forth between the niece’s home and her own house during the next 21 days.  This contradicted the 
account in the Appellant’s narrative.  These accounts were further contradicted by the Appellant’s 
niece’s letter, which states that she sheltered  the Appellant from sometime in March, 2017 until 
she left Nigeria to go to the United States.4  This letter additionally  conflicts with the Appellant’s 
BOC in another way, because the Appellant states there that she returned back to her own home 
with her husband from her niece’s place prior to leaving the United States.

 [20]  I disagree with the Appellant’s submission that the inconsistencies  in her evidence  are 
limited to confusing various dates that all took place in March, that she confused dates because 
she was under pressure, and that any inconsistencies in the evidence are minor.  Aside from the 
inconsistencies in dates, on which I place less importance than the RPD and acknowledge that 
there could be confusion about, based on my review of the recording o f the hearing and other 
evidence, I agree with the RPD’s finding that there were a number of other more substantive 
inconsistencies in the Appellant’s account of when she left her home and where she went when 
she left.  There were a number of different ver sions of this narrative in evidence before the RPD:  
a) the Appellant left her home to go to her family home on March 1, 2017, returned to her 
own home and then her niece’s home.  Based on discussions between her family and her 
husband, she agreed to return to  her own home and husband before fleeing Nigeria to the 
United States (from the Appellant’s BOC);  
b) the Appellant left her home to stay with her niece at the beginning of March 2017, and then 
shuttled back and forth between there and her own home for the nex t 21 days, when her 
husband was away travelling.  She did not go to her family home during this time 
(Appellant’s oral testimony);  and  
c) the XXXXXXXXX went to her niece’s home in March 2017 and left directly from there to travel 
to the United States (niece’s  letter).  
[21]  I agree with the RPD that these inconsistencies, which were not adequately explained, are 
not minor but central to the XXXXXXXXX’s narrative, as they relate to her account of domestic 
violence and need to flee her husband, and that they seriously  damage  the credibility of  the 
Appellant’s narrative of domestic violence and threat of forced religious conversion.  
Inconsistencies regarding the XXXXXXXXX’s report to the police  
[22]  The RPD also found that there were inconsistencies in the evidence regarding  the 
XXXXXXXXX’s claim that she reported the domestic violence to the police.  It found that there were 
three different dates provided for when the XXXXXXXXX reported to the police.  Further, it found that 
there were inconsistencies regarding the results o f the police report.

 [23]  The Appellant argues that although there were inconsistencies in the dates, the overall 
series of events was consistent.  I disagree with her argument, and I agree with the RPD that there 
was a significant inconsistency regarding the  result of the report to the police.  Based on my 
review of the recording of the hearing, I agree with the RPD’s finding that the XXXXXXXXX testified 
that her husband suffered no consequences from his behaviour and from the authorities.5  When 
confronted w ith the fact that the police report she provided stated that the XXXXXXXXX’s husband 
had been “detained in our facility” overnight from March 17, 2017 to March 18, 2017 and warned 
to desist from this behaviour “or face severe consequences for his actions,”6 the Appellant 
amended her testimony to state that he was called to the police station and then they were told by 
the police to go home together to settle their issues.7  I do not agree with the Appellant’s argument 
that there was no inconsistency in thes e two accounts.  She submits that the response by the police 
as described in the police report was “mild” and “effectively non -consequential for her husband”, 
which was consistent with her testimony that he faced no consequences from the authorities.  I 
find that detention overnight and a serious warning “of severe consequences” for any further 
abuse is a significant, if inadequate, consequence for the allegations of abuse, and inconsistent 
with the Appellant’s oral evidence that her husband suffered no con sequences from her report to 
the police, and find that this further damages the credibility of her narrative.   
Omission regarding assault by husband after return home  
[24]  The RPD found that the XXXXXXXXX’s adjusted oral testimony, in which she claimed that he r 
husband beat her after they returned home together from the police station, was inconsistent with 
the police report, which stated that he was detained overnight.  Further, it found that this beating 
was significant, since it happened when she was about t o leave the country, but was omitted from 
the Appellant’s BOC, which further undermined her credibility.  
[25]  The Appellant argues that the RPD placed too much significance on this omission, as this 
incident was not the reason she decided to leave the country.   Rather, she decided to leave 
because the police failed to protect her from her husband.

 [26]  I do not find that the RPD placed too much significance on this contradiction and 
omission.  Based on my review of the evidence, I agree with the RPD’s finding, and  find that it is 
appropriate to consider this in its assessment of the Appellant’s credibility.   
Medical documentation  
[27]  The RPD found that medical documentation provided by the Appellant regarding a 
number of scars and dental issues did not demonstrate tha t they were caused by domestic 
violence.  The Appellant argues that the RPD should have considered whether the reported 
injuries were consistent with her testimony.   
[28]  I disagree, and find that the medical information does not confirm the injuries were caus ed 
by domestic violence.  Although the reported injuries may be consistent with the Appellant’s 
claim, I find that the reports do not outweigh the other credibility concerns discussed above.   
CONCLUSION  
[29]  On the basis of the findings outlined above, I dismi ss the appeal.  I agree with the RPD 
that there were significant credibility concerns regarding the Appellant’s claim, and that she did 
not establish her allegations on a balance of probabilities.   
[30]  As a result, I confirm the determination of the RPD pursuant to paragraph 111(1)( a) of the 
IRPA. The appeal is dismissed.

Introduction and Issue  
 
[1] The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, appeals pursuant to section 63(1) of the Immigration 
and Refugee Protection  Act1 (IRPA ) from a decision of the visa officer not to issue a permanent 
resident visa to her spouse, XXXXXXXXXXX , step -daughter, XXXXXXXXXXXX and step -son XXXXXXXXX  
(the applicant s), on the basis that the marriage is not genuine and that it was entered into 
primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the IRPA . 
 
[2] The issue is whether the appellant has proven that the applicant is to be considere d her 
spouse, and therefore a member of the family class, pursuant to Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Regulations2 (Regulations ) sections 117(1)(a) and 4 (now 4 (1)).  
 
[3] At the time of the refusal by the visa officer, section 4 of the Regulations  read as follows:  
 
4. For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse, a 
common -law partner, a conjugal partner or an adopted child of a person if the marriage, common -
law partnership, conjugal partnership or adoption is n ot genuine and was entered into primarily for 
the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act.3 
 
[4] Effective September 30, 2010 section 4 of the Regulations  was amended and section 4(1), 
the new provision dealing with “bad faith” marriages, co mmon -law partnerships and conjugal 
partnerships, reads as follows:  
 
4.(1) For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse, a 
common -law partner, or a conjugal partner if the marriage, common -law partnership, conju gal 
partnership  
 
(a) was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the 
Act; or  
(b) is not genuine.4

[5] Under section 4 of the Regulations , as it read prior to September 30, 2010, to succeed on 
appeal the appellant had to prove either  that the marriage is genuine or that it was not entered 
into primarily for the purpose of the applicant gaining any status or privilege under the IRPA .  To 
dismiss the appeal the panel had to find that the marriage is not genuine and  was en tered into 
primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the IRPA . 
 
[6] However, under section 4(1) of the Regulations , as it reads on or after September 30, 
2010, to succeed on appeal the appellant has to prove that the marriage was not  entered into 
primarily for the purpose of the applicant gaining any status or privilege under the IRPA  and  that 
it is genuine.  To dismiss the appeal the panel must find that the marriage was entered into 
primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the IRPA  or that it is not 
genuine.  
 
[7] At the hearing of the appeal in this matter the test set out in former section 4 (now section 
4(1)) of the Regulations ) had been changed.  While the word order is different, the test remains 
the same except for the change from “and” to “or”.  A two -pronged conjunctive test for being 
excluded from the family class under former Regulation  4 has become a disjunctive test under 
Regulation  4(1).  
 
[8] Due to the findings it has made on the primary purpose and th e genuineness of the 
marriage, the panel has determined that the result of the appeal is the same under former section 
4 and current section 4(1) of the Regulations . 
 
Decision  
 
[9] Having considered the evidence and submissions of the parties, the panel finds that the 
appellant has not met the burden of proof in this appeal provided for in former section 4 and in 
current section 4(1) of the Regulations .  The panel finds that the marriage was entered into 
primarily for immigration purposes and is not genuine.  T he applicant is therefore not a member 
of the family class.

Credibility of the Witnesses  
 
[22]  In co nsidering the reliability and credibility of witnesses in the case of inconsistencies 
and an absence of supporting evidence, “...The trial judge should not consider the plaintiff’s 
evidence in isolation, but must look at the totality of the evidence to ass ess the impact of the 
inconsistencies in that evidence on questions of credibility and reliability pertaining to the core 
issue in the case.”14 
 
[23]  It is true that the panel had the benefit of observing the appellant and hearing the 
applicant testify under aff irmation.  In general, t here is a presumption of truth in sworn evidence, 
unless there is some reason to doubt that truthfulness.15  In this case, however, there were 
sufficient inconsistencies and implausibility that overcame that presumption.  Both the 
appellant’s and the applicant’s evidence were hesitant, vague, evasive, self -contradictory, and in 
some aspects, defies common sense and logic.  The panel therefore does not find either the 
appellant’s or the applicant’s evidence credible, trustworthy or rel iable.

Genuineness of Marriage  
 
[24]  The genuineness of a marriage can be affected by a number of different indicia .16  These 
are not identical in every appeal as the genuineness of the marriage can be affected by any 
number of different factors in each appeal . 
 
[25]  These can include, but are not limited to, such factors as how the relationship developed; 
the intent of the parties to the marriage; the length of the relationship; the amount of time spent 
together; conduct at the time of meeting, at the time of an en gagement and/or the wedding; 
behaviour subsequent to a wedding; the level of knowledge of each other’s relationship histories; 
levels of continuing contact and communication; the provision of financial support; the 
knowledge of and sharing of responsibilit y for the care of children brought into the marriage; the 
knowledge of and contact with extended families of the parties; as well as the level of knowledge 
about each other’s daily lives.  All of these factors can be considered in determining the 
genuinene ss of a marriage.

Primary Purpose of Acquiring Status under IRPA  
 
[103]  The importance of membership in the family class by marri age is that the applicant is 
largely exempted from other requirements.  The advantage sought in spousal appeals is generally 
entry to Canada and the granting of permanent resident status to the applicant as a member of the 
family class.  Whether the relati onship was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring 
any status or privilege under IRPA  is self -evident and self -explanatory.  
 
[104]  The Federal Court states in XXXX , “...if the evidence leads to a finding that the marriage is 
not genuine, then there i s a presumption that it was entered into for the purpose of gaining status.  
The burden of establishing a contrary purpose should be placed squarely on the applicant.”64 
 
[105]  Having found the marriage not to be genuine, and in light of the witnesses’ lack of 
credibility overall, the lack of credible explanations as to their intentions for such a marriage, the 
panel finds that this burden has not been met in this case.  The panel therefore concludes, on a 
balance of probabilities, that the evidence demonstrates t hat the acquisition of status under IRPA  
was the primary purpose for this marriage.

Conclusion  
 
[106]  The onus is on the appellant to satisfy this panel, on a balance of probabilities, that this 
marriage is not caught by former section 4 or the current section  4(1) of the Regulations .  In 
considering the totality of evidence, the panel is not persuaded that the appellant has met that 
burden in this case.  
 
[107]  The panel has considered the evidence and submissions in this case, including the 
documentary evidence, the  appellant’s visits to China, the photographs submitted, the telephone 
invoices, the length of time since marriage, and the parties’ testimony at the hearing.  
 
[108]  This case, as in other cases of this nature, rests largely on the credibility of the parties.  
As stated, the panel finds both the appellant’s and the applicant’s evidence vague, evasive, 
inconsistent, contradictory and not credible in general.  The panel specifically does not find their 
evidence on the introduction and development of their relations hip credible.  The logical 
inference is that the relationship, and hence the marriage, is not genuine, and was entered into for 
gaining status or privilege under the IRPA . 
 
[109]  Having considered all the factors and submissions and weighed the evidence, the pan el 
finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the marriage was entered into primarily for the purpose 
of acquiring status or privilege under the IRPA  and is not genuine.  The appellant has not 
discharged the onus under section 4 of the Regulations  as it re ad prior to September 30, 2010, 
and section  4(1) of the Regulations  as it reads after the amendment effective September 30, 
2010.  
 
[110]  The appeal is dismissed.

REASONS FOR DECISION  
BACKGROUND  
[1] At the conclusion of the evidence and submissions, I dismissed this appeal with reasons 
to follow. These are those reasons.  
[2] On September 24, 2013 , the appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXX, filed an application for a travel 
document. In the course of the assessment of the appellant’s eligibility to enter Canada, it was 
determined by the Deputy Program Manager in the Embassy of Canada in Ankara, Turkey that 
appellant is inadmissible pursuant to section 41(b) of the  Immigration and Refugee Protection 
Act1 (IRPA ) for failing to comply with the residency obligation mandated b y section 28 of the 
IRPA  and there were insufficient humanitarian and compassionate grounds, taking into account 
the best interests of a child directly affected by the determination,  to warrant special relief.  
ISSUE AND DECISION  
[3] Appellant does not dispute that he did not meet the residency obligation in that he did not 
spend more than 237 days in Canada in the five years prior to the date his application for a travel 
document was received. Accordingly, I find the Deputy Program Manager’s decision is valid i n 
law. The issue therefore is whether, taking into account the best interests of a child directly 
affected by those decisions, sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant 
special relief in all the circumstances of the case.

The Appellant bears the burden of proving her case on a balance of probabilities. Background  
 
[1] This is the hearing of a sponsorship appeal brought by XXXXXX  (the “appellant ”), from the 
refusal to issue a permanent resident visa to his wife, XXXXXXXXXXXX (the “applicant ”), who resides 
in China, because the appellant was found by the visa  officer to be an ineligible sponsor.  
 
[2] The appellant became a permanent resident of Canada on landing on April 2002 as a 
skilled worker. He was 29 years old.  He is now a Canadian citizen.  
 
[3] To be issued a permanent  resident visa as a member of the family c lass , the sponsorship 
undertaking made with respect of the sponsorship of a foreign national must be in effect and the 
sponsor who gave the undertaking must meet the requirements of section 133  of the Immigration 
and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the  “Regulations ”).1  Under section 133(1) (a) of the 
Regulations  the sponsorship application shall only be approved by an officer if , on the day on which 
the application for permanent residence was filed and from that day until the day a decision is made 
with respect to the application, there i s evidence that the appellant complies with section 130  of the 
Regulations .  Under subsection 130(2)  of the Regulations  a Canadian citizen who is a sponsor and 
who does not reside in Canada may sponsor an application for permanent residence made by their 
spouse if the spouse will become a permanent resident when the applicant becomes a permanent 
resident.  
  
[4] In this case th e appellant is a Canadian citizen whose wife applied for permanent residence 
as a sponsored spouse on November 26, 2010 at the Canadian visa office located in Hong  Kong.   
The appellant was resident in Hong Kong on that date and on June 27 , 2011 , when the a pplicant ’s 
application was refused.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
OVERVIEW   
[1] XXXX XXXX  (the Principal A ppellant) , XXXX XXXX  (the Associate Appellant),  
XXXX XXXX XXXX  and XXXX XXXX  (the Minor  Appellants),  citizen s of Romania , appeal a 
decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated  February  6, 2019 , rejecting their 
claim s for refugee protection.  The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (the RAD) to set 
aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a determin ation that they are Convention 
refugees.  In the alternative, the Appellants request a hearing before the RAD or a 
redetermination by the RPD.  
DETERMINATION  
[2] The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph  111(1)( b) of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Act  (IRPA), the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own 
determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees.  
BACKGROUND  
[3] The Appellants allege that they  face persecution in Romania due to their Roma ethnicity. 
Specifically, th ey allege  that they have been refused service, abused,  discriminated against  and 
threatened due to their ethnicity. In general, the Appellants  allege that the Roma are segregated 
and/or denied services in housing, schooling, and healthcare, that Roma in Romania do not enjoy 
the same freedom of movement throughout the country that other Romanian citizens do , and that 
they are subject to violence and abuse . The Appellants fled Romania on XXXX XXXX , 2018  
and brought their claims in Canada which were heard on January 25, 2019 and rejected on 
February 6, 2019 , as the RPD found the Appellants lacked credibility.  The Appellants allege that 
the RPD erred  in the following ways:

[4] The Appellants have submitted eight  pieces of evidence in a section they title “New 
Evidence” in their record.1 They have not clearly explained how these eight pieces of evidence 
meet the require ments for admission , as their written statement makes no mention of the new 
evidence ,2 and their memo makes only a generic statement about new evidence.3 Nevertheless , I 
have considered the evidence and find that only one of the eight pieces of evidence is admissible 
and that the requirements for convening an oral hearing are not met.  
Positive RPD decisions for the XXXXXXXXXX’ family contained in the RPD record are not 
new evidence  
[5] The XXXXXXXXXX submitted two decisions of the RPD made in claims brought by the 
XXXXXXXXXX’ family members which were already contained in the RPD record, as the XXXXXXXXXX 
submitted them to the RPD.4 As these were before the RPD , they are not new evidence but are 
before me as part of the RPD record.  Therefore, although these docu ments are not new evidence , 
they will be considered on appeal.  They cannot be the subject of a decision to convene an oral 
hearing , as they are not new.  
The news articles and decision of the RPD which pre -date the decision are not admissible  
[6] The Appellants  submitted four news articles about country conditions for Roma in 
Romania from 2013 and 2014 and one RPD decision accepting Roma from Romania as refugees 
from September, 2018.5 These documents were not contained in the RPD record.  The Appellants 
have prov ided no evidence as to why these documents could not have been provided prior to the

[7] The Appellants submitted a decision of the RPD which post -dates the rejection of their

[9] When reviewing the R PD’s decision, the RAD is required to independently assess

 ANALYSIS  
[10]  The following issues are d eterminative of this appeal:  
(a) The RPD’s credibility assessment was microscopic, overzealous and 
misapprehended the evidence;  
(b) The Appellants face a risk of persecution on a Convention ground;  and  
(c) The Appellants do not have access to state protection or an internal flight 
alternative ( IFA ). 
The RPD’s credibility assessment was microscopic, overzealous and misapprehended the 
evidence  
[11]  The RPD made numerous credibility findings on issues as wide -ranging as the length of 
validity of the XXXXXXXXXX’ passports to the Appellants’ knowledge of the actions of their family 
members who left Canada and information about previous marriages of the adult Appellants.9 
The Appellants argue that this assessment was microscopic and related to peripheral issues and 
misapprehende d some of the evidence.10 Looking at the record in its totality, I agree with the 
Appellants.  The RPD’s approach to assessing credibility was incorrect and cannot be sustained.  I 
will give several examples.  
[12]  First, many of the credibility findings made by th e RPD are not related to the claim and 
are so peripheral as to demonstrate an overzealous attempt to discredit the Appellants.  For 
example, the RPD found the Appellants lacked credibility because their passports had only been 
issued for one year.11 Absent a  finding that the passport is fraudulent, which the RPD did not 
make, the length of the validity of the passport is not relevant to the Appellants’ claim, and the 
Appellants cannot be expected to know why the government issued the passport as it did.  
Addit ionally, the RPD found it lacked credibility that the Appellants did not accurately know 
how many Roma were in Romania.12 Given the Appellants’ lack of sophistication, this is not 
surprising, nor does it have any bearing on whether the Appellants experience d the problems 
they allege or are at risk.  Similarly, the RPD focused on a lack of documentation for the adult

that the Appellants did not have these documents,  but even if it were, the previous marriages are 
not relevant to the claims.   
[13]  Second, many of the credibility findings are based on a misapprehension of the evidence.  
For example, the RPD found it lacked credibility that the Appellants did not make a refug ee 
claim in the United Kingdom, despite the fact that Romanians cannot do so, as members of the 
European Union ( EU ).13 Moreover, as the Appellants argue, the RPD ’s finding that it was not 
credible that the Principal Appellant did not know there was a law re quiring all children to go to 
school ignores the documentary evidence that shows a high rate of Roma drop -outs due to 
discrimination.14 
[14]  These are just several examples out of many credibility findings which are irrelevant or 
incorrectly made.  For these reas ons , the RPD’s credibility assessment cannot be sustained and I 
am conducting my own credibility assessment.  
The Appellants face a risk of persecution on a Convention ground  
[15]  For the following reasons, I find that the Appellants have credibly established th at they 
face a risk of persecution on the basis of their Roma ethnicity, which is a Convention ground.  
[16]  First, I note that the RPD accepted that the Appellants are Roma , and I see no reason to 
disturb this finding.15 Second, the RPD did not find any material  inconsistencies, and I see none 
either, upon a review of the record.  Looking at the record and the oral testimony in its totality, I 
find that the XXXXXXXXXX were credible particularly based upon their profile which demonstrates 
that they are not sophisti cated or educated individuals.16 While the RPD faulted the Principal 
Appellant for answering, “I don’t know” to many questions, I do not find this to be evidence of a 
lack of credibility from an individual with only two years of education.17 Having reviewed the 
testimony, I find that it is consistent with the allegations and reflective of the Appellants’ 
personal circumstances.  Moreover, from the point at which they made their claim , the Appellants 
have consistently stated that they fear racists in Romania an d that they have had problems in

with evidence about attacks on their family members and the positive refugee decisions for those 
family members.19  
[17]  Furthermore,  the Appellants’ allegations are corroborated by the country conditions 
documents which demonstrate that Roma face police violence, societal discrimination, poor 
access to government services, shortage of employment opportunities, high rates of school 
attr ition and inadequate healthcare.20 Roma face a lower life -expectancy, difficulty in securing 
property documents, discriminatory language used against them, school segregation, incidents of 
property destruction and forced evictions.21 The Roma population in R omania is described as 
“poor, vulnerable, and socially excluded,” and they face systemic discrimination by society in 
areas including education, housing, health and employment as well as facing violence.22 When I 
take this evidence together with the XXXXXXX nts’ evidence , I find that the Appellants are credible 
and have established their allegations , on a balance of probabilities.  
[18]  I note that the XXXXXXXXXX spent time in the UK and returned to Romania, but I accept 
their explanations that they went there for the birth of their children and had no knowledge about 
any ability to stay there permanently.  Therefore, I find that this re -availment does not undermine 
my finding of credibility.  
[19]  I also find that the evidence that I have reviewed is sufficient to establish that the 
Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution based upon their Roma ethnicity, which is a 
Convention ground.  As reviewed, the Appellants faced instances of discrimination in school, 
healthcare, exclusion from public spaces , and co untry documents also indicate that Roma face a 
risk of violence. I find that this evidence more than meets the test for persecution or persecution 
on the basis of cumulative discrimination.  
[20]  Guidance from the UNHCR Handbook23 on determining refugee status an d Canadian 
jurisprudence24 indicates that discrimination can amount to persecution cumulatively when the 
following conditions are met. First, there must be a number of discriminatory acts which take 
place in a general atmosphere of insecurity in the country  of origin. The discriminatory acts must

serious restrictions on the right to earn a livelihood or to access normally available educational 
facilities. Where the  cumulative nature of the discrimination results in an insecure future for the 
person concerned, this constitutes persecution. When making this assessment, I must consider 
the personal circumstances and vulnerabilities of the Appellants, as I have done abo ve. Given the 
systemic nature of the discrimination of Roma, the risk of violence, and educational segregation, 
and given the young age of the Minor Appellants, I find that the test is made out in this case.  
[21]  For these reasons , I find that the Appellants fa ce a risk of persecution on a Convention 
ground.  
The Appellants do not have access to state protection or an IFA  
[22]  For the following reasons , I find that the Appellants do not have access to state protection 
or an IFA.  
[23]  With regard to state protection, I have reviewed the evidence, and I find that , while there 
is some evidence of efforts to protect Roma, at this time, state protection is not adequate at the 
operational level.  Document ary evidence  shows  that the police con tinue to perpetrate violence 
against Roma ; state authorities are implicated in instances of harassment and forced evictions of 
Roma, and that , in instances where Roma are the victims of crime , they often end up being 
blamed.25 Government officials have made  discriminatory statements against Roma and have 
been involved in attacks against Roma, and, while there are laws prohibiting discrimination, 
these are not enforced where Roma persons are concerned.26 While some sources note that there 
has been an improveme nt of the relationship between police and the Roma community, Romani 
groups indicate that police harassment and abuse continues to be routine , and reports of ethnic 
profiling of Roma continue.27 Therefore, I find that the Appellants would not have adequate state 
protection in Romania.  
[24]  Similarly, the country conditions evidence shows that the situation for Roma is the same 
across Romania, and , therefore, there is no viable internal flight alternative for the Appellants.

1 Reasons for Decision  
 
[1] The claimants,  XXXX XXXX XXXX  and his daughter, XXXXXXXXXXXXXX , are 
citizens of Djibouti. They are claiming refugee protection under section  96 and subsection  97(1) of 
the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).  
 
ALL EGATIONS  
[2] The allega tions in support of this claim are found in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) 
filed by the principal claiman t (PC),  Mr. XXXX  (the PC), and the forms and attachments that they 
submitted with their refugee protection claims. The co-claimant  is asking the panel to refer to the 
PC’s account for her claim. The alleged facts can be summarized as follows.  
[3] The XX and his daughter are citizens of Djibouti and members of the XXXXXXXXXXXXX  tribe . 
They fear political pers ecution . They left their country on XXXX XXXX XXXX  2016 , and arrived 
in the United  States on XXXX XXXX XXXX  2016 ; they then travelled to Canada on the 13th of 
that month and claimed refugee protection.  
[4] He claim ed that he fears the Djiboutian authorities because of his support for the 
opposition , [translation]  “more specifically, the USN party. I supported the opposition by, among 
other things, lending a bus to protestors for their demonstrat ions , as well as through financial 
support,” as he state d in his account . 
[5] In 2012, the police searched his business and his home and took four  computers and some 
invoices. The  police accused him of funding the parti renouveau démocratique [democratic 
renewal party], known as the USN. He received a summons  to appear on XXXX XXXX , 2012, 
and he was arrested, detained and tortured for XXXX  days.  
[6] Upon leaving prison , he went to the hos pital  and tried to receive compen sation for the harm 
he suffered by contacting members of parliament. He asked that his computers be returned to him, 
but he receive d no answer. He learned that he was not allowed to leave the country when he tried 
to go to Ethiopia to visit relatives. The authorities eventually allowed him to travel between the 
two  countries, but he had to undergo additional examinations when he travelled. He allege d that 
the police continu ed to harass his businesses .

DETERMINATION  
[10]  The claimants are not “Conventi on refugees” or persons in need of protection under 
sections  96 o r 97 of the Act .  
 
IDENTIT Y

US visas in their passports ( Exhibit  A-1). 
[12]  Their respective identities were established af ter their documents and the various forms 
submitted as part of their claim were verified in their presence.

highly vulnerable and fr agile. He may have difficulty answering detailed questions about his past 
as he complains of memory and concentration difficulties and episodic confusion. These symptoms 
are common in persons suffering from XXXX  and XXXX  failure.”

ANALYS IS 
[16]  The determinative factor in this refugee protection claim is the credibility  of the claimants’ 
account . 
[17]  The two  key witnesses contradicted each other on fundamental aspects at the hear t of the 
refugee protection claim : when they learned  that the principal claimant was on a list of people 
being targeted by the country’s authorities.  
[18]  A narrative attached to a BOC Form cannot be concocted  by people who are not in the 
claimant’s country and who are far from where the incidents took place. Th e BOC Form and the 
narrative must establish, as faithfully as possible, the story as told by the claimant or credible 
witnesses. It is only in the absence of a witness and in exceptional circ umstances that the panel 
must accept an account written by someon e else in place of one from the person concerned .  
[19]  The claimants did not establish a serious possibility of persecution in Djibouti on a 
Convention ground . 
 
CREDIBILITY

refugee protection claim : when they learned that the principal claimant was on a list of people 
being targeted by the country’s authorities .

4 [21]  The principal claimant testified in a laconic manner . He often stated that he had forgotten 
certain informa tion indicated in his narrative. The panel wonders how, if this claimant really has 
memory problems, he could have written a seven -page narrative containing so many specific facts . 
[22]  The PC’s BOC  Form and narrative, on which the co-claimant ’s claim  is based , give rise to 
many questions as to their reliability. It appears from the evidence that the account in them was 
written by the PC’s family members, who live in different countries and did not witness the alleged 
facts .  
[23]  The panel questioned the co-claimant  further  and grants considerable probative value to her 
testimony. For one thing, according to the evidence, the co-claimant  is 27 years old, she went to 
school for  11 years, and she was living with her father in that  country. For another, she stated that 
she witnessed the 2012 incident and that she was aware of her father’s political problems .  
[24]  Regarding the witness,  XXXX XXXX XXXX , he has lived in C anada since 2010 , and he 
travelled to Djibouti in XXXX  or XXXX  2015, according to his testimony. He did not witness any 
of the alleged inci dents , and he stated that he often spoke to another sister who lives in that  
country. The panel does not find his testimony credible because he did not witness the events, and 
because hi s testimony was vague and contained serious contra diction s on two  key aspects: the 
writing of the narrative  attached to the BOC  Form in this claim, and when he learned about the list 
of people being targeted by the authorities, including the PC.  
[25]  Finally, the panel concludes that the PC  and the co-claimant  did not behave like people

8 [49]  The witness spoke only about one  list. He alleged that he frequently spoke to his family in

[67]  About the BOC Form, the panel notes th at the co-claimant  is 27  years and is an adult. She  
has 11  years of education, and she stated that she completed her forms in French and that she had

11 Ethnic p ers ecution  
[73]  According to the evidence, the principal claimant frequently went to E thiopi a and returned 
to h is country each time. When asked about this, he stated that the Ethiopian authorities have 
agreements to arrest fugitives from Djibouti. The panel does not believe that the principal claimant 
fears persecution in his country. If that were the case, he would not have made so many trips 
abroad an d returned to Djibouti each time . 
[74]  The PC  alleges that he fears pers ecution by reason of his membership in the Yonis  Moussa  
tribe, which is known for its opposi tion to the current regime. Yet, the male claimant stated that he 
fears the authorities only by reason of his membership in the opposition and because he was 
accused in 2012 of trading in XXXX , a substance that he could not describe for the panel. He 
stated that t he authorities said that XXXX  is used to make [translation]  “atom ic bombs.”  
[75]  The evidence does not establish that the claimants were persecuted or would be in the 
future by reason of their ethnicity . 
 
CONCLUSION  
[76]  Based on the above, the panel believes that t he PC was arrested in 2012 because of his 
membership in the opposition party. In 2013 , the p olice seized his truck, and he received fine s for 
various offences relating to his transport company. This is not political persecution . 
[77]  The evidence does not enabl e the panel to conclude that the principal claimant or his 
daughter were persecuted by reason of their ethnicity or their political opinion . 
[78]  Given all the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimants did not establish a serious 
possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would 
be personally subjected to a danger of  torture, a risk to their lives, or a risk of cruel and unusual 
treatment or punishment should they return to Djibouti.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  (the Appellant), a citizen of Ecuador , appeals a decision of 
the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.  He has 
submitted no new evidence in support of his appeal. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal 
Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the RPD and  to substitute that decision with a finding 
that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, 
the Appellant asks that the matter be sent back to the RPD for re -determination by a different 
panel.  
DETERMINATIO N 
[2]  Pursuant to Section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA), 
the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the 
Appellant  is a Convention refugee . 
Background  
[3] The A ppellant alleged before the  RPD that he is a gay man and fears discrimination and 
worse in Ecuador, due to the masculine and machismo culture of the country. The XXXXXXXXX’s 
family are staunch Christians who believe that homosexuality is immoral, criminal, and contrary 
to the cultur e of Ecuador.  
[4] The XXXXXXXXX hid his sexual orientation, but one day in 2014 was seen by two co -
workers when the XXXXXXXXX kissed his same sex friend. The XXXXXXXXX was beaten and 
threatened by the co -workers. The Appellant did not report the beating to his employers or to the 
police because he feared having his lifestyle exposed even further.  
[5] The Appellant applied to Canada for a visa which was issued on December 4, 2014 and a 
short time later, the Appellant received the visa (on December 22, 2014). On XXXX XXXX , 
2015, he flew to Canada. On February 27, 2015 the Appellant applied for protection at an inland 
office.

ANALYSIS  
Role of the RAD  
[7] The RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision, in Huruglica ,1 provides the RAD 
with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized 
tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first -level administrative tribunal. Justice XXXXXX 
states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision:  
 [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD’s decision on 
the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons 
above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects 
of the RPD’s decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the 
claimant is a Conventi on refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its 
assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own 
decision.  
[55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of 
the RPD on such issues as credibil ity and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular 
advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate 
court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an “overriding and palpable 
error.”  
[8] Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its o wn assessment of the RPD’s decision and come 
to an independent assessment of whether the XXXXXXXXX is a Convention refugee or a person in 
need of protection. The RAD will recognize and respect the credibility findings of the RPD or to 
other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions.  
The RPD’s Findings  
[9] The Appellant argues that the documentary evidence which was before the RPD 
establishes that, for homosexuals in Ecuador, such as the Appellant, the level of state protectio n

[22]  The RPD did not find that the XXXXXXXXX was not a homosexual, but only that he failed to 
seek state protection and ther efore failed to rebut the existence of adequate state protection. 
Given the evidence on file in support of the Appellant's sexual orientation, the RAD therefore 
accepts that the XXXXXXXXX is in fact a homosexual man from Ecuador and must make a decision 
based on that fact.  
[23]  Much of the documentary evidence is contradictory. In one item,15 the RAD reads that the 
state has closed down as many as 18 of the clinics which are violating the law regarding the 
mistreatment of homosexuals. In another document,16 the RA D reads that scores of these clinics 
continue to operate with impunity throughout Ecuador. Yet another document tells of how a 
candidate for President is punished by the electoral system for making disparaging remarks about 
LGBT people.17 
[24]  The most telling d ocument18 the RAD has read —which stands out amongst the others —
was quoted by the Appellant in his Memorandum and is taken from the Board's own National 
Documentation Package.19 The statistical fact that 71% of those interviewed —in what amounts 
to a statistic ally accurate sampling of 2,805 members of the LGBT community —have

 experienced some sort of discrimination, including family rejection and violence, 44 % had faced 
discrimination in the workplace, 40% in education and 34% in health care. Further, 66% have 
reported violence against them when dealing with the public. These figures speak loudly to the 
Appellant's statement of the machismo mentality in Ecuador.  
[25]  The Appellant is a member of a particular social group as a homosexual and therefore has 
a nexus to the Convention.  
[26]  As the  I.R.P.A. specifies that the Appellant must have a nexus to one of the Convention 
grounds in order to be considered under section 96) of the IRPA and then also have a well -
founded fear, it remains only for him to rebut the existence of state protection. The Act states:  
96. A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well -founded fear of 
persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular 
social group or political opinion,  
(a) is outside each of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reason of 
that fear, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of each of those countries; 
or 
(b) not having a country of nationality, is outside the country of their former 
habitual residence and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to return to 
that country.  
[27]  The test is whether or not there is more than a mere possibility that the person will face 
persecution should he return to his home country. The test is not "on a balance of probabilit y" 
which is a far greater burden to prove. In this case, the RAD finds that there is more than a mere 
possibility that the Appellant would face persecution in Ecuador should he return and try to live 
openly as a gay man.  
[28]  The panel made reasonable inferenc es from the documents and came to its independent 
decision. The RAD does not find that the panel necessarily erred in making the conclusion that it 
made; however, the RAD disagrees with that conclusion after conducting its own analysis of the 
evidence. For  that reason, the RPD decision will not stand.

REASONS FOR DECISION  
INTRODUCTION  
[1] XXXXXXXXX , a citizen of Haiti, is appealing the decision rendered by the Refugee 
Protection Division  (RPD) on September  29, 2019, rejecting her claim for refugee protection 
under sections  96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA).  
[2] The RPD concluded that the appellant i s excluded from Canada’s protection under Article  1E 
of the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees  and section  98 of the IRPA. The appellant 
submits that the RPD erred when it analyzed the rights associated with  permanent resident status in 
Brazil a nd the risk she will face in both Brazil and Haiti. The appellant is asking the Refugee Appeal 
Division  (RAD) to allow the appeal or refer the matter to the RPD for re -determination.  
OVERVIEW  
[3] The appellant alleged that she is at risk in Haiti by reason of her political activities.  
[4] In XXXX  2010, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX supporters broke into her home i n search of her husband 
and brother. Her husband was a supporter of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  and led  a group in his neighbourhood 
in Gonaïves that had supported her  candidacy in the 2010 elections. The appellant and her brother 
had helped him with his activities.  
[5] Following the event in XXXX  2010, the appellant fled to a friend’s home. She left Haiti and 
went to Brazil on XXXX XXXX , 2011. She obtained permanent residence  in Braz il. 
[6] The appellant alleged that she worked without pay for three months for her employer, who 
also apparently threatened her with a gun in XXXX  2015. She left Brazil and went to the United 
States on XXXX XXXX XXXX  2016. She then came to Canada to claim refugee protection on 
July  26, 2017.

 DETERMINATION  
[7] After conducting an independent analysis of all of the evidence on the record, including the 
recording of the hearing, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err when it concluded that the 
appellant is excluded from Canada’s protection.  
[8] The appeal is dismissed.  
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION  
[9] The RAD is required to conduct its own analysis of the evidence in light of the arguments 
put forward by the appellant in order to assess whether the RPD acted correctly with respect to 
each alleged error of law, error of fact or error of mixed fact and law. While the RAD may show 
deference to the RPD’s assessment in some exceptional cases, the applicable standard of review 
in this case is the correctness standar d.1 
ANALYSIS  
Exclusion  
[10]  The RAD disclosed the most recent national documentation packages  on Brazil and Haiti 
to the appellant from September  1, 2020, giving  her the opportunity to provide additional 
observations before November  4, 2020. To date , the appellant has not submitted a response.  
     Rights attach ed to permanent resident status  
[11]  The appellan t argues  that her status as a permanent resident in Brazil was not substantially 
similar to that of Brazilians with regard to employment.  
[12]  According to the documentary evidence, permanent residents of Brazil have the same rights 
as Brazilians. In this respect, the Brazilian Constitution  states that:  
Art.  5. All persons are equal before the law; without any distinction whatsoever, 
Brazilians a nd foreigners residing in the country being ensured of inviolability of 
the right to life, to liberty, to equality and to property …

 Art.  6. Education, health, work, leisure, security, social security, protection of 
motherhood and childhood, and assistance  to the destitute, are social rights, as set 
forth by this Constitution (ibid.  1988).2 
[13]  The documentary evidence shows that Brazil adopted laws prohibiting racism and 
discrimination based on skin colour and nationality, and that guarantee non -discriminatory  access to 
work, housing, education and the other rights and freedoms set forth by  their constitution.3  
[14]  It also states that measures have been put in place at the federal and local levels to strengthen 
access to these rights, such as a federal secretariat  for human rights, an ombudsman and a national 
assistance line to report humans rights violations,4 which are “reviewed, treated and forwarded to 
the responsible bodies.”5 
[15]  Based on the objective evidence, I am of the opinion that the laws in Brazil provide  permanent 
residents with rights that are substantially similar to those of Brazilian citizens. These rights are 
granted to permanent residents based on their status, not o n their origin  or race.  
[16]  According to the appellant, [transl ation]  “although the Brazilian c onstitution grants 
Brazilians and foreigners the same employment rights, in reality, there is an enormous difference. 
A right that is not protected in practice is of no benefit  to the individual who consequently does 
not enjoy it.”6 
[17]   This argume nt relates to  the protection and respect of the appellant’s rights in practice, which 
I will address below.  
     Prospective risk in Brazil  
[18]  The appellant cited the documentary evidence, which states that: “the permanent resident, 
even if highly qualified,  is in reality a temporary resident who may only do his/her job in the 
company which he/she was hired to work for, at least during the first mandate.”7  
[19]  I note that this passage has been taken out of context, as the conditions cited therein are not 
aimed a t those who have obtained permanent resident status but rather at holders of a “permanent 
visa,” which is valid for a period of five years. Furthermore, the concept of a “permanent visa” no

Permanent residents have the same rights as citizens with regard to private -sector employment.9  
[20]  The appellant cited the following passage in support of the argument that Haitians’ rights 
are not protected like those of Brazilians:  
According to another documentary source, in 2016, out of a total of 39,961 foreign 
nationals, 18,742 Haitian nationals were hired, and out of a total of 50,810 foreign 
nationals, 26,466 Haitian nationals were dismissed; in 2015, out of a total of 56,678 
fore ign nationals, 29,737 Haitian nationals were hired, and out of a total of 48,934 
foreign nationals, 22,176 Haitian nationals were dismissed.10  
[21]  In my opinion, the statistics cited by the appellant in no way establish that Haitians’ rights 
are not protected like those of Brazilians. All that can be understood from these statistics is that 
Haitians make up a significant part of the foreign workforce in Brazil. It can also be noted that 
many Haitian workers were dismissed in 2016 and 2015. However, no informati on is provided 
about  the cause of these dismissals.  
[22]  The appellant refers to the same source to point out that most Haitians only have casu al, 
odd jobs despite being well educated and that Brazilians are paid three times as much for doing 
the same job.11  
[23]  It is true that the documentary evidence refers to  discrimination against the Afro -Brazilian 
population in every aspect of society and reports of incidents involving discrimination and violence 
against immigrants, including Haitians.12 Difficulties related to the quality of the jobs available to 
Haitians include discrimination, not speaking Portuguese, lack of legal status in the country and the 
economic crisis that Brazil has faced since 2016. The Ministry of Labour and Employment refe rred 
to extremely precarious work conditions that could be called slavery, but there are no statistics on 
this matter.13  
[24]  I note that the appellant has held three jobs in Brazil since her arrival to the country. For 
example , in her IMM5669  form,14 she states that she worked at a XXXX  and a XXXX  in Brazil 
from 2011 to XXXX  2016. She did not allege that she had experienced any problems in relation to 
these jobs. The harm she suffered in Brazil was related to her last job in construction. According to  
the appellant, she worked in very difficult conditions and her employer did not pay her for XXXX

 months. When she asked for payment, he pointed a gun and threatened to kill her, which forced her 
to leave the country.  
[25]  I agree with the RPD that this inciden t, although very alarming, is actually an isolated case. 
The appellant did not allege that she had experienced other problems in Brazil during the five years 
she lived there.  
[26]  In addition, the appellant failed to establish that she could  not live in anothe r region of Brazil 
without facing a risk from her former employer. Nor did she  establish that she could not find a new 
job in Brazil. As the RPD noted, other than the single telephone call the appellant made to the police, 
she did not attempt to exhaust al l of the recourses available to her to obtain protection from the 
Brazilian authorities.  
[27]  Contrary to the appellant’s arguments,15 I am of the opinion that neither the documentary 
evidence nor the event described by the appellant establish that there are su stained or systemic 
violations of Haitians’ fundamental human rights in Brazil which amount to persecution.  
[28]  Consequently, the appellant failed to establish a prospective risk in Brazil within the meaning 
of section  96 of the IRPA by reason of her race or nationality. She also failed to establish, on a 
balance of probabilities, that she would be subject to a risk to her life, to a danger of torture or to a 
risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment within the meaning of section  97 of the IRPA if 
she were to return to Brazil.  
[29]  In short, I agree with the RPD that the appellant’s departure from Brazil and relinquishment 
of her permanent resident status cannot be characterized as involuntary. This weighs in favour of 
exclusion.  
     The prospective risk in  Haiti  
[30]  The RPD concluded that the appellant failed to credibly establish her allegations 
concerning the events in Haiti.  
[31]  The appellant argues that the RPD conducted an examination that was confusing, 
repetitive, microscopic , biased and misleading by subjecting her to misleading descriptions of the 
evidence.  She submits  that she responded to all relevant questions from the RPD and made no

 omissions with regard to the important aspects of her claim.  The RPD asked about facts and details 
that were not re quested in the Basis of Claim  Form but that constitute general, contextual 
information. As such, the non -credibility findings are based on secondary details.16 
[32]  First and foremost, I am of the opinion that the appellant’s arguments concerning the 
member’s ex amination are unfounded. Members are afforded wide latitude with regard to their 
questions so that they are able to establish the facts of a case. Although the member’s questions 
were repetitive at some points, I note that this was necessary given that the  appellant gave vague, 
confusing testimony at times. Be that as it may , I cannot conclude that the member conducted an 
examination that was misleading, biased, confusing or microscopic .  
[33]  The RPD identified the following issues with respect to the appellant ’s credibility:  
 Lack of knowledge regarding the date of the presidential elections in 2010;  
 The fact that the appellant did not vote in the elections and did not know whether her 
husband had voted;  
 The lack of corroborating evidence establishing their involvement in 
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX’s party or that they had worked on her electoral campaign;  
 The contradiction concerning the date the criminals broke into her home, as the 
appellant stated at the hearing that it had been before the elections, whereas the 
evidence shows that it took place after the elections;  
 The contradiction concerning the date and circumstances of the death of her brother 
XXXX , who was also being pursued for his political activities; and  
 The RPD also did not believe the appellant about  the fire at her house.  
[34]   Contrary to the appellant’s arguments, I am of the opinion that the issues raised above are 
significant enough to undermine her credibility with regard to the events in Haiti.  
[35]  It should be noted that the appellant bears the burden of establishing her allegations, on a 
balance of probabilities.  
[36]  The appellant alleged a risk of persecution by reason of the political activities of her 
husband, who was apparently the head of the group that supported the candidate XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX 
in their n eighbourhood. She alleged that the party paid her husband to put up posters in their

in [translation]  “mobilization” for the same party and had helped her husb and with his role.  
[37]  However, the appellant was not able to state when the elections had taken place, whether 
there had been several rounds of elections or whether her husband had voted, nor was she able to 
provide any other details on the election process.  In my opinion, these elements are important in 
order to be able to establish the political profiles of the appellant and her husband and their 
involvement in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX election campaign. Contrary to the appellant’s argument, these

[38]  I also consider it problematic that the appellant stated that the attack at her home had taken 
place prior to the elections yet also stated that she does not know when t he elections took place. 
This further undermines her credibility.  
[39]  In addition , I am of the  opinion that her brother’s death is a central element of the 
appellant’s prospective risk in Haiti. She stated that her brother had been killed by the same 
assailant s because he had also helped them to put up XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX posters.        
[40]  However, I agree with the RPD that the appellant was unable to satisfactorily explain why 
she stated at the hearing that her brother had been found dead in the hospital in 2014.  According 
to her written account, her brother had allegedly been found XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  and 
according to the sequence of events, this had happened before she left Haiti in 2011.  
[41]  When confronted on this inconsistency, the appellant simply responded tha t her brother is 
dead [translation]  “because he went to get me when I left in 2010.” When asked why she did not 
provide a copy of the death certificate in support of her refugee protection claim if her brother had 
died at the hospital, the appellant respon ded that she had not asked for one. In my opinion, the 
RPD did not err in finding that this further undermines the appellant’s credibility.  
[42]  I also note that the appellant did not attempt to provide any corroborating evidence before 
the RPD or the RAD, despite the credibility issues that were raised. I consider it reasonable to 
expect the appellant to provide evidence from XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX pa rty concerning their 
involvement with the said party, especially if her husband had been paid to help with the electoral 
campaign.

 [43]  With regard to the fire at her house at the end of XXXX  2011, the appellant testified that 
Haitians who had arrived in Brazil  told her that her house had been burned down. However, the 
appellant stated that she does not know the names of these people even though they were her 
neighbours in Haiti. The appellant also allegedly forgot to ask them any information about their 
identit ies, despite the fact that the concerned individuals had located her in Brazil and had given 
her such important information. I consider the appellant’s allegations extremely vague and 
consequently give them no probative value.  
[44]  I also note that the appellan t did not  provide any corroborating evidence from the alleged 
witnesses of the fire. Nor did she attempt to provide evidence in support of her allegations from 
the landlord who rented them the house that had allegedly burned down in Haiti.  
[45]  Therefore, for t he above reasons, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err when it 
concluded that the appellant failed to credibly establish her allegations concerning the events in 
Haiti.  
[46]  Furthermore, in my opinion, the appellant also failed to establish that her li fe would be at 
risk if she had to return to Haiti today. If in fact she was  involved in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX party, her 
involvement was minimal and took place in the context of an electoral campaign. The appellant 
and her husband left Haiti more than nine ye ars ago. Neither the documentary evidence nor the 
appellant’s evidence supports the conclusion that there was any interest in them following their 
departure or that their political activities in 2010 could put the appellant at risk today.  
[47]  For all of these  reasons, I conclude that the appellant failed to establish a serious possibility 
of persecution in Haiti by reaso n of her political involvement.  
[48]  I also agree with  the RPD that the appellant failed to establish a serious possibility of 
persecution by reaso n of being a woman. The appellant did not challenge this conclusion, which I 
consider to be correct.  
[49]  Furthermore, no prospective risk was established under section  97 of the IRPA.  
[50]  That weighs in favour of exclusion.

      Whether she can return to Brazil  
[51]   The appellant alleged that, contrary to what is required in Zeng ,17 the RPD neglected  to 
analyze a determinative factor, namely, whether she can return to Brazil.  
[52]  It is true that the RPD failed to analyze this factor; however, that error is not determinati ve 
in this case. Although the appellant argued that she does not have the right to return to Brazil 
according to the documentary evidence,18 that is not the only factor to consider when conducting 
an exclusion analysis.  
[53]  As explained above, the appellant voluntarily lost her permanent resident status in Brazil 
and cannot return there. However, she failed to establish a prospective risk in Haiti. Therefore, I 
conclude that Canada will have complied with its international obligations with respec t to 
non -refo ulement should the appellant return to her country of origin. As a whole and in light of 
the factors established in XXXX , these conclusions weigh in favour of exclusion.  
[54]  In my opinion, the RPD was correct in concluding that the appellant is excluded from 
Canada’s protection under Article  1E of the Convention and section  98 of the IRPA.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are th e reasons and decision of the Immigration Appeal Division in the appeal by 
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the “appellant”) from a determination made against her on 21 June 
2011 .  The appellant was found to have failed to comply with the residency obligation 
require ments of section 28 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act . 
 
[2] The appellant was represented at this hearing by her niece, Ms. XXXXX, who served as an 
unpaid representative .  The appellant testified through the use of an interpreter .  The appellant’s 
testimony was overall credible, clear and consistent with the documentary evidence.  
 
[3] At the time of the determination made by an Immigration Officer at the Canadian 
Consulate in Buffalo on 21 June 2011, the appellant was found to have zero days of residenc y in 
Canada .  The appellant conceded that she is in breach of the residency requirement and has not 
met her residency obligation under section 28  of the  Immigration and Refugee Protection Act .  
The officer’s determination is valid in law.  
 
[4] At this appeal the appellant testified that she became a permanent resident of Canada on 
29 March 1976, but that her mother returned to Colombia with the appellant  while the appellant 
was a young teen .  The appellant settled in Colombia, married, had two daughters, and is well -
established financially and socially in that country as her husband is employed as a doctor and 
she herself is a painter .  The appellant and her husband travel internationally on a regular basis.  
 
[5] The appellant did not endeavour to return to Canada until 1997, and then only as a visitor, 
for the purpose of introducing her husband and children to her sisters in Canada .  The appellant 
was in fact  issued a visitor visa at that time and visited her family in Canada for just over 20 
days, returning to Colombia thereafter .  When applying for this visitor visa in 1997 a visa officer 
at the Canadian Embassy took the appellant’s Record of Landing documen t and did not return it 
to her .  At that time, despite the issuance of a visitor visa to the appellant, her Permanent 
Residence status was not relinquished.
