[6] At this hearing, the appellant’s testimony about whether she relinquished her permanent 
residence in 1997 was confus ing, and with good reason:  the appellant’s experience in 1997, the 
withholding of her Record of Landing and the issuance of a visitor visa, all suggest that she was 
no longer a Permanent Resident thereafter .  The fact of this appeal, how ever, confirms she 
remained a Permanent Resident .  Why the appellant was never clearly given the opportunity to 
relinquish her Permanent Resident status is unclear, although it appears this may have occurred, 
though without finality, in 1997 .  In any event , the appellant’s subsequent visitor visa 
applications were refused, and although financial matters may be an issue, the fact of this appeal 
establishes that that the appellant’s Permanent Residence status was clearly still a concern.  
 
[7] The appellant has tw o sisters and their families in Canada .  By contrast, in Colombia the 
appellant has her spouse, daughters, granddaughter, as well as three brothers, three sisters and 
their respective families .  The appellant possesses no assets or property in Canada .  In Colombia, 
the appellant ’s family own an apartment valued at over 360 million Colombian pesos  and a car.  
 
[8] The appellant’s daughter entered Canada and claimed refugee status in the past but 
voluntarily returned to C olombia following the refusal of her claim .  The appellant’s own 
immigration history establishes that she has no interest in remaining in Canada permanently, but 
rather, that she wishes to enter Canada as a visitor .  She has entered Canada as a visitor in 1997 
for a period of just over 20 days, ret urning to Colombia thereafter .  As noted, t he appellant is 
well established socially and financially in Colombia ; she also possesses the funds and ability to 
travel internationally often, with her spouse, returning to her home country of Colombia 
following  her trips abroad.  
 
[9] The appellant testified that she had no interest in residing in Canada as a permanent 
resident .  Rather, she merely wishes to be able to visit her sisters and their families in Canada .  
One of the appellant’s nieces in Canada suffers fr om cancer and being prohibited from seeing her 
niece in light of these medical concerns has caused the appellant hardship .  The panel hopes that 
the dismissal of this appeal will facilitate a Canadian visitor visa application that will be 
unencumbered by t he appellant’s Permanent Resident status.

[10]  There is no evidence of any undue hardship that the appellant would face by losing her 
Canadian Permanent Residence status; to the contrary, the appellant’s testimony established that 
she wished to have this statu s finally disposed of so that she may be able to apply for Canadian 
visitor status, which is the only type of status she is interested in attaining in Canada at this time.  
There are no minor children whose best interests would be impacted by this decision . 
 
[11]  For all of the above reasons, the appeal is dismissed.

The appeal is dismissed .

 ANALYSIS  
 
[10]  The applicant was born in 1992. The appellant became a permanent resident in 2005. He 
acknowledges that he did not declare the applicant at the time of h is own application for 
permanent residence. As a result she was not examined.  
 
[11]  The appellant claims that he and the applicant’s mother parted ways before they knew she 
was pregnant. The applicant’s mother died in 2003. The appellant reportedly did not lea rn of his 
daughter’s existence until August 6, 2011. Their relationship was confirmed by DNA testing. 
The appellant began to support the applicant.  
 
[12]  At the time of the appellant’s application for permanent residence the applicant was not 
disclosed. The app ellant’s explanation is that at the time he was unaware of the applicant’s 
existence. These circumstances are similar to the facts addressed by the Federal Court in Adjani .3 
In Adjani,  Mr. Justice XXXXXXXXX found:  
 
[31]  In my view the impugned provision do es not allow for such an 
interpretation. The language is clear and unambiguous, subjective knowledge of 
the misrepresentation or non -disclosure is not contemplated in the regulation. The 
Court of Appeal in Azizi , above, at paragraph 28 of its reasons, inte rpreted the 
provision as follows: “It simply provides that non -accompanying family members 
who have not been examined for a reason other than a decision by a visa officer  
will not be admitted as members of the family class.” (My emphasis) This 
interpretati on is consistent with decisions of the Federal Court. As stated above, in 
XXXX  at paragraph 11, the motive is unimportant, a failure to disclose which 
prevents examination of the dependent precludes future sponsorship of that person 
as a member of the fami ly class. See also Jean -Jacques v. M.C.I ., 2005 FC 104 at 
paragraph 9.  
 
[32]  In my view, the meaning, scope, purpose and application of the impugned 
regulation have been comprehensively dealt with in the jurisprudence.  The scope 
of the regulation is not l imited to deliberate or fraudulent non -disclosure but to 
any non -disclosure which may prevent examination of a dependent. Non -
disclosed, non -accompanying family members cannot be admitted as members of 
the family class.

 [13]  I am bound by the decision of Mr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in Adjani . At the time of the 
appellant’s application for permanent residence the applicant was not examined, nor even 
disclosed. The explanation for the non -disclosure does not overcome the requirement for 
examination in paragraph  117(9)( d) of the Regulations . The applicant cannot be admitted as a 
member of the family class.  
 
[14]  The respondent submitted that the appeal should also be dismissed because the applicant 
does not meet the definition of dependent child in that she was overage at the  time of application. 
The application was “locked -in” on August 22, 2014. The applicant turned 19 years of age on 
December 8, 2011. The appellant provided money transfer receipts as proof of financial support. 
Some of those receipts pre -date the applicant turning 19 years,4 including as early as January 12, 
2011, seven months before the appellant reportedly learned of the applicant’s existence. In any 
case, those money transfers are addressed to the appellant’s mother, not the applicant. There was 
no other proof of financial support before the applicant turned 19 years of age.  
 
[15]  On October 29, 2014, the visa office gave written notice to the appellant that the 
applicant did not meet the definition of dependent child. The visa officer’s notes set out their 
ana lysis of the facts related to that ground of refusal. However, that ground of refusal was not 
cited in the final refusal letter. The IAD letter of February 16, 2015, did not request submissions 
on that issue, and appellant’s counsel did not provide any.  
 
[16]  Appellant’s counsel attached a written submission to the Notice of Appeal. In that 
submission c ounsel acknowledged that paragraph  117(9)(d) of the Regulations  may apply, and 
requested special relief on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Parliament has not granted 
the IAD the ability to consider humanitarian and compassionate factors in these types of cases. 
Section 65 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act 5 states:  
In an appeal under subsection 63(1) or (2) respecting an application based on 
mem bership in the family class, the Immigration Appeal Division may not 
consider humanitarian and compassionate considerations unless it has decided

Court decision in XXXX . The Court found:  
Once the IAD determines that the foreign national is a non -family member (or the 
sponsor is not a defined sponsor), that ends its jurisdiction in respect of any claim

DETERMINATION

(“IRPA”),  the appeal is dismissed. On an independent assessment, I agree with the RPD that the 
Appellant’s allegations lack credibility. The Refugee Appeal Division (“RAD”) therefore 
confirms the RPD’s negative determination.

 Role of the Refugee Appeal Division  
[7] The jurisprudence establishe s that the RAD is required to undertake an independent 
assessment of the evidence and reach its own determination. Deference is owed to the RPD only 
where the RPD held a meaningful advantage in assessing evidence.1 
[8] In the present case, I see no reason to s how deference to any of the RPD’s findings. I 
have applied a correctness standard and arrived at my own independent findings based on the 
evidence before me.  
Admissibility of New Evidence and Request for an Oral Hearing  
[9] The Appellant submits a number of documents as new evidence. Those include:  
 An affidavit from her daughter, Ms. XXXX2 
 Medical documents and birth certificate relating to Ms. XXXX  reasons for failing to 
appear as a witness at her mother’s RPD hearing3 
 A le gal opinion concerning the reliability of the affidavits from Nigeria that were 
provided by the Appellant in support of her claim4 
[10]  The affidavit from Ms. XXXX , the medical documents, and the birth certificate are all 
inadmissible, however the legal opinion  has been admitted as new evidence.  
[11]  The IRPA  limits the ability of appellants to present new evidence on appeal to the RAD. 
Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA  states that, on appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal 
may present only evidence that ar ose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably 
available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to 
have presented, at the time of the claim’s rejection. If the new evidence meets the requirements  
of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA , the RAD must then consider factors around the credibility, 
relevance, and newness of the evidence .5 
[12]  The affidavit from Ms. XXXX is not admissible. Although I accept Ms. 
XXXX explanation for her inability to appear at her mo ther’s hearing as a witness, I note that Ms.

 Background

Analysis

REASONS FOR DECISION  
INTRODUCTION  
[1] This is an appeal by the appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, from a removal orde r dated 
September 4, 2012 issued against him by a Member of the Immigration Division who found him 
inadmissible pursuant to section 36(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 
(IRPA) . The appellant has been convicted of aggravated assault contr ary to section 268 of the 
Criminal Code of Canada ,2 which carries a maximum sentence of fourteen years imprisonment . 
The appeal is based on section 63(3) of the IRPA . 
BACKGROUND  
[2] The appellant was born in Guyana and is 29 years old.  He is single and has bee n in 
Canada as a permanent resident since October 25, 2005 at the age of 20.  
[3] Upon conviction for aggravated assault the appellant was sentenced on April 5, 2011 to 9 
months and one week pre -sentence custody (attracting a credit of 1.5 to 1 days served for  a total 
of 14 months) and probation for 2 years, a section 109 prohibition for 10 years and registration of 
his DNA.  
ISSUE AND DECISION  
[4] There was no challenge to the validity of the removal order, which I find is valid in 
law.  Consequently the issue in th is appeal is whether, in accordance with sections 67(1)(c) and 
68(1) of the IRPA , sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special 
relief in light of all  the circumstances of the case.  The appellant has the burden of meeting this 
statutory test.  
[5] For the reasons set out below the appeal is dismissed.

[1] These are the reasons for  a decision rendered under Section 45 of the Immigration and

report alleges that Mr. XXXXXX is a permanent resident of Canada inadmissible to Canada for

XXXXXX is not a Canadian Citizen.

employee of GS Telecom (Nigeria) and therefore did not meet the definition of dep endent child 
under IRPA  and the Regulations ,2 and therefore has engaged in a direct misrepresentation of a 
material fact.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
OVERVIEW  
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  (the Appellant) , a citizen  of Syria , appeal s a decision of 
the Ref ugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his  claim  for refugee protection.  He alleges that 
he will  be detained and tortured  if he returns to Syria because  he has  not  fulfilled his mandatory 
military ser vice . He also fears persecution in Syria as part of the ongoing civil conflict because 
he is a Sunni Muslim.   
[2] For the reasons that follow, I find that the RPD erred by failing to consider the country 
conditions in Syria, mischaracterizing the evidence, and focusing on peripheral issues. I find that 
the Appellant’s allegations are credible on a balan ce of probabilities. Accordingly, I allow the 
appeal and find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.  
BACKGROUND  
[3] From 2007 –2013 , the Appellant  had tem porary residency  status in Qatar . In 2013 , he 
traveled to the United States (US) . He stayed in the US  past the expiration of his visa and  
married  an American  in 2014 . They intended  for her to sponsor him  to become a US citizen. 
However,  they discovered she  had insufficient means to do so  after t he XXXXXXXXX had been in the 
US for more than a year and was no longer eligible to apply for asylum . Therefore,  in 2017, the 
Appellant  decided to come to Canada to make a refugee claim.   
[4] The RPD rejected the XXXXXXXXX’s claim finding that he lacked credibilit y because of his 
delay in seeking asylum , inconsistencies reg arding the date of his marriage , and the omission of 
a return trip to Qatar from the US from his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative.  The XXXXXXXX t 
submits  that the RPD erred by failing to reference country conditions in Syria and by basing its 
decision on an unreasonable analysis of the Appellant’s testimony  and evidence regarding the 
US process for sponsorship.

 DETERMINATION  
[5] The appeal is allowed.  Pursuant to section 111(1)( b) of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Act  (IRPA),  the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own 
determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.  
ANALYSIS  
Role of the RAD  
[6] The RAD  review s RPD decisions on  a standard of correctness. In limited circumstances 
the RPD may have a meaningful advantage over the  RAD in assessing evidence that was before 
the RPD. In those  cases the RAD will show deference to the RPD . In this appeal I  have applied 
the correctness standard  unless stated otherwise.   
Admissibility of New Evidence  
[7] The Appellant submits new evidence in the form of an affidavit from the Appellant dated 
October 19, 2017 , in which he makes statements concerning his Sunni faith, his fear of 
persecution in Syria , and his delay in claiming asylum . The Appellant has  included the following 
documents originating from the Immigration and Refugee Board as supporting exhibits to his 
affidavit : 
- The Expedited Policy – Designation of New Country which states that 
claims from Syria have been designated eligible for processing under this 
policy.1 
- Chairperson Guideline 1: Civilian Non -Combatants Fearing Persecution 
in Civil War Situations (the Civil War Guideline).2  
- National Documentation Package (NDP) fo r Syria versions 31 March 
2017 and 29 September 2017.3 
[8] Counsel argues that the affidavit and exhibits meet the new evidence criteria because they 
contain information responding to speculative RPD findings, which could not reasonably have

Merits of the Appeal  
Credibility and Delay in Claiming Asylum  
[11]  The RPD found that the determinative issue in this case was the Appellant’s behavior and 
that his behavior showed a lack of subjective fear and undermined the credibility of all of his 
allegations regarding the risks of returning to Syria.5 The Appellant alleges that this finding lacks 
objective support an d was incorrect in light of the present conflict in Syria which has included 
the use of chemical weapons and allegations of crimes against humanity. I agree with the

Trip to Qatar  
[12]  When questioned by the RPD, the Appellant testified that he returned to Qatar i n late 
2013. The Appellant stated that he arrived in the US in April 2013 and travelled back to Qatar 
several months later to look for a job. However, his previous sponsor refused to renew his status 
in Qatar so, after approximately 15 days in Qatar, he fo und himself obliged to go back to the US 
before his US visa expired.6 The Appellant claims that he made the trip to Qatar because he had 
a valid US visitor visa, could legally enter Qatar at the time, and that he did not leave the US 
after his visitor visa  expired on April 3, 2014 .7  
[13]  The RPD found that the Appellant should have disclosed all of his travel earlier and 
mentioned this trip to Qatar in his initial refugee claimant interview with the Canada Border 
Services  Agency .8 The Appellant claimed that he did not mention this trip in his interview 
because he thought he had been asked if he had left the US since coming back to the US for the 
last time.9 Whether or not he understood the interviewer’s travel questions , a claimant cannot be 
faulted for not clai ming asylum while in status.  Therefore, I find that the RPD erred when it 
made a negative credibility inference because the Appellant did not claim asylum in the US 
while in the US under a valid visitor visa.  
Marriage  and US spousal sponsorship process

from 2014 –2017 showed a lack of subjective fear and also undermined his credibility.  
[15]  With regard to when the XXXXXXXXX met and married his wife, he claims that any 
incon sistencies were the result of typographical errors which were repeated in the text that had 
been copied. He testified and stated in his affidavit that the couple met around December 2013, 
not December 2014, and married in October 2014. I find that this exp lanation is credible on a

[16]  The courts have held that it is reasonable to expect people fleeing persecution to claim

Furthermore, delay alone cannot undermine the credibility of the Appellant’s subjective fear 
given the ongoing civil war and humanitarian crisis in Syria , which are recognized in the national 
documenta tion and should have been assessed  by the RPD in its reasons.12 
[17]  The Appellant has only a high school education. In his affidavit he states that he initially 
thought he could obtain temporary residency in the US if he was sponsored by an employer, but 
that h is employer did not tell him about the US laws and took no steps to sponsor him. The 
Appellant claims that he was not able to understand the refugee and immigration system in the 
US , or afford to access the system , until important deadlines had passed.  The  Appellant testified 
that in 2014 –2016, he was working illegally in the US and being paid less than minimum wage. 
It took him until early 2015 to save enough money for an immigration lawyer. He testified that 
his lawyer told them he needed a sponsor but th at his wife, who had a young child from a

[18]  The Appellant testified that given their situation, he continued to work illegally in the US 
and sometime  later, a new employer said that he would be a financial guarantor so his wi fe could 
sponsor him. The Appellant submitted the medical examination he completed to start the process 
as corroborating evidence.14 He claims that, at the time , he was earning approximately

Risk of harm in Syria  
[19]  The Civil War Guideline states that the definition of Convention refugee may be applied 
to claimants fearing return to situations of civil war where the harm feared constitutes 
persecution.16 The Guideline also states that when determining whether persecution is based on a 
convention ground , the applicant can show that the fear he had results not from reprehensible 
acts committed or likely to be committed directly against him but from reprehensible acts 
committed , or likely to be committed , against members of a group to which he belongs.17  
[20]  The Appellant submits that he faces subs tantial risks of harm in Syria, which are not 
general consequences of the civil war in Syria, and for which there is no internal flight 
alternative because the risk is throughout the country and the state is the main agent of 
persecution, which are all con siderations under the Guideline. He alleges that he fears return to 
Syria because he has not paid the military service exemption fee and therefore would be detained 
as a deserter upon arrival in Syria. He objects to paying the substantial fee because the m oney 
would go to supporting the current Syrian regime which is killing civilians. Furthermore, he 
claims that there is no guarantee that paying the fee would protect him from having to serve in 
the military because of the ongoing need for soldiers. Finally , the Appellant alleges that he fears 
persecution in Syria by extremist forces and XXXXX forces because he is a Sunni Muslim.

 [21]  The Appellant has submitted an affidavit dated May 24, 2017 from XXXX XXXX , an 
Arabic interpreter and translator. Attached to the  affidavit as exhibits are a copy of the 
Appellant’s Syrian Military Book in Arabic and an English translation of the book.18 The 
document contains a record of postponements the Appellant received for his military service 
while he was in secondary school, d uring his brother’s service, and while he was a resident in 
Qatar.  
[22]  The national documentation indicates that Syrian nationals who try to evade military 
service face imprisonment or forced conscription , and may be seen as treasonous and against the 
regime a nd subjected to torture.19 The UNHCR has noted intensified efforts by the Syrian 
government to recruit reservists and conscripts including a rise in the targeting of certain groups , 
such as religious minorities , and the revocation of service exemptions .20 Based on the 
Appellant’s testimony, documentary evidence , and the objective national documentation , I find 
that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant belongs to the particular social group of young 
men who have been conscripted into the Syrian army . As such, h e faces a serious possibility of 
being persecuted  in the form of imprisonment or torture  by the state for evading military service . 
Accordingly, I find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee under s.  96 of the IRPA.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the rea son s and  dec ision of th e Immi gration Appeal Division (IAD) pertaining

(IRPA),1 by Hassan NAZIL  (Appellant), from the refusal of the sponsorship applicatio n for a 
permanent r esident visa of h is spouse  XXXXXXXXXXXXX  (Applican t), from Fiji . 
 
[2] The application was refused under subsection 4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Regulations  (IRPR).2  The de tails o f the refusal  are set out in the refusal  letter and  
Glo bal Case  Ma nagement Syste m (GCMS)  notes of the immigration officer.3  
 
[3] For the re asons that follow, I am dismissing  this appeal.  
 
 
BACKGROUND  
 
[4] The Appellant is a 36-year -old  Canadian Citizen.   Thi s is his first mar riage.   The 
Applicant is 37 years old.   This is her second marriage  and she also had one previous de facto  
relationship .  She has two children  from previous relationships.  
 
[5] The Appellant and the Applicant w ere married on June 2018.  An application to sponsor  
the Applicant to Canada  was filed in December 2 018.  The Applica nt was invited to an interview 
with  the visa office  in November  2018.   The application  was refused on December 5, 201 9 as the  
visa officer was not satisfied  that the marriage  was genuine and/o r not entered primarily for the 
purpose  of acqu iring status o or  privilege  under the IRPA .    
 
[6] The visa officer identified concerns related to the quick timeline of this relationship,  that 
the couple married without meeting in person, they have spent littl e time together in their whole  
relationship (ab out two months) , the Applicant gave generic reasons why she liked the Appellant

ISSUE  
 
[14]  The issue in this appeal is whether su bsection 4(1)  of the IRPR applies, there by exclu ding 
the Applicant as  a member of the family class. The two tests set out in subsection 4(1 ) of the 
IRPR are that the marriage:

under the Act; or

DECISION  
 
[15]  Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Appella nt has not met  the bur den of 
proof.  I find, on a balance of probabilities, the marriage is not genuine .  The a ppea l is dismissed . 
 
 
ANALYSIS  
 
[16]  There are some well -established and objective f actors that th e IAD h as developed to 
assess whether a marriage is genuine.  Those factors , co nfirmed by the courts ,5 facilita te the task 
of deciding if a relationship falls within t he a mbit of sub section 4( 1) of the IRPR .  XXXXXXXXXXX  
behaviour before and during the  marriage, the evidence of contact, communication  and 
intera ction before and after the marriage, their depth of knowl edge of each ot her, their con tact 
with extended families, their activ ities of d aily life, intermingling  of finances, and shared 
responsibil ity for the care of children brought into the marriage, are all considerations that assist 
evaluating whether a marri age is genuine.  
 
[17]  The second t est articulated in section 4(1)(a) of th e IRPR  – whether the relationship was 
entered into primarily for the p urp ose of acquiring any s tatus or privilege under the IR PA  – is 
self-explanatory. The indications of such intent will  be gleaned fro m examining th e 
circumstances of the marria ge or will be exposed  incidentally while exam inin g the evidence and 
testimony abo ut the genuineness  of the marriage .

Is the  marriage genuine?  
 
[19]  There is insufficient credible, reliable testimony  and documentary evidence  to prove, on  a

[22]  Although I find the GCMS notes to be reliable evidence, I find that a principle of natural

visa officer’s concerns pertaining to the alleged misinformation in the 2006 applications , as the 
procedural fairness letter did not mention the discrepancy in the 2006 applications.  This is a 
breach of natural justice.   Based on  my finding of a breach of natural justice, I find that the 
refusal is not legally valid.  
[23]  Section 67(2) of the Act  requires the Panel to set aside the original decision and substitute 
a determination that , in its opinion , should have been made , or refer  the matter to the appropriate

probabilities that the Applicants’ family composition consists of six children located in Sri

 [1] These are the  reasons in the sponsorship appeal by FoluXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the appellant) from the refusal to approve the permanen t resident visa applications made by Ifeoluwa XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX & ToluwalolXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, (the applicants), from Nigeria.  [2] The applications for permanent resident visas were refused on October 17, 2005 because, pursuant to section 117(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the Regulations), the visa officer at the Canadian High Commission, Accra, Ghana found the applicants did not meet the definition of “a de pendent child of the sponsor.”  Section 117(1)(b) reads,  
117(1) Member — A foreign national is a member of the family class if, with respect to a sponsor, the foreign national is   (b) a dependent child of the sponsor …
 
 [3] "Dependent child" is defined in section 2 of the Regulations to be:   
"dependent Child", in respect of a parent, means a child who  (a) has one of the following relationships with the parent, namely,  (i) is the biological child of the parent, if  the child has not been adopted by a person other than the spouse or common-law partner of the parent,   (b) is in one of the following situations of dependency, namely,   (ii) has depended substantially on the financial support of the parent since before the age of 22 — or if the child became a spouse or common-law partner before the age of 22, since becoming a spouse or common-law partner — and, since before the age of 22 or since becoming a spouse or common-law partner, as the case may be, has been a student   (A) continuously enrolled in and attending a post-secondary institution that is accredited by the relevant government authority, and   (B) actively pursuing a course of academi c, professional or vocational training on a full-time basis 
 [4] Pursuant to section 12(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA), “a foreign national may be selected as a member  of the family class on the basis of their

 relationship as the spouse, common-law partner, child, parent or other prescribed family member of a Canadian citizen or permanent resident.”  [5] Pursuant to section 11(1) of IRPA, in order to be issued a visa to enter Canada “a foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an  officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document shall be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act.”  [6] As the applicants did not meet the definition of dependent children, they were not considered to be a member of the family class and therefore were considered to be inadmissible and the visas to immigrate were refused.  [7] The appellant appeals these refusals.     Decision  [8] For the reasons set out below, the appeal is dismissed.     Substantive Issues  [9] The onus is on the appellant to demonstrat e that on a balance of probabilities the applicants meet the definition of dependent child ren and are therefore not inadmissible; that is, the refusal is not valid in law.  To establish th at the refusals were invalid in law the appellant must meet a three part test.  If the appellant fa ils on any one of the tests the appeal must fail in law.  [10] The onus is on the appellant to demonstrate that on a balance of probabilities that: (1) the applicants were her biological children; (2) that if over the age of 22 years, they had depended

 substantially on the financial support of a parent since before they were the age of 22; and (3) they had been continuously enrolled in an accredited (by a relevant government authority) post- secondary institution actively pursuing a course of  academic, professional or vocational training on a full-time basis.   [11] The panel, in considering appeals under these provisions of IRPA, does not have any discretionary jurisdiction to consider human itarian and compassionate grounds to allow the appeal because the exercise of the panel’s discretionary jurisdiction can only take place after a person or persons have been found to be member s of the family class and who are otherwise deemed inadmissible.   Analysis  [12] The panel heard oral testimony from the appell ant.  The panel considered the Record and documentary evidence disclosed by the appella nt as Exhibits A-1, A-2 and A-3 and the respective submissions of the parties.  [13] While the testimony of the appellant was for th e most part credible, a major evidentiary problem was encountered which was fatal for the appeal.    [14] The appellant testified that she had four child ren, two boys and two girls.  She testified to having come to Canada on a visitor’s visa in  2002 and then applying for Convention refugee status, which she received in September 2004.  The appellant testified that she had sponsored her sons, born in 1984 and 1986.  She subsequently s ponsored her two daughters, the applicants, born in 1981 and 1982.  At the time of the applic ation they were 23 and 24 years old, which is above the age limit for sponsorship unless the applicants could be shown to meet the exception set out in the definition of a dependent child noted above.

 [15] The appellant testified that she had b XXX widowed in December 2000.  The panel considered a death certificate and published obituary attesting to the fact of the death of the appellant’s husband and finds this to be proven.  [16] The appellant testified that since the deat h of her husband her daughters have been dependent upon her, relying on her for financ ial support, including the cost of tuition.    [17] In support of her appeal the appellant proffered numerous documents which purported to attest to various aspects of the validity of claim that her daughters were, from before they were 22 year old, dependent children in full-time educa tion at accredited post-secondary institutions in Nigeria.  According to the appellant, these docum ents originated two ways, either directly from the appellant herself in Canada or from the app licants who obtained them from various sources in Nigeria.  They were submitted either with th e sponsorship application made in Canada or at the time the visa applications were delivered directly to the visa post in Accra, Ghana.  [18] Several documents distinguish themselves.  Fi rst, both applicants swore Affidavits of Loss of Documents on August 17, 2005 attesting to the fact that certain documents, including educational records and the birth certificates, had been lost in July 2005.  Second, the supposedly lost copies of the registrations of birth of the applicants issued August 13, 1981 and February 23, 1983 respectively were, according to the appellant 's testimony, submitted by the appellant with her sponsorship application.  Third, the app licants each apparently submitted a Statutory Declaration of Age issued by the Customary C ourts of Oyo State of Nigeria on August 26, 2005 directly to the visa office to replace the supposedly lost birth registrations.  The later two documents were sworn by an “E.XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX which the appellant had identified was her late husband’s name.  The Statutory Declara tions of Age state respectively that “Miss XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is my Daughter,” and that “OXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is my Daughter.”  Given that the appellant’s husband had been  dead since December 2000, the latter two documents cannot be true.  [19] The appellant testified that she brought all the documents respecting her children with her to Canada.  She testified that she had no invol vement with the production of the Statutory

 Declarations of Age, speculating that "ma ybe my children asked somebody to make these documents."   [20] The panel cannot rely upon the documentary ev idence as confirmatory of the appellant’s testimony because it has a valid reason not to do so.  The issue of the validity of the documents, especially the documents relating to education we re raised by the visa officer as one of the grounds of refusal.  The existence of false documen ts throws the reliability of all the documents into question.  The appellant’s testimony provide s the panel with no reasonable or credible explanation for the existence of false documents.  The Affidavits of Loss of Documents suggest that the Statutory Declarations were created solely for the purpose of bolstering the applications which inevitably leads the panel to the conclusion  that the remaining documents were themselves created simply to bolster the claim of continuing education since before the applicants turned 22 years of age.  The panel therefore can place no weight on these documents.  [21] Furthermore the appellant has not been able to satisfactorily address the visa officer’s concerns that neither applicant had a good knowledge of the course s they were studying and that although both claimed to be studying computers scienc e, neither has used a computer more than a few times during several years of study.  This sugge sts to the panel that the applicants were in fact not in school.  [22] Therefore, the appellant cannot meet the onus on her to demonstrate that on a balance of probabilities the applicants are members of the family class for the purposes of immigration.  [23] The appeal is dismissed

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
INTRODUCTION  
[1] XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the appellant), a 57-year -old female Canadian citizen, married her 
husband, XXXXXXXXXXXX  (the applicant) , a 30 -year -old Pakistani citizen , on October 1, 201 5.  It 
was the second marriage for the appellant and the first for the applicant.   In Decem ber, 2015, the 
applicant submitted his application for permanent residency.  This application was refused on 
December 21 , 2016 because the visa officer in Saudi Arabia, where the applicant was resident 
and working,  was not satisfied that the rela tionship between the applicant and appellant was 
genuine or not entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring status in Canada.   
ISSUE  
[2] The issue at appeal is whether the applicant is excluded from membership in the family 
class pursuant to the bad faith marriage provision outlined in section 4 of the Immigration and 
Refugee Protection Regulations  (the  Regulations ) or whether the appellant  has shown that the 
applicant is to be considered her spouse and therefore a member of the family class pursuant to 
subsection 12(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA ) and particularly 
considering section 4(1) of the Regulations.1 
DETERMI NATION  
[3] The appeal is allowed. I find that the appellant has met her onus of establishing that, on a 
balance of probabilities, the applicant is not excluded by section 4(1) of the Regulations .  
[4] The evidence establishes on a balance of probabilities that thi s marriage is genuine and 
was not entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring status in Canada for the reasons that 
follow.

belonged.  At that time the applicant was working in Saudi Arabia.  He had not applied for a visa

Is the marriage genuine or was it entered into primarily for the purpose of obtaining a 
status under IRPA?  
[13]  The Regulations provide that in order for a Canadian citizen or permanent resident to 
sponsor an applicant to come to Canada as a spouse, the marriage must be both genuine and not 
entered into for the purpose of obtaining any immigration status or privilege.6  The marriage 
must be gen uine for both parties and it is up to the appellant to establish that the applicant is a 
member of the family class, and thus can be sponsored to Canada.7  Furthermore, while the 
intention of both parties is relevant in our examination of the appeal, the i ntention of the 
applicant is a key determinant.8  Finally, in order to meet her onus on a balance of probabilities, 
the evidence provided by the appellant must be clear, convincing and cogent.9

[3] In XXXXX  2009, the claimant’s grandmother died of cancer.  A m onth later, the claimant 
was summoned to the Umphakatsi which is an administrative sub -division headed by the chief of

had not introduced him to the chief and the elders of the Umphakatsi.  The claimant was also told 
that he could not be allowed to remain in the chiefdom because the Umphakatsi had information 
that h e was gay.  The claimant was shocked because the accusations that he was gay were not true 
and because he believed he was entitled to his grandmother’s prope rty.  He was told by the 
Umphaka tsi that he had no option in the matter.

 ANALYSIS  
[10]  The claimant has established his identity , on a bal ance of probabilities , based on his passport 
and  National Identity Card , and based on his testimony.  
[11]  Although the claimant has established on a balance of probabilities  his parents and 
grandmother’s death , he has not established the other elements of his c laim on a balance of 
probabilities.  
[12]  The claimant’s port -of-entry (POE) notes reference the land dispute between the claimant 
and the chieftaincy in his grand mother’s village , but do not refer to the claimant having been 
targeted because of his perceived ho mosexuality.  As far as the claimant’s allegations that he was 
persecuted prior to his departure because of his perceived sexual orientation as a homosexual, the 
claimant’s Personal Information Form ( PIF ) narrative2 is inconsiste nt with the claimant’s form  
IMM  5611 found in the POE notes.3 
[13]  The claimant testified of the existence of documents presented  to him in or about XXXXX  
2010 regarding his grandmother’s property and about a note left for him a fter his grandmother’s 
home  was burned  down.  He did not dis close these documents.  
[14]  The claimant provided an affidavit sworn by Pastor XXXXXXXXXX  on XXXX , 2011.4  
This affidavit reiterates the claimant’s allegations set out in his PIF narrative and appears to rely 
exclusively on information provided by the claimant . 
[15]  The claimant testified that he did not know why his grandmother had not dealt with the 
formalities to ensure that the claimant could inherit her property.  Neither the claimant no r pastor 
XXXXX  provided any documentary proof that the claimant’s grandmothe r was the owner of land 
which she was entitled to transfer upon death or that the claimant was the natural heir to her 
property.  The claimant stated during testimony that when his grandmother passed away he felt he 
should get her land.  Asked if she left a will, he answered that she did not.  Asked whether she had 
money, the claimant stated that she did not tell him where she kept her money.

 [16]  The claimant was asked why he had to sign documents allowing the chief to demolish his 
grandmother’s home if the chief believed that he had no right to his grandmother’s property.  The 
claimant explained that the men may have wished to use his objection s against him in whatever way 
they wished if he in fact refused to sign.  This explanation is devoid of meaning and is not 
reasonable.  
[17]  Asked whether he had called upon a lawyer to sort out his property issues, the claimant 
stated that he did not think that a lawyer would be able to help him and that he could not afford 
legal help.  
[18]  The claimant has not established, on a bal ance of probabilities, that he was entitled to his 
grandmother’s property when she passed away or that he was denied his rightful inheritance by 
village officials.  
[19]  The right to property is not one upon which a claim of refugee protection can be founded  
and  the claimant’s claim that the village chief and elders wish to get rid of him because he would 
not relinquish his grandmother’s property does not establish a nexus to one of the grounds 
enumerated in section 96 of the IRPA . 
[20]  The claimant alleges that there  is another basis for his claim, namely , that he was threatened 
and forced to leave his grandmother’s village because he was perceived to be gay by the chief and 
elders of his village.  Other than the affidavit prepared by the Pastor which appears to be en tirely 
based on reports made to the pastor by the claimant, reports which do not appear to have been 
independently verified by the pastor, the claimant did not submit any evidence to support his 
allegations that he was perceived to be gay by the leadership  and members of his community.  Nor 
was it clear from the claimant’s PIF and oral testimony why the misconceptions about the 
claimant’s sexual orientation could not be put to rest.  The claimant testified that the source of the 
misunderstanding about his s exual orientation was his friendship with classmates who were gay yet, 
according to the claimant, he also had a girlfriend who was a classmate from 2005 on.

 [21]  When asked what he had done with the note left for him by those who had burned the house, 
XXXXXXXXXXXXX stated that he had given it to police when he went to report the fire.  It was unclear 
from the claimant’s testimony why the police would have kept the anonymous note since they 
refused to help the claimant because he could not prove that the house ha d been burned 
intentionally or that any particular person had left him the anonymous note.  The claimant’s failure 
to establish the existence of written threats made toward him or that he reported the fire and threats 
to the police negatively impacts his c redibility.  
[22]  A friend of the claimant whom the claimant alleges was gay, XXXXXXXX , was reportedly 
assaulted because of his sexual orientation as he waited for the claimant’s return home from his 
meeting at the village palace.  Asked whether he had tried to contact his friend  to obtain his account 
of the events , the claimant advised that he had but that his friend would not take his calls.  
[23]  Having considered all  of the evidence in this claim, the panel finds that the claimant has not 
established , on a balance of probabilities , that he was entitled to his grand mother’s property when 
she died;  that he was threatened and his grandmother’s home burned down to pressure him into 
renouncing his rights to the property ; that he was perceived to be gay and threatened wit h harm as a 
result ; and  that he sought police protection.  
[24]  The panel having determined that the claimant’s allegations and testimony were not credible 
determines that the claimant has not established that there is a serious possibility that he will be 
perse cuted if removed to Swaziland  today . 
[25]  The claimant also claims that he will face a danger of torture, a risk to his life and /or of 
cruel and unusual treatment o r punishment if he is removed to Swaziland.  As the panel did not find 
the claimant’s allegations  and testimony, credible, the claimant has not established on a balance of 
probabilities that he will face a danger or torture, personal risk to his life and or personal risk of 
cruel and unusual treatment or punishment wi thin the meaning of section 97 (1) of the IRPA  if 
removed to Swaziland.

Material s filed in evidence indicate that he had limited family support when he arrived in Canada in 1999.  While he resided with an aunt during that period, he was unhappy in that home. Mate rials indicate that he attended school in Canada, however, he had some difficulties due to challenges in learning English and his lack of competence in the French language. [5] Having considered all the evidence and submissions from both the counsel for the 
appellant and the Minister of Immigration , Refugees and Citizenship  (the Minister);  the Panel 
finds that the appellant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the marriage is genuine and 
that it was not entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under 
the IRPA . The appeal is allowed pursuant to subsection 66(a) of IRPA .  
 
[6] Since the Panel has determined that the marriage is genuine  and therefore the applicant is 
considered the spouse of the appellant and a member of the family class , the ground of refusal 
pursuant to paragraph 36(2 )(a) of the IRPA , which was conceded by counsel for the appellant, is 
determined to be valid in law. Notwithstanding this inadmissibility, there are sufficient 
humanitarian and compassionate grounds to allow the applicant entry to Canada.

ANALYSIS  
 
[20] A Canadian citizen or permanent resident of Canada may sponsor the application of a 
foreign national as a member of the family class; a spouse is a member of the family class.20 
However, if the marriage was entered in bad faith, under subsection 4(1) of  the Regulations, that 
spouse is excluded from the family class.  
 
[21]  With respect to  the genuineness of a marriage  for the purposes of the Regulations , the 
Panel examined a number of factors21 and took into account additional evidence that was not 
before th e immigration  officer.22 For example, the length of the parties relationships prior to their 
marriage, their age difference, their former marital or civil status, their respective financial 
situation and employment, their family background, their knowledge of one another’s histories, 
their language and their respective interests. The appellant bears the burden of proof in this 
regard. The Panel finds that the indicia do weigh positively in favo ur of the appellant. The Panel 
is cognizant of the immigration objectives, that being “to see that families are reunited in 
Canada.”23  
 
[22] In considering the reliability and credibility of witnesses in the case of inconsistencies 
and an absence of suppor ting evidence, “[T]he trial judge should not consider the plaintiff’s 
evidence in isolation, but must look at the totality of the evidence to assess the impact of the 
inconsistencies in that evidence on questions of credibility and reliability pertaining t o the core 
issue in the case .”24

[24] In the assessment of this marriage, the appellant advises that the applicant was residing 
with her parents and brother in Guelph, Ontario shortly after entering Canada illegall y in October

would respond about her pregnancy as she was unmarried. The appellant’s mother , who was

[25]  Throughout the applicant’s time in Canada, that being 39 months, he has resided with the

notwithstanding his precarious immigration situation in Canada. The evidence does not suggest

permanent residence. In other words, that the marriage was entered into primarily for him to 
acquire status or privilege which appeared to be so on its face. This is a case where an 
assessment into the merits of the marriage has to be looked at deeper given the applicant’s 
immigration history in the United States and Canada.  
 
[26] Having said that,  the Panel, by no stretch of the imagination is not naive to the fact that

within Canada on his behalf. It is a negative factor that th e applicant did not provide the 
residential address of his wife and son who he resided with when he completed the refugee 
application. This concealment of facts was likely done to avoid complicating his refugee claim.

ROLE OF THE RAD  
[6] The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Huru glica1 provides guidance in relation to 
the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal , such as the RAD, to 
decisions of the first -level administrative tribunal.  
[7] The Court stated that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fa ct and law) which 
raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions by applying 
the correctness standard. Pursuant to s. 111(2)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD may refer the matter back 
to the RPD for redetermination if it is “of the opinion” that it cannot make a decision confirming 
or setting aside the RPD ’s decision without hearing the evidence presented before the RPD. This 
recognizes that there may be cases where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD 
in making fin dings of fact or mixed fact and law, because those cases require an assessment of 
credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. It further indicates that , although the 
RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituti ng its own determination, 
the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case -by-
case basis.  
[8] Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its assessment of the RPD’s decision on the basis of 
the principles outlined above.

 REASONS AND  DECISION  
[1] XXXX (the principal Appellant), his wife XXXX (the associated Appellant) and their 
children XXXX and XXXX (the minor Appellants) appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection 
Division (RPD) denying their claim s for refugee protection.  They have submitted no new 
evidence in support of their  appeal . The Appellant s ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to 
set aside the determination of the RPD and either find them to be protected persons or refer the 
matter back to the RPD for redetermination.  
DETE RMINATION  
[2] These appeals are allowed. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Act  (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re -determination by a 
differently -constituted panel.   
Background  
[3] The principal Appellant alleg ed before the RPD that he worked in Kosovo for a XXX non -
governmental organization; his job was to XXX to assist minorities in matters such as XXXX. In 
2004, he began to receive threats from an extremist organization, which accused him of 
supporting minori ty rights. His vehicle was later vandalized, and he received threatening phone 
calls. He was attacked by masked men who called him a Serbian spy and a traitor. He and his 
family fled to the United States in 2005, and sought asylum; however, they were not s uccessful, 
and in 2011, were told to leave the country.   
[4] They  returned to Kosovo, but found themselves in conflict with fundamentalist Muslim 
parents at the school attended by the minor Appellants. The principal Appellant also opposed the 
building of a ne w mosque in the area. He began to receive threatening e -mail messages and phone 
calls accusing him of being an infidel, in addition to threats from people who knocked on his door 
in the night. In XXXX of 2013, the principal Appellant went to the police wit h a copy of a 
threatening email; they did not make a report, and the Appellant subsequently sought help from

ANALYSIS  
Role of the RAD  
[7] What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD ? 
[8] The Appellants make no submissions on the role of the RAD or the standard to be applied 
to the RPD’s decision.  
[9] While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not 
specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.  
[10]  The RAD has, in respect of proceedings brought before it under the IRPA, sole and 
exclusive jurisd iction to hear and determine all questions of law and fact, including questions of 
jurisdiction.1 While the RAD is a relatively new tribunal, it has by now rendered more than a 
thousand decisions on the merits of appeals. It has experience in interpreting the IRPA, its home 
statute and one with which it has particular familiarity. It is therefore appropriate for the RAD to

Legislation  
[11]  The legislative history of the RAD is carefully detailed in XXXXXXX ,3 and will not be

[12]  While the IRPA  does not specifically set out the purpose of the RAD, it does describe the 
purposes of the legislation with respect to refugees:4 
(a) to recognize that the refugee program is in the first instance about saving lives 
and offering protection to the displaced and persecuted;  
(b) to fulfil Canada’s international legal obligations with respect to refugees and 
affirm Canada’s commitment to international efforts to provide assistance to those 
in need of resettlement;  
(c) to gr ant, as a fundamental expression of Canada’s humanitarian ideals, fair 
consideration to those who come to Canada claiming persecution;  
(d) to offer safe haven to persons with a well -founded fear of persecution based on 
race, religion, nationality, political op inion or membership in a particular social 
group, as well as those at risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or 
punishment;

(f) to support the self -sufficiency and the social and economic well -being of refugees

Canadian society; and  
(h) to promote international justice and security by denying access to Canadian 
territory to persons, including refugee claimants, who are security risks or serious 
crimin als.  
[13]  While all  of these objectives are generally relevant to the RAD, ( e) is specifically 
applicable to the appellate tribunal, which must be cognizant of the requirement to establish fair 
and efficient procedures that will maintain the integrity of the re fugee protection system while at 
the same time upholding respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms.  
[14]  The IRPA sheds some light on the purpose of the RAD in Section 110(1):  
Subject to subsections (1.1) and (2), a person or the Minister may appeal, in  accordance 
with the rules of the Board, on a question of law, of fact or of mixed law and fact , to the 
Refugee Appeal Division against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division to allow or 
reject the person’s claim for refugee protection  (emphasis add ed.)  
[15]  This suggests that the RAD must consider questions arising from the RPD’s decision.  
[16]  Section 110(2) of the IRPA restricts access to the RAD. Those without the right of a RAD 
appeal include designated foreign nationals, refugee claimants whose claims were found to have 
no credible basis or to be manifestly unfounded, and individuals who have lost their refugee status 
through vacation or cessation.  
[17]  Section 110(3) requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD’s 
record, though i t may also accept documentary evidence and submissions from both the Minister 
and the subject of the appeal. Section 110(4) imposes restrictions on new evidence filed by the 
subject of the appeal, who “ may present only evidence that arose after the rejecti on of their claim

[18]  Section 110(6) sets out the exceptional circumstances in which the RAD may hold an oral 
hearing: where there is new evidence (a) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility 
of the person who is the subject of the appeal; (b) that is central to the decision with respect to the 
refugee protection claim; and (c) that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee 
protection claim.  
[19]  Section 111(1) provides the RAD with a broad range of remedies: it must either confirm 
the determination of the RPD, set that determination aside and substitute its own determination, or 
refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. According to Section 111(2), the RAD is 
only to refer a matter back i f the decision of the RPD is “ wrong in law, in fact or in mixed law 
and fact ,” and if it cannot confirm or substitute “ without hearing evidence that was presented to 
the Refugee Protection Division .” In the RAD’s view, these provisions suggest both an emph asis 
on finality and a desire to avoid duplication between the RAD and the RPD.  
[20]  Section 165 provides that members of the RAD have the powers and authority of a 
commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act,  and may do any other thing they consider 
necessa ry to provide a full and proper hearing.  
[21]  Section 171 sets out provisions in respect to proceedings before the RAD, including that 
the Division is not bound by legal or technical rules of evidence, and that it may receive and base 
a decision on evidence tha t is adduced in the proceedings and considered credible or t rustworthy 
in the circumstances . It also allows the RAD to take notice of facts that may be judicially noticed, 
of any other generally recognized facts, and of information or opinion within its sp ecialized 
knowledge. Section 171(c) provides that a decision of a three -member RAD panel has 
precedential value for the RPD and for single -member panels of the RAD.  Where the RAD

Jurisprudence  
[23]  As a new tribunal, the RAD did not initially have the benefit of any jurisprudence 
specifically dealing with its role, its relationship to the RPD, or the nature of an appeal. In 
hundreds of cases, the RAD rather consistently determined that it should apply a standard of 
review of reasonableness, deferring to the RPD’s findings of fact and mixed fact and law , while 
applying a standard of correctness to questions of law, natural justice, and procedural fairness.  
[24]  The Federal Court first spoke to the RAD’s role in Iyamuremye .8 In that case, the Court 
found itself entirely in agreement with the RAD that the stand ard of review to be applied to 
decisions of the RPD was one of reasonableness, though it found that the RAD had erred by 
failing to conduct an independent review of the evidence in order to assess whether the RPD’s 
decision was in fact reasonable. The Cour t also recognize d that it would be absurd, and contrary 
to subsection 110(3) of the IRPA,  to require the RAD to re -examine in every instance whether 
claimants are in fact refugees or persons in need of  protection.  
[25]  In the subsequent case s of XXXXXXX  and XXX , the Court clarified the role of the RAD in 
relation to the RPD.9 It held that the RAD is not to undertake a process of judicial review,  but 
rather must conduct  its own assessment of the facts in order to determine whether the RPD made 
an error of law or mis-assessed the facts to the point of making a “palpable and overriding 
error” .10 In the Court’s view, the lower tribunal’s ability to hear evidence viva voce  makes it

 [76]  To put it simply, it is not helpful in the RAD context to determine the scope of deference 
on the basis of issue categories. Instead, the RAD will determine deference based on categories of 
evidence.  
[77]  The RAD will show deference to the RPD’s findings where the RPD was in an 
advantageous position to reach such findings. The RPD’s advantage comes from seeing claimants 
and witnesses and hearing oral testimony. As such, credibility findings arising from that oral 
testimony are deserving of deferen ce, as are other findings of fact based on oral evidence, as are 
findings based on the RPD’s specialized knowledge of a particular matter where the RAD does 
not have its own specialized knowledge with respect to the same factual issue.  The RPD’s 
advantage may even extend to personal documents in situations where it has questioned the 
claimant or witness about such documents and where the resulting testimony gives rise to 
credibility concerns.  
[78]  Not every finding relating to credibility warrants deference. Whe re the RPD has made a 
finding of implausibility, for example, it has no advantage where that determination of plausibility 
is based on the RPD’s own reasoning, or on objective documents, and does not arise directly from 
the oral evidence.68  Similarly, wher e the RPD draws an inference —a credibility finding based on 
deduction and reasoning, rather than a contradiction in evidence —the RAD may see no reason to 
show deference, as the appellate tribunal can be expected to have equal expertise in the inferential 
process.69  
[79]  Where the RPD was in an advantageous position to reach a conclusion, the RAD will 
recognize and respect that finding. Where the RPD did not enjoy such an advantage, the RAD 
will apply a standard of correctness.

 [85]  How then is “recognize and respect” to be defined? In XXXXXXXX,  the Supreme Court 
discussed two elements of a deferential review: process and outcome. 73 Despite the difference 
between judicial review and a RAD appeal, it seems appropriate for the RAD to adopt those 
elements.  
[86]  Even where the RAD is to show deference to findings of the RPD, those findings must 
still be the result of a comprehensible reasoni ng process. The RAD must be able to read the 
RPD’s decision and understand how the RPD’s conclusions were reached.  
[87]  Further, the outcome of that process must be a result that is based on and supported by the 
evidence that was before the RPD. For this reaso n, it is particularly important, as repeatedly noted 
by the Federal Court, that the RAD engage in its own review of the evidence in the RPD’s record, 
in order to determine whether the RPD’s finding is supported by that evidence.  
[88]  “Recognize and respect” is therefore a level of deference that will not interfere with the 
RPD’s findings where such conclusions result from the RPD’s distinct advantages or from a 
comprehensible reasoning process whose premises are rooted in such advantages.  If either the 
process o r the outcome does not meet these requirements, the RAD will determine the findings to 
be in error or, in the language of Section 111(2), “wrong.”  
[89]  On matters where the RAD owes no deference, it will consider the RPD’s findings and 
conclusions on a standard  of correctness: it will conduct its own review of the evidence and 
undertake its own analysis of the question. If this does not lead the RAD to the same conclusion 
as the RPD, the RPD’s finding is wrong.

the RPD. It will assess all of the evidence, both that in the RPD’s record and any admissible new

[2] The reasons for refusal were contained in a letter dated February 5, 2009 from the High Commission of Canada, Immigration Section in New Delhi.  The reasons for refusal were two-fold; first, in the opinion of the visa officer the marriage in question between the appellant and applicant was not legally valid in that the applic ant was not free to marry according to local law as set out in the Hindu Marriage Act,1955.  Consequently, the marriage in question could not be considered a marriage under section 2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations since the word “marriage” must be a marriage that  is valid both under the laws of the jurisdiction where it took place and under Canadian law.  [3] The second reason for refusal was that in the opinion of the visa officer the marriage in question between the appellant and applicant was not in accordance with section 4 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  in that it was not a bona fide marriage and was entered into primarily for the purpose of  gaining status or privilege under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.  [4] The administrative background to this appeal is as follows.  On July 21, 2010 the panel heard evidence from 1:15 p.m. to 4:10 p.m., mainly on the bona fide nature of the marriage.  On September 29, 2010 the resumption was held; howeve r the appellant was not present and counsel indicated that the appellant was sick.  How to proceed administratively was then dealt with by the panel and both counsel.  The panel pointed out that its mandate was soon over and if this matter was not dealt with today it would either go de novo or if a counsel for the applicant so desired it could go by way of a new member taking over and using the transcript as a basis for a continuation.

[10] The sole question therefore for the panel is  whether the marriage between the appellant and applicant which took place on May 9, 2008 was a valid marri age and was in contravention of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.  [11] Evidence establishes that both appellant a nd applicant are Hindu and in order for the marriage to be valid, according to section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, neither party could have a spouse living at the time of the marriage.
1  Therefore in order for this marriage to be valid the previous divorce between the appl icant and her husband must also be valid.  [12] The visa post made a determination that the marriage in question was not valid because the applicant was not properly divorced.  Once a deci sion like this is made it is well established that to rely on foreign law the party asserting the foreign law must provide expert evidence to prove it.  [13] It is true that case law has indicated that th e rules of evidence do not have to be adhered to strictly in the context of administrative pr oceedings.  The decision-maker may rely on expert evidence if it is available but also can rely on foreign and domestic statutory provisions and the totality of the evidence, both oral and documenta ry, to come to a conclusion.  Notwithstanding this “liberalization” of the law in regard to administrative tribunals, the onus is still on the appellant to prove the case, and the difficulty the panel has here is that there seems to be almost no attempt to provide any evidence to re fute the opinion of the visa officer.  [14] No knowledge of foreign law can be imputed to the decision-maker; the decision-maker needs oral evidence, affidavit evidence or expert evidence in order to come to its decision.  The only attempt to provide a document to refute th e position taken by the visa post is the legal document found at pages 1 to 29 of Exhibit A-1.  An examination of this document shows that as a result of the legal difficulties the appellant an d applicant were having, the applicant went back to court to get a divorce document through the courts of India.  When one examines this document one sees that as a result of this document the senior civil judge determines at page 13 of Exhibit A-1, that both parties are now free to marry and determines that they are free to enter

[17] The option available to the appellant and ap plicant is if this marriage is indeed a bona fide one, the appellant would be free to re-sponsor th e applicant in order to have her join him in Canada.  [18] Having come to this conclusion it is not necessary for any other member of the Immigration Appeal Division to hear any further evidence on the bona fide nature of this marriage.  Therefore, for all the above reasons this appeal is dismissed.

Disponible en français  REASONS FOR  DECISION  
 
[1] XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  is appealing1 a removal order issued against him by a Minister’s 
delegate for failing to comply with the residency obligation .  
ISSUE  
[2] The appellant is a citizen of Leban on. He acknowledges his failure to comply with the 
residency obligation and cites humanitarian and compassionate considerations to retain  his 
permanent residen t status . He obtained that status in Canada in Decemb er 2006, under the skilled 
worker categor y.2 
[3] Und er the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA), a permanent resident must 
accumulate 730 days of residence over a five -year period.  In this case, the period comprises the 
five years immediately before the examination on July  12, 2020 .3 Mr. XXXX cites , on a balance of 
probabilities, humanitarian and compassionate considerations and the panel must review this issue . 
[4] With 32 days of presence over the relevant  period, the failure to comply with the residency 
obligation is extreme . The appel lant stayed abroad for reasons that can hardly be considered  
humanitarian  and compassionate  considerations . The panel notes that he made no attempt to return 
here to settle at the first reasonable opportunity . His current establishment is very weak . The 
Immigra tion  Appeal Division  (IAD ) foresees fairly little dislocation  in the event that permanent 
residence is lost . What is more, the best interest s of the child does not weigh in favour of retaining 
status here .  
[5] The presence in Canada of family through marriage  weighs marginally in favour of the 
appeal, but does not outweigh all the other criteria .  
DETERMINATION  
[6] The appeal is dismissed .

[29]  What is more, the argument on relevance is hard for the undersigned to follow when it 
seems erroneous  not to take into consid eration the fact that a person created false documents and 
lied repeatedly in his past immigration process . An employee of Citizenship and I mmigration 
Canada notified the appellant that [translation]  “the record of the interview and the false statements 
he made will be added to his file and will follow him for all f uture initiatives. ”27  
[30]  With the withdrawal of his citizenship application, Mr.  XXXX obtained a permanent 
resident card valid  for five years , but some periods of presence in  Canada remained unclear to the 
immigration authorities,28 which adds to the relevance of accepting the document ary evidence . 
[31]  The N ovemb er 2017 IAD decision29 makes no mention of the fact that  the appellant 
committed  fraudul ent actions to obtain Canadian citizenship .  
[32]  To successfully invoke the doctrine of res judicata, there needs to be a decision tying  the 
same parties to the same issue. In this case, the IAD decision of November 2017 ties together the 
same parties, but the issue is completely diff erent. The removal order of July  2020 is not that of 
March  2014. I t is not the same five -year period and the analysis of humanitarian and 
compassionate considerations must be reconsidered accordingly. What is more, the IAD member 
who made the decision in 2017 made absolutely no  mention  of the evidence of fraud the appellant 
committed in order to obtain his permanent resident card and Canadian citizenship. He did in fact  
hear such evidence at the hearing, including during the cross -examination of the appellant who 
admitted to committing  fraud.30  
[33]  It goes without saying that the panel does not accept the res judicata argument . On the 
contrary, the undersigned considers that  Mr.  XXXX was given many chances. He got away with 
committing fraud for his permanent  resident card and for his citizenship application without 
charge, and was able to keep his permanent  resident status without investigation into his

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons and decision of the Immigration Appeal Division (the “IAD”) in an 
appeal by XXXXXXXXXXXXX (the “appellant”) against the refusal of the sponsored application for a 
permanent resident visa for her spouse, Sheik XXXXXXXXXXXXX, also known  as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the “applicant”), a citizen of Fiji.  
 
BACKGROUND  
 
[2] There were two grounds of refusal. The first was section 4(1) of the Immigration and 
Refugee Protection Regulations  (the “ Regulations ”).1 The visa officer found that the marriag e 
between the appellant and applicant is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose 
of the applicant acquiring status under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the “ Act ”).2 
 
[3] The second groun d of refusal was pursuant to section 36(2)(b) of the Act . The applicant 
was determined to be inadmissible on grounds of criminality for having been convicted outside 
Canada of offences that, if committed in Canada, would constitute indictable offences.  
 
[4] The appellant is a 31 -year -old citizen of Canada. The applicant is a 40 -year -old citizen of 
Fiji. The couple married on May 27, 2012. They have each been married previously.  
 
Administrative History  
 
[5] This matter has a convoluted administrative history. The app lication was refused on 
June  30, 2014. The Notice of Appeal was filed on July 31, 2014. Due to a medical condition the 
appellant claimed she was unable to participate in scheduling conferences. The IAD sent letters

[7] On April 12, 2016, the appellant applied in writi ng to have the hearing proceed without

[8] Counsel for the Minister o f Citizenship and Immigration (the “respondent”) appeared at 
the scheduled hearing. The appellant did not. The respondent provided oral submissions on three 
options: (1) the appeal be declared abandoned; (2) the hearing be postponed; or (3) the

 [9] If the applicant is found to be a member of the family c lass, the IAD has jurisdiction to 
grant special relief based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations in respect to  the 
applicant’s inadmissibility for criminality. It was ordered that submissions only be provided on

[10]  The appellant provided eviden ce, including documents and a  compact disc ( CD ), and 
written submissions.3 The respondent provided documentary evidence4 and written submissions. 
There was no oral testimony. I have taken into consideration the contents of the Record, the 
documentary evidence and the parties’ submissions.  
 
ISSUES  
 
[11]  The issue is whether subsection 4(1) of the Regulations  applies, thereby excluding the 
applicant from consideration as a member of the family class. The tests set out in subsection 4(1) 
of the Regulations  are whether the marriage:  
a) was entered into primaril y for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege 
under the Act ; or,  
 
b) is not genuine.  
 
[12]  Only one test needs to be met to disqualify a spouse. The onus of proof is on the 
appellant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the applicant is not disqualified as a 
spouse.

 DECISION  
 
[13]  I find the appellant has not met the onus on her of establishing, on a balance of 
probabilities that the marriage was not entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring a status 
or privilege under the Act . I find  that the applicant is not a member of the family class. The 
appeal is dismissed.  
 
ANALYSIS  
 
[14]  The applicant entered Canada on December 23, 2007, on a temporary resident’s visa 
(“TRV”). On July 18, 2008, an application to extend the TRV was denied. During t he course of 
that application Citizenship and Immigration Canada found that the applicant had been refused 
work permits three times since his arrival in Canada. On August 19, 2008, the applicant made a 
refugee claim. On November 2, 2010, the applicant was arrested for harassing his former wife, a 
Canadian resident. On December 21, 2010, the applicant’s ref ugee claim was denied. On 
March  30, 2011, he was ordered deported.  
 
[15]  In August 2011 the appellant and applicant met through an online dating site. They me t in 
person on September 10, 2011. In February 2012 they began to live together. They were legally 
married on May 27, 2012. There was no religious ceremony. The applicant was deported the next 
day.  
 
[16]  The applicant was interviewed by the visa officer on Jul y 8, 2013. The visa officer 
initially concluded that the marriage was genuine. The visa officer continued processing the 
application. They learned about the applicant’s history, including name changes, his immigration 
history in Canada and other countries,  his criminal charges in Canada, and apparent 
misrepresentations on prior applications. Based on all the information before them, the visa 
officer concluded that the applicant entered into the marriage primarily to gain status in Canada.
