[17]  The applicant’s immigration history is sordid. He made an unsuccessful asylum claim in 
Australia. He later applied to enter New Zealand and was refused. He changed his name and was 
granted entry to New Zealand under that name. He was discovered and charged with 
misreprese ntation. He was convicted and deported from New Zealand. He applied for a Canadian 
TRV and was denied. He changed his name again and was successful in obtaining a TRV in the 
new name. He was refused three work permits and an extension to his TRV. He then m ade a 
refugee claim. That claim was refused and he was ordered deported. In his many applications to 
Canada he never disclosed his name changes or criminal history. While in Canada he was 
accused of criminally harassing his ex -wife.  
 
[18]  The appellant provided  proof of ongoing communication; proof of financial support; 
photos; and, letters of support from friends and family, including the appellant’s parents. The 
appellant provided a lengthy written submission. The applicant provided two letters, one dated 
Febr uary 20, 2015, and the other September 5, 2014, explaining his immigration history and 
attesting to the bona fides  of the marriage. The couple reportedly lived together for three months 
prior to their legal marriage. This is evidence of genuineness.  
 
[19]  The crux of this case is whether the applicant entered into the marriage primarily for the 
purpose of acquiring status under the Act .  Evidence that a marriage is genuine can show that a 
marriage was not entered into primarily for the purpose of immigration, h owever it is not 
decisive. Assessing the primary purpose of a marriage requires assessing the evidence to draw 
conclusions about the parties’, most importantly the applicant’s, state -of-mind.

 [20]  In this case there is no oral  testimony to assess. The appellant chose not to testify and not 
to call the applicant as a witness. The applicant’s version of events comes primarily from his two 
letters. The applicant has a history of failing to disclose material facts in immigration 
applications. The applicant testified before the New Zealand court. The judge in that proceeding 
found the applicant’s testimony to be “a tissue of lies”.5 The applicant’s letters are unsworn. The 
February 20, 2015, letter includes an explanation for his off ences in New Zealand – the very 
explanation the judge found was fabricated. The applicant was not available to be cross -
examined on the information provided. For these reasons, I give the applicant’s written 
explanations no weight.  
 
[21]  The applicant has famil y in Canada. I find that is a pull factor. The applicant has a history 
of attempting to gain status in Australia, New Zealand and then Canada by hook -or-by-crook. 
The applicant admitted to the visa officer that he lied on his original TRV application. He w as 
not intending to come to Canada for a temporary visit; he was coming for the purpose of going 
into business with his brother -in-law. The applicant withheld material facts on his applications. 
The applicant was facing removal when he met the appellant. XXXXX were legally married the day 
before the applicant was scheduled for deportation.  This evidence leads to the conclusion that the 
applicant entered into marriage  primarily for the purpose of acquiring status or privilege under 
the Act . The onus is on the  appellant to provide evidence to show that this conclusion is wrong. I 
find that the appellant has not provided sufficient evidence to discharge her onus.  
 
[22]  I find that the applicant entered into the marriage primarily for the purpose of acquiring 
status o r privilege under the Act . 
 
[23]  Minister’s counsel submitted that an adverse inference should be drawn from the fact that 
no oral testimony was provided. The appellant’s explanation for not wishing to call evidence was 
her medical condition.   She provided medi cal information to support her contention that it would

 be difficult for her to testify. I find that, given her medical condition, no adverse inference should 
be drawn from the appellant  not testifying. However, the applicant’s intention in entering into t he 
marriage is pivotal to this appeal. It would have been natural for him to testify. His motivation in 
entering into the marriage was at issue. His credibility was in question. Only he could testify to 
the circumstances of his negative immigration history . He provided information on those issues 
in his written statements but the respondent could not cross -examine him. I draw a negative 
inference from his failure to testify.  
 
[24]  I make no finding in respect to subsection 4(1)(b) of the Regulations  – genuinenes s of the 
marriage.  However, in my assessment of the primary purpose of the marriage I have taken into 
consideration the evidence tending to show that the marriage is genuine, including the period of 
co-habitation, proof of ongoing communication, proof of f inancial support, photos and letters of 
support. I find that the evidence of genuineness is insufficient to overcome the compelling 
evidence that the marriage was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring a status or 
privilege under the Act . 
 
[25]  Hav ing found that the marriage was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring 
status or privilege under the Act , it is unnecessary to make a decision in respect to the second 
ground of refusal – criminality outside Canada.  
 
CONCLUSION  
 
[26]  On the whole of the evidence before me, I find the appellant has not met the onus on her 
of establishing, on a balance of probabilities that the marriage was not entered into primarily for 
the purpose of acquiring a status or privilege under the Act . I the refore find that the applicant is 
excluded as a member of the family class.

Introduction

RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the 
Appellant is a Convention refugee. This appeal is allowed.

of her ex -husband, XXXXXXXXX . The abuse, both physical and sexual, became serious in 2005

[31]  The RPD’s decision cannot stand as it contains err ors in its assessment of the Appellant’s 
credibility, the treatment of the documenta ry evidence, and its consideration of an IFA.  
[32]  Having conducted my own analysis of the record, I must now determine if I am able to 
substitute the correct decision in this Appeal, or if I must return the Appeal to the RPD for a 
determination.  
[33]  The RPD and the Appellant’s lawyer canvassed some elements central to the Appellant’s 
claim during the two sittings at the RPD. This testimony was uncontested by the RPD and 
maintains a presumption of truth unless there are valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness. I w as 
struck by many of the details she provided in her testimony and her BoC – for instance, how she 
linked her husband’s abusive periods to his use of alcohol, holidays and association with his 
friends. How after the attack on the XXXXXXXXX and her father i n 2005 her ex -husband tried to make 
it up to her parents by repairing their roof. Her story has a ring of truth to it. I also have carefully 
reviewed copies of the documentary evidence the XXXXXXXXX supplied in support of her claim. I 
believe that she was abused by her ex -husband.  
[34]  On the question of state protection, the documentary evidence is clear that domestic 
violence, while widespread, is not taken seriously in Ukrainian society.

 Canada in Danyluk6 has given clear direction that the rules governing res judicata should not be mechanically applied.  Even if the criteria for res judicata are met, the issue of whether res judicata ought to be applied in any given case is within the Immigration Appeal Division’s (the “IAD”) discretion to determine.  Genera lly, in cases where the criteria for res judicata are met, the doctrine will be applied, unless an overriding quest ion of fairness is raised in order to avoid a potential injustice.  Such circumstances would dictate that a rehearing is required.  Recent Federal Court jurisprudence
7 confirms these principles. [8] It is with these principles in mind that I turn now to the facts of this case.  The respondent submitted the appeal should be dismissed on the basis of res judicata.  The respondent submitted that the same issue was decided in the first appeal , the decision in the first appeal was final, and the parties in the present appeal are the same pa rties that took place in the previous appeal.   [9] The appellant’s counsel submitted that there was no valid adoption “the first time around”.  Instead he submitted that the “new” adoption is the only valid adoption and the “new” adoption has never been the subject of an appeal previously.  Accordingly, the principle of res judicata should not be applied to an adoption which was not the subject of any litigation previously.  However, although I noted a second adoption ceremony took place in 2001, there is no evidence the 1998 adoption has been  rescinded or cancelled.  There is no evidence before me that establishes the second adoption is recognized by the authorities as conferring any status on the parties. Test  relating to exclusion under Article  1E of the  Convention  
[13]  Article  1E of the Convention states the following : 
This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent 
authorities of the country in which he has taken resid ence as having the rights and 
obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country . 
[14]  In XXXX ,6 the Federal Court of Appeal sets out the following test to be applied in 
determining whether Article  1E of the Convention is applicable in a given case : 
Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have 
status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country?  If the answer 
is yes, the claimant is excluded . If the answer is no, the next question is whether the 
claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed 
to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the 
answer is yes, the RPD must consider and  balance various factors. These include, but 
are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether 
the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the 
home country, Canada’s internatio nal obligations, and any other relevant facts.  
[15]  Before considering  the application of the test to the case at hand, it is important to 
determine where the burden of proof lies with regard to exclusion under Article  1E of the 
Convention .

ANALYSIS  
[9] In the XXXXXXX  case, the Supreme Court of Canada set out the three preconditions for 
assessing whether the doctrine of res judica ta may apply:  (1) that the same question has been 
decided in earlier proceedings; (2) that the earlier judicial decision was final; and (3) that the 
parties to that decision or their privies are the same in both the proceedings.2 
[10]  If the moving party succes sfully establishes these preconditions, a court must still 
determine whether, as a matter of discretion, issue estoppel ought to be applied.   Justice XXXXXX, 
writing for the unanimous Court, also noted the observations of the British Colombia Court of 
Appe al in a similar matter:3 
It must always be remembered that although the three requirements for issue 
estoppel must be satisfied before it can apply, the fact that they may be satisfied 
does not automatically give rise to its application.   Issue estoppel is an equitable 
doctrine, a nd as can be seen from the cases, is closely related to abuse of 
process.   The doctrine of issue estoppel is designed as an implement of justice, 
and a protection against injustice.   It  inevitably calls upon the exercise of a 
judicial discretion to achiev e fairness according to the circumstances of each 
case.  
[11]  Counsel  agree that the three XXXXXXX  preconditions are met in this case.  We have the 
same parties, the same issue, and the IAD decisions of 2016 and 2018 were final decisions. The 
question is thus wh ether I should exercise my discretion not to dismiss the appeal to protect 
against injustice.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons for the decision in the appeal of XXXXXXXX who appeals the refusal 
to approve the permanent resident app lication made by his spouse, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.  The 
application was refused by the visa officer pursuant to Section 4(1) of the Immigration and 
Refugee Protection Regulations  on the basis that the marriage was entered into primarily for the 
purpose of acquiring status or privilege under Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) . 
 
[2] Having considered all of the evidence , the panel finds that the appellant has proven on a 
balance of probabilities that the marriage is genuine and that it was not entered into primarily to 
acquire any status or privilege under IRPA . Counsel for the respondent has ha d an opportunity to 
review the R ecord and disclosures .  He had an opportunity to examine the appellant and the 
applicant’s sister who appeared as a witne ss when we were here in January.  He had an 
opportunity to witness the full examination of the appellant , and the witness and he also had an 
opportunity to witness the direct examination of the applicant.  
 
[3] Having considered all of the evidence before the M inister , he presented the position that 
the appellant has provided sufficient credible evidence to establish the genuineness of the 
marriage.   Consequently,  the M inister has consented to the appeal being allowed.  
 
[4] In consi deration of the consent of the M inister, as well as the totality of the ev idence 
before me including the R ecord and disclosures, I find that the appeal should be allowed as the

INTRODUCTION  
[1] These are the  reasons for the decision in a preliminary issue in the appeal of GXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the appellant) from a removal order made by Member XXXXXXXXXXX  of the 
Immigration Division in Toronto on May 29 2007.   The removal order came about as a result of 
the appellant's conviction for unauthorized use of a computer contrary to  section  342.1(1)  of the 
Criminal Code of Canada.   
[2] On December 7, 2016, while on a stay of removal, the appellant was convicted of credit 
card fraud  contrary to section  342(3) of the Criminal Code of Canada .  As the sentence for such 
an offence  can include imprisonment of up to ten years, the conviction falls with the definition of 
serious criminality found in section 36(1)(a)  of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (the 
Act ). Section 68(4) of the Act  provides:  
Termination and cancellation

resident or a foreign national who was found inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality or 
criminality, and they are convicted of another offence referred to in subsection 36(1), the stay is  
cancelled by operation of law and the appeal is terminated.

on that appeal has yet been rendered. In a post -hearing letter provided to the Immigration Appeal

heard on April 3, 2020 and a decision rendered three to four weeks after that.1  
[4] In a decision dated December 21, 2017, IAD Member XXXXXXXX found that the IAD has no 
jurisdiction to hear the appellant’s appeal, as per section 68(4) quoted above  and denied the 
appellant’s request that the stay continue pending the outcome of the appeal of his conviction to 
the Ontario Court of Appeal.  
[5] The appellant sought and was granted l eave for judicial review of that decision by the 
Federal Court of Canada.

 [19]  The Minister acknowledges that an appellant cannot re -open an appeal that has been 
disposed of, unless there is breach of natural justice, as per section 71 of the Act . However,  he 
posits that i f the appellant’s conviction is overturned, that he could launch a second appeal based 
on the same removal order, and ask the IAD to abridge the time for filing the appeal, which the 
IAD can do as per Rule 58 . Thus , there is a remedy for a n unjust removal.  
[20]  The question in this application really comes down what is most consistent with the intent 
and spirit of the legislation and the rules and where to strike the balance between  the interest and 
rights of the appellant with the interests an d rights of the Canadian public.  
[21]  The termination of an appeal and the cancellation of a stay  conviction of a serious crime 
certainly suggests that Parliament envisioned swift removal from Canada of such persons.  
[22]  At the same time, as suggested by Madam XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the procedural rights of 
appellants must be protected when she found that the IAD had not turned its mind to  the 
importance of the decision to the individual affected .  
[23]  There is no question that the decision whether or not to grant a postpo nement is of great 
importance to the appellant. A dismissal has the potential to render an injustice to the appellant. 
However, at this point that is speculative. I do not know the merits of the appeal being advanced 
and I am in no position to predict the outcome. The Chairperson’s Guideline discourages 
postponements to await the outcome of an appeal of a conviction on criminal charges.  
[24]  The language of section 68(4) is plain. Parliament could have added language to the 
effect that the appeal will not be te rminated until all avenues of appeal have been exhausted. It 
did not do so.  
[25]  At the same time , there is now a set date for the hearing of the appeal, which is less than 
two months away. If the removal process is put into play and the conviction overturned, this 
could result in an injustice to the appellant, not to mention unnecessary expense to Canada’s 
immigration system.

INTRODUCTION  
[1] XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (Appellant) appeals the exclusion order issued against him on May 
26, 2016,  by the Immigration Division (ID).1  He was found to be inadmis sible for 
misrepresentation because he did not disclose his prior deportation from Canada in his 
application for permanent residence .  In addition, the Appellant failed to disclose a number of 
other matters on his permanent residence application.   The Immigration and Refugee Protection 
Act (IRPA )2 sanctions misrepresentations of material facts on rele vant matters that induce or 
could induce errors in the administration of the immigration legislation.  
[2] The Appellant is 36 years of age and a citizen of Saint Lucia .  He became a permanent 
resident of Canada in July 2010  through a spousal sponsorship  by XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX .3 
[3] Appellant’s counsel indicated that his client was not challenging the validity of the ID’s 
finding.  As such, the hearing focused on whether there are sufficient humanitarian and 
compassionate (H&C) considerations to allow the appeal.  
[4] The Appellant testified in English at the hearing in Toronto.  
DECISION  
[5] After considering the testimony, documentary evidence and submissions, I find that, 
taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, there are 
sufficie nt humanitarian and compassionate considerations warranting special relief in light of all 
the circumstances of the case . 
[6] The removal order is stayed for a period of five years.

weapon and the other charges against him were stayed because  he was scheduled to be removed 
from Canada.  He was eventually deported in March 2007 and needed an Authorization to Return 
to Canada (ARC) to re -enter this country.  This did not dissuade the Appell ant in his efforts to 
enter Canada once again.  
[13]  The Appellant’s name at the time  of his deportation  was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (his 
mother’s name), so he acquired another passport with the name XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (his father’s 
name) and re -entered Canada in December 2007.  When he entered at that time he did not 
disclose to immigration officials that he was previously deported from Canada, that he used a  
different name to get a new passport and that he needed an ARC.  As a result, the Appellant was 
allowed to enter Canada at that time on a Visitor Record, which required him to depart by 
January 18, 2008.  The Appellant did not comply with that requirement  and stayed in Canada.

Even were the panel to conclude that the legislation envisaged return travel to Canada for the purpose of preparing for an upcoming appeal hearing, which it does not, the case has not been made out that this appellant would be unable to adequately prepare for the hearing in the absence of his physical presence in Canada prior to hearing. [6] The panel finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees. The determinat ive issue is 
state protection and the included issue of the credibility of the claimant s’ evidence on state

ANALYSIS  
Identity

State Protection  
[8] The Supreme Court in Ward5 stated that absent a complete breakdown of state ap paratus, 
states are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens. A refugee claimant who is alleging 
that state protection is inadequate bears the evidentiary burden of adducing evidence to that effect.  
The standard of proof applicable is the balanc e of probabilities. The presumption of state 
protection is rebutted by clear and convincing evidence and the claimant must approach his or her 
state for protection, if state protection might reasonably be forthcoming.  Simply asserting a 
subjective belief o f a lack of state protection is not sufficient.  State protection need not be perfect.  
In assessing the state protection available to any individual among the factors to be considered are 
the profile of the alleged agent of persecution, the efforts the clai mant took to seek protection 
from authorities and the response of the of the authorities along with the available documentary 
evidence .6 
[9] Counsel submitted that Colombia is a failed state unable to protect its citizens.  This is 
contradicted by country condi tion documents which describe the country as a democracy with

CONCLUSION  
[21]  Considering  the totality of the evidence and the findings as set out a bove, the Panel finds 
the claimants have failed to present evidence that is credible on a balance of probabilities to 
support the allegations which form the basis of their claims, and therefore are not Convention 
refugees pursuant to s. 96 of IRPA, nor are  they persons in need of protection under s. 97(1) of 
IRPA. The state protection analysis and related credibility findings apply to consideration of the 
claims under both sections . The claim s are  rejected.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] Pursuant to subsection 63(1) the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (the IRPA ),1 
SaXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the appellant) appealed the refusal concerning the sponsored application 
for permanent residence of h er spouse, DavidXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  (the applicant), which was 
issued on March  2, 201 7. 
[2] In addition to the reasons for the refusal to issue an applicant a permanent resident visa, 
citing subsection s 41(b) and 52(1)2 of the IRPA, for not having an Authorization to Return to 
Canada, the Minis ter submitted an application seeking that section 4.1 of the Immigration and 
Refugee Protection Regulations  (Regulations ) should be added. On the opening of the appeal, the 
Minister’s application was granted. As such, there are two grounds of refusal.  
ISS UE AND DECISION  
[3] At issue  in this appeal  is whether the applicant falls within the class of persons described 
in sub section s 41(b) and 52(1) of the IRPA as well as subsection 4 .1 of the Regulations ,3 thereby 
excluding him  from consideration as a spouse for the purpose of the Regulations.  
[4] Having  considered the evidence and the submissions from the appellant’s counsel and the 
Minister of Immigration , Refugees and Citizenship (Minister), the Panel finds that the appellant 
has not proven, on a balance of probabi lities that section 52(1) of the IRPA is not valid in law for 
not having the written authorization to return to Canada even though there  is an incorrect 
reference to sub section 41(b) of the IRPA. There was no dispute that the applicant was under a 
deemed d eportation order which was enforced on July 31, 2010 and that he did not have the 
consent or authorization to return to Canada.  
[5] Also, having  considered the evidence and submissions from both the counsel for the 
appellant and the Minister, with respect to s ection 4.1 of the Regulations,  the Panel finds that the 
appellant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that section 4.1 does not apply.   
[6] For the following  reasons, t he appeal is dismissed pursuant to subsection 69(1) of the 
IRPA .

INTRODUCTION AND DECISION  
[1] The following reasons explain why I am dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX  
(the Appellant).  The Appellant has appealed the Refugee Protection Division’s (RPD) April 9 , 
201 9 decision that rejected his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has asked that I 
substitute the RPD’s decision with my own finding that the Appellant  is a Convention refugee or 
a person in need of protection, or that I return the file to the RPD for redetermination. I find that 
the RPD was correct to determine that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee and that he is not 
a person in need of protect ion.  
BACKGROUND  
[2] The Appellant has made the following key allegations in his Basis of Claim (BOC) forms 
and at the RPD hearing:  
 That he is a citizen of Pakistan and no other country.  
 That he provided information to the police which aided in the capture and prosecution of 
several members of the religious extremist group Lashkar -e-Jhangvi (LeJ).  
 That LeJ members threatened, attacked, and kidnapped the XXXXXXXXX and that LeJ 
members attacked and threatened the XXXXXXXXX’s family.  
 That the XXXXXXXXX fled to the United States of America (USA) and subsequently crossed 
into Canada, where he made his refugee claim.  
[3] The RPD found that the XXXXXXXXX’s claim failed because  of credibility problems.  
Specifically, the RPD found that several material omissions and inconsis tencies in the Appellant’s 
evidence and testimony undermined his allegations that he had ever suffered past persecution.

[1] These are the reasons of the decision of the Immigration Appeal Division in File

status or benefit under the Act.   The relationship was , therefore , one described in sub section 4(1)

admissible to Canada as a member of the family class accor dingly.  
 
[3] Today, I received the oral evidence from the appellant in person and from the applicant 
via teleconference.  At the conclusion of testimony, counsel for the appellant argued that the 
evidence before me was such that the decision of the immigration  officer should be set aside.  
The Minister was of the opinion that the appellant had not met the burden of proof falling on her.

put forward the best evidence.  I also turned my mind to the Act,  which tells me that the 
Immigration Appeal Division (IAD)  may base a decision on evidence adduced in the 
proceedings that it considers credible or trustworthy in the circumstances .

REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX  (the Appellant), a citizen of Iran, appeals a decision of the Refugee 
Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.  He has submitted no new 
evidence in support of his appeal , nor is requesting an oral hearing . The Appellant asks the 
Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to reverse the decision of the RPD a nd find that the Appellant is 
a Convention refugee or a  person in need of protection or i n the alternative, that the RAD refer the 
matter back to the RPD, to a different member, for  a redetermination.  
DETERMINATION  
[2] Pursuant to Section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA), the 
RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant 
is a Convention refugee.  
Background  
[3] The Appellant alleged before the RPD that as a practicing Christian converted from Islam, 
he faces severe persecution in Iran as an Apostate. Details of his claim will be fo und in his Basis 
of Claim (BOC) form and the transcript of the hearing in the Appell ant’s record.  
[4] The Appellant’s application for refugee protection was heard on March 4 and 12, 2014 , 
and a decision in writing was issued on July 23, 2014 denying the claim. The decision was based 
on credibility issues described in the reasons for that deci sion. The RPD did consider the claim in 
the context of a sur place  claim ; however , found that there was insufficient evidence to support 
the Appellant’s claim to be a true Christian.  
[5] The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its assessment of the sur place  nature of this 
claim. This is the only issue on which the Appellant is seeking his appeal.

 The Role of RAD  
[6] Counsel has made some submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review 
of an RPD decision. However, the RAD finds that the re cent Federal Court decision, in 
Huruglica ,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be 
applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first -level administrative 
tribunal. Justice XXXXXX states  in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision:  
[54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD’s decision on the 
standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the 
RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the 
RPD’s decisio n and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant 
is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment 
departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.  
[55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of 
the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular 
advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate 
court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an “overriding and palpable 
error.”  
[7] Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD’s decision and come to 
an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need 
of protection. Deference will be a fforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other 
findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions.

missed the first meeting because of transportation related issues. The second meeting , which it is 
alleged the Appellant missed , was actually cancelle d by the Church due to a scheduling conflict 
for space , so the Appellant submits that it is unreasonable to blame the Appellant for missing a

REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons for the decision in the appeal of Nirmala Devi RamXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX for non -compliance with the residency obligation prescribed in section 28 of the 
Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA ). 
[2] Section 28 of the IRPA  requires per manent residents of Canada to be physically present 
in Canada for at least 730 days in a five -year period.  The counting of that five -year period can 
be triggered in a number of ways.  In this case, the counting is linked to  the Appellant’s 
application for  a Permanent Resident Card .2  The relevant five -year period is December 8, 2010 
to December 8, 2015 .3  The Appellant has 575  days in Canada during the relevant period.4  The 
Appellant did not challenge the legal validity of the residency obligation determination and no 
exceptions to physical presence in Canada are relevant in this ca se.  As such, the hearing focus ed 
on whether there are sufficient humanitarian and compas sionate (H&C) considerations to allow 
the appeal.  
[3] The Appellant is 37 years of age and a citizen of Guyana  who was granted permanent 
residence in Canada in May 1994 .5  She testified in person at the hearing  in English.   The 
Appellant’s mother, SXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXWitness), testified in English at the hearing.  
DECISION  
[4] After considering the testimony, documentary evidence and submissions, I find that, 
taking into account the best interests of a child directly affect ed by the decision, there are 
sufficient H&C  considerations warranting special relief in light of all the circumstances of the 
case .  The appeal is allowed .

ANALYSIS  
[5] Where permanent residents are in breach of the residency obligation under the IRPA,  they 
may avail themselves of the H&C jurisdictio n of the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD).  The 
granting  of H&C relief under section 67(1)(c) of the IRPA  requires me to consider all the 
circumstances of the case, including the best interests of any children impacted by the decision.  
[6] IAD decision -makers  have considered the following factors when determining whether 
there are sufficient H&C considerations to grant special relief:  
 extent of non -compliance;  
 the reasons for the appellant’s departure from Canada;  
 reasons for the lengthy stay abroad;  
 ties to the foreign country;  
 the appellant’s degree of establishment in Canada;  
 whether the appellant or their family would suffer hardship if the appeal is  
          dismissed;  
 whether there are unique or special circumstances present in the case, and;  
 the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision.  
These  factors are not exhaustive and the weight assigned to each factor varies according to the 
circumstances of t he case.  
Humanitarian & Compassionate Considerations  
 Extent of non -compliance  
[7] The Appellant has 575  days in Canada in the releva nt five -year period.  This is a  
moderate breach of the residency obligation requiring a commensurate level of H&C factors to 
justify the granting of special relief.  
 Reasons for the appellant’s departure from Canada and prolonged stay abroad  
[8] Although a citizen of Guyana, the Appellant  left for Barbados when she was 9 years of 
age.  Her parents had separated and her father lived in  Barbados.  She resided in Barbados from 
1989 to 1993 on a student visa.  Her parents decided that she should stay with her father for a 
number of reasons, including his financial stability.

[12]  After witnessing  her mother’s challenges the Appellant wanted to stay with her to be

probabilities, the Appellant reasonably believed that she no longer had status in Canada when 
she was issued a visitor visa in 2000.  
[14]  The finding above should not be taken as a blanket excuse for ap pellants to plead 
ignorance of the law  in order to avoid their obligations as permanent residents of Canada.  This

actions of state agents contributed to creating  a subjective belief that she no longer had status in 
this country.  Moreover, this was reinforced when the Appellant was issued a second visitor visa.  
The Appel lant’s  actions demonstrate that she sincerely held this belief, because she went to  the

permanent resident .  The visit to the MP’s office  crystalizes the time for assessing whether the

CONCLUSION  
[34]  Minister’s counsel suggested that the Appellant may have engaged in misrepresentation 
with respect to her 2013 visitor visa application because she subsequently attempted to maintain 
her permanent resident status.  As such, the suggestion is that the XXXXX lant did not intend to 
leave Canada when she entered using a visitor visa.  This proposition assumes that the Appellant 
knew she had status in Canada.  Firstly, intentions can change.  At the time of the visitor visa 
application the Appellant may have inte nded to come for a visit and go back to Barbados, but 
when she saw how her mother was doing she decided to make inquiries about sponsorship.  The 
Appellant was credible and forthright about this course of events.  Moreover, if she did have an 
intent to rem ain in Canada when she applied for visitor visa, it does not follow that she would go 
to the MP’s office to look into sponsorship requirements.  Rather, it is reasonable to expect that 
she would have simply proceeded with the Permanent Resident Card applic ation on her own.  
Secondly, since there is no evidence suggesting that the Appellant engaged in misrepresentation.  
[35]  Minister’s counsel provided me with two cases in support of her submissions.11  Those 
cases are distinguishable from this case because they  deal with permanent residents  who 
voluntarily relinquished  their  status  and the scope of the IAD’s  jurisdiction  in that regard.  I n this 
case , the IAD has jurisdiction and  the issue regarding  status turns on the Appellant’s  subjective 
view of her status , th e role immigration officials’ actions played in reinforcing her subjective  
belief and when the first opportunity to retu rn crystalized for XXXXXXXXX.  
[36]  The XXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXX were credible, consistent and forthright.  
[37]  The XXXXXXXXX left Canada as a child a nd eventually held a sincere belief that she no 
longer had status in Canada.  Immigration officials contributed to that belief and when she 
realize d that she has status in Canada the Appellant acted promptly and diligently to maintain her 
status.

 REASONS FOR DEC ISION  
 
[1] These are the reasons and decision of the Immigration Appeal Division  (the “IAD”)  in 
the appeal of SXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ( the “appellant ”), of the refusal to approve the permanent 
resident visa application made by Am XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ( the “applic ant ”), from India, 
who was sponsored by the appellant.  
 
[2] The details of the refusal are set out in the refusal letter and the visa officer's notes are as 
shown in the Record.  
 
[3] Counsel to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration ( the “respondent ”), argued  that 
the doctrine of res judicata  applies in this case, therefore preventing the IAD from hearing this 
appeal.  
 
[4] By way of background, the appellant is 35 years old and w as landed in Canada on July 
29, 2005. She was previously married in January 19 99 and w as divorced on June 11 , 2007.  
 
[5] The appellant is 37 years old and lives in India and this is his first marriage.  
 
[6] The appellant and the applicant were married in India on June  11, 2008.  
 
[7] The panel entered three disclosures from the appellant into evidenc e. There was also a 
copy of the Record before us and the panel heard oral arguments from counsel to both parties in 
advance of its decision. Both parties indicated that they had nothing more to add prior to my 
decision being rendered.  
 
[8] Counsel to the resp ondent made an oral application that I find that the doctrines of res 
judicata  prevent me from hearing this appeal, based on the grounds of refusal, that is Regulation  
4(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the “ Regulations ”).1

 [9] The is sue of res judicata  is the only issue I am deciding in the present decision.  
 
[10]  The doctrine of res judicata  and the associated concept of estoppel  are designed to 
advance the interests of justice by promoting finality in judicial decision making. The doctr ine 
applies when these three conditions are satisfied: first, the parties in the previous proceeding are 
the same; second, the previous decision was final;  and , third, the issue is the same.  
 
[11]  The purpose behind the doctrine of res judicata  was summarized in the case of Danyluk 
vs. Ainsworth Technologies Inc .2 as follows, and I quote:  
18.  The law rightly seeks a finality to litigation. To advance that objective, it 
requires litigants to put their best foot forward to establish the truth of their 
allegations  when first called upon to do so. A litigant, to use the vernacular, is 
only entitled to one bite at the cherry. The appellant chose the ESA as her forum 
and she lost. An issue, once decided, should not generally be re -litigated to the 
benefit of the losin g party and the harassment of the winner. A person should only 
be vexed once in the same cause. Duplicative litigation, potential inconsistent 
results, undue costs and inconclusive proceedings are to be avoided.  
 
[12]  The case of XXXXXXX  also confirmed the app lication of res judicata  to administrative 
proceedings such as those at the IAD.  
 
[13]  In the case at bar, all three of the conditions for res judicata  are answered in the 
affirmative. The previous IAD decision is a final adjudication of the same matter, the p arties to 
the previous appeal are the same, that is the appellant and the Minister of Citizenship and 
Immigration, and the issue is whether the marriage was captured by the bad faith prohibition 
found in Regulation  4(1).  
 
[14]  Generally , res judicata  applies i n public law to prevent applicants from re -applying, ad 
infinitum , with the same application, which would constitute an abuse of the process of 
administrative tribunals.

 [15]  Jurisprudence, such as the Federal Court  (the “Court”)  case of XXXXXX ,3 confirms  that a 
tribunal has jurisdiction to control its process and to prevent abuse, and may, therefore, consider 
whether to summarily dispose of an appeal that is an abusive attempt to re -litigate what was 
already decided.  
 
[16]  However, the Court also confirmed that the doctrine should not prevent an applicant from 
launching a second application based on changes of circumstances provided, that the change of 
circumstances is relevant to the matter to be decided.  
 
[17]  The appellant proposed the application on the grounds t hat the appellant and the applicant 
were now parents of a child and that that development, in itself, constituted special 
circumstances. Counsel to the appellant produced some medical evidence and also expressed the 
appellant's willingness to undergo deoxy ribonucleic acid  (DNA ) testing.  
 
[18]  For his part, the respondent argued that in her decision of December 17 , 2010, my 
colleague, Member XXXXX, dismissed the appeal in the face of evidence that the appellant and the 
applicant planned to have a baby, and that the appellant may even have been pregnant with the 
applicant's child at the time of the hearing.  
 
[19]  Member XXXXX found, based on a decision of the review of the evidence before her, that 
both tests in Regulation  4(1) were met, i.e. primary purpose and genui neness.  
 
[20]  I find that the fact that the appellant and the applicant were planning to have a baby did 
not prevent her from rendering her decision, and even if sufficient credible evidence were before 
me now, to establish that the appellant and the applicant  have a child from their union, this 
would not be a determinative factor in any decision I might take, particularly with respect to 
primary purpose.  
 
[21]  The other argument made by counsel for the appellant is that a breach of natural justice 
occurred due to an allegation that the appellant's prior counsel was incompetent.

 [22]  I had no evidence before me, however, to indicate that previous counsel had been notified 
of these allegations or that a complaint had been filed with the Law Society.  
 
[23]  In summary, the law  requires application of the doctrine of res judicata  to this appeal, 
unless special circumstances warrant making an exception, and whether taking into account all of 
the circumstances, applying the principle of res judicata  would cause an injustice.  
 
[24]  For  example, res judicata  may be overcome where fresh new evidence, previously 
unavailable, conclusively impeaches the original results.  
 
[25]  As I pointed out earlier, however, I am satisfied that Member XXXXX took her decision on 
the understanding that it was t he appellant's and the applicant's intent to become parents. 
Accordingly, that a child has now been born, would not have changed her finding.  
 
[26]  The preconditions for res judicata  do apply in this case and the appellant has not 
established that there are sp ecial circumstances to overcome that application. Furthermore, it has 
not been established that the integrity of the justice system would be enhanced by re -litigation or 
that an injustice would result if the doctrine of res judicata  is applied.  
 
[27]  In the cir cumstances and for reasons set out above, this appeal is dismissed because the 
doctrine of res judicata  applies and prevents a rehearing of this case.

Introduction [1] The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXX, appeals from  the refusal of an application for a permanent resident visa made by the appli cant, XXXXXXXXXXXXX. The appellant married the applicant and sponsored the applicant as a member of the family class. The application was refused because a visa officer determined that the marriage is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring status under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (the “IRPA”).
 
Issue and Decision [2]  At the time of the refusal, section 4 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (the “Regulations”) read as follows: 
4. For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered a spouse, a common-law partner, a conjugal partner or an adopted child of a person if the marriage, common-law partnership, conjugal partnership or adoption is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Act.

REASONS FOR DECISION  
INTRODUCTION  
[1] These are the reasons for the decision in the appeal of Mary Ronisiya ANXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXthe appellant), who appeals the refusal to approve the permanent resident 
application made by her spouse, RaymXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXthe applicant). The sponsored 
application for a visa was refused on the basis that the marriage of the appellant and applican t is 
not a genuine marriage and was entered into primarily for the purposes of acquiring status or 
privilege in Canada under the Immigration and Refugee Protection  Act  (IRPA)1. 
[2] In addition, the visa officer also found the applicant inadmissible to Canada for financial 
reasons, under section 39 of IRPA as there is insufficient evidence that adequate arrangement for 
his care and support, other than those that involve social assistance, have been made.  
ISSUE  
[3] The issue in this appeal is whether sub section 4(1)  of the Immigration and Refugee 
Protection Regulations  (IRPR)2 applies, thereby excluding the applicant from consideration as a 
member of the family class.  There are two com ponents: the foreign national shall not be 
considered a spouse if the marriage is not genuine or if it was entered into primarily for the 
purpose of acquiring any privilege under the IRPA . To succeed on the appeal, the appellant has 
to demonstrate that neither component applies to her relationship.   
[4] The issue pertaining to the financial inadmissibility of th e applicant pursuant to 
section  39 of the IRPA will only be  considered if it is determined that the applicant is a member 
of the family class.

[5] I have come to the conclusion that on a balance of probabilities, the marriage is genuine

the IRPA.   
[6] The appellant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that the applicant is not 
described by section 3 9 of the IRPA .  The appeal is  allowed for the following reasons.  
BACKGROUND  
[7] The appellant was born on April 9th, 1981 , in Sri Lanka and is now a Canadian citizen.  
The applicant was born on July 19th, 1975 , in Sri Lanka and is still living there.  This is their first 
marriage and they have one son together, born in 2008.  The marriage, an arranged one, took 
place on August 25, 2007.  
[8] In 2005, following the tsunami, the applicant applied for permanent residence as a 
refugee, under the special program that was put in to place b y the Canadian government. That 
application was refused on credibility issues.  
[9] This is the appellant ’s second application to sponsor her husband.  The  first one was 
presented in 2007.  After the interview, the officer, satisfied about the relationship, refused the 
application for misrepresentation.  He came to the conclusion that the applicant had made false 
declarations in his Tsunami application, render ing the applicant inadmissible to Canada for a 
period of two years. The appellant appealed the decision but withdrew her appeal once the 
two -year bar had elapsed and presented another sponsorship application which was received on 
October 10th 2012.

ANALYSIS  
[11]  In addition to the credibility of the witnesses, the factors listed in Chavez4 may guide the 
assessment that must be made as to the genuineness of the marriage.  These factors are not 
exhaustive. The weight given to each factor can vary from one  appeal to another depending on 
the circumstances of the case.  
[12]  In this appeal, the following factors were addressed: the arranged marriage, the visits, the 
mutual knowledge, the financial support and the implication in son’s life.   
Credibility of the wi tnesses  
[13]  I have heard evidence over the course of two and a half days – the first day and a half on 
January 25 and January 26, 2017 and the second one on April 25, 2017.   Both the appellant and 
the applicant testified with the help of a Tamil interpreter. The appellant and the applicant have 
been subjected to cross -examination.

4 [14]  There is no question that the applicant has demonstrated a desire to come to Canada in 
the past, as he admitted making false declarations in his 2005 Tsunami application to come to 
Canada. This, for the Minister, provides a strong motive to enter into a relationship in order to be 
sponsored to come to Canada.  That being said, it is important to evaluate the current file in its

and who had a child together.  Considering the length of time of the relationship, I find that it is 
not abnormal, when looking at events that occurred ten years ago, to find some inconsistencies 
between the forms and  the testimonies.  
[15]  For that reason, even though there were some discrepencies, I find that they were credible 
and believable witnesses who answered questions, on balance, in a direct and straightforward 
manner.  The applicant hesitated a few times and quest ions needed to be repeated from time to 
time.  Because of that, the Minister stated during submissions that the applicant’s testimony was 
difficult, that questions needed to be repeated or that he was not answering.  Taking into

The arranged marriage  
[16]  The visa officer mentioned that it was not clear as to whom exactly had arranged the 
marriage.  The appellant and the applicant explained during their testimony how the marriage was 
arranged and by whom.   After reviewing all the evidence, the forms and hearing the testimonies, 
I am satisfied that there is no contradiction on that subject.  The sponsor’s mother was looking for

also looking for a life partner for her son.  They discussed, looked at the charts and determined

[18]  The appellant declared that she did not know before the marriage that her husband had 
tried to come to Canada before, nor that he had made false declarations in his tsunami

8 [28]  This couple have  an eight -year -old son  together  and have been married for almost ten

Financial inadmissiblitiy  
[29]  Because I am satisfied that the mariage is a genuine marriage, the financial 
inadmissibility needs to be addressed.   
[30]  In appeals of refusals pursuant to section 39 of the IRPA , the applicant’s ability and 
willingness to support himself and his dependents and any arrangements for t he applicant’s 
support in Canada have to be examined. The relevant legislative section is set out as follows:  
39. Financial reasons - A foreign national is inadmissible for financial reasons if 
they are or will be unable or unwilling to support themselves or any other person 
who is dependent on them, and have not satisfied an officer that adequate 
arrangements for care and support, other than those that involve social assistance, 
have been made.  
 
 
[31]  To sponsor, the appellant is not subject to the requirement to meet the Minimum 
Necessary Income test, however the IRPA requires that she meet s her Sponsorship Undertaking 
not to hold Canada or a province liable and to repay any social assistance paid to or on behalf of 
the sponsored foreign national pursuant to se ction 132 of the Regulations .  
[32]  The Minister argued that the appellant was willingly on welfare from 2008 and 2012, that 
she went back to work in 2012, just before submitting the new sponsorship application, thus 
showing that she only started to work again to be able to sponsor her spouse.  The appellant 
stopped working before the birth of her child and testified that , because she is a single mother, 
she did not want to send her child to daycare, she only went back to work in 2012.  One might not 
agree with th e reasons provided for not going back to work, but one cannot judge the reasons 
behind someone else’s decision.  We also need to keep in mind cultural background.  I estimate

9 that the reasons she mentioned for not going back to work are satisfying.  What the evidence also 
shows is that the appellant has been working for the same employer since 20129, does her 
income tax return every year, and is even able to save some money, as shown by her bank 
account statement10. The fact that the appellant has been working for the last five years, with the 
same employer, is a positive factor in the file.  
[33]  As for the applicant, the Minister, because of the past misrepresentation, had a lot of 
concerns regarding his employment.  The applicant has admitted he made false representations  in 
his t sunami application.  He is now working and there is no indication in the evidence that he has 
made any false declaration again.  The applicant has not indicated an unwillingness to work, 
stated he has been working since his father die d in 1993 and evidence was provided to show that 
he has a job offer for when he comes to Canada11. If the legislator had wanted to prevent people 
from applying again after having misrepresented themselves, he would have written the IRPA 
accordingly, this is  not the case.    
[34]  The above, does not support a conclusion that the applicant is a person described by 
section 39 of the IRPA.    
CONCLUSION  
[35]  I find on a balance of probabilities that pursuant to subsection 4(1) of the IRPR, the 
marriage was not entered into primarily for the purpose of immigration and that it is genuine.  
[36]  I find that the applicant is not described by section 39 of the Act .  
[37]  The appeal is allowed.

 [1] The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, appeals th e refusal of the sponsored application for a permanent resident visa of the applicant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, her spouse.  The application was refused because the visa officer concluded that th e applicant was a person described in section 4 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations  (the Regulations).  The visa officer held that the applicant entered into the marriage pr imarily for the purpose of acquiring status or privilege under the Act.  [2] The Regulations operate to exclude applicants fr om consideration in particular circumstances.  Section 4 of the Regulations provides that if the marriage is not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of acquiring any status or privilege under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA), the applicant is not a spouse under the IRPA.  The onus is on the appellant to demonstrate that the applicant is not caught by the excluding section of the Regulations.   [3] In order to be caught by section 4 of the Regulations, the preponderance of reliable evidence must demonstrate that the relationship is  not genuine and was entered into primarily for the purpose of the applicant acquiring any status or privilege under the IRPA.  In order to succeed on appeal, the appellant need only establish one of the prongs of the test has not been met.  [4] The appellant contended that the refusal is no t valid in law.  Further, that the relationship with the applicant is bona fide and the marriage was not entered into primarily for the purpose of the applicant gaining admission to Canada as a me mber of the family class.  She also submitted that the applicant intends to reside permanently with her.  Minister’s counsel urged the panel to dismiss the appeal.    [5] The appeal commenced on December 1, 2006 having been heard previously on July 5, 2006 before another member.  The matter was to be resumed by the other member in order to hear testimony from the applicant at the conclu sion of the appellant’s evidence.  A resumption

completely discordant with what the Applicant told the vi sa officer.  
[23]  I note as well that the cousin XXXXXX has not provided any evidence in this proceeding 
and that the Appellant was in Tanzania when the Applicant signed the TRV application.  
[24]  The Appellant testified that XXXXXX had assisted with the spousal spons orship 
application as well, in which  the Applicant indicate d that she had never previously been refused 
a TRV.14 If the Appellant’s testimony is true, XXXXXX would have certainly been aware of the 
prior application. (In her testimony, the Applicant indicate d that it was not XXXXXX, but her 
sister, who had assisted with her application for permanent residence.)  
[25]  With respect to this TRV issue, the Applicant testified at the appeal hearing that she 
signed the application but did not understand what was in the f orms. When asked by her counsel 
what she thought she was signing, she claimed that her cousin XXXXXX told her it was a visa 
application, but nothing more. She did not even know what country it was for. At the visa post 
interview, as noted, the Applicant ha d claimed that the TRV application was not prepared by her 
cousin but by an agent.15 
[26]  When asked about the “husband” listed on the TRV application, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, 
the Applicant denied knowing this individual.

[27]  When asked about what discussions she has since had with her cousin who she claims is 
responsible for the TRV documents, she testified that she told him he had made trouble for her 
by filling out the forms as he did. However, she claims that he did not provide any explanation 
for the falsehoods in  the applications, other than to say that he wanted to surprise her with a

[28]  The Applicant’s testimony that she had no idea about the forms her cousin had her s ign in

When the application was filed, I applied with an agent. I gave information

CONCLUSION  
[29]  As confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in F.H. v. McDougall ,17 the evidence 
must always be clear, convincing and cogent in order to satisfy the balance of probabilities test . 
Such was not the case in this appeal. Indeed, the evidence of the Appellant and Applicant was so 
confused and contradictory that none of it can  be considered reliable.  
[30]  The Appellant has failed to establish that section 4(1) of the Regulations does not apply 
to this relationship.   Neither witness was  credible and I am satisfied that the Applicant filed a 
TRV application in 2015 that was completely  fraudulent in an effort to go to Canada.  As held by 
the Honourable Mr. Justice Shore:18 
An Applicant who trifles with the truth in legal proceedings cannot expect to 
be successful; thus, a Court may discredit even true statements, not knowing 
where the tru th begins and ends, and a climate of uncertainty then prevails.  
[31]  The appeal is dismissed.

[1] XXXXXXX  (the Appellant), a citizen of Ghana,  appeals a decision of the Refugee 
Protection Division (RPD) rejecting  her claim for refugee protection.  
[2] The Appellant  submit ted documents  to be considered as new evidence  pursuant to 
s.110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act or IRPA) in support of her  
appeal. However, the Appellant did not request a hearing before the Refugee Appeal Division 
(RAD) pursuant to section 1 10 (6) of the Act.  
[3] The Appellant requests that the RAD set aside the RPD’s decision and  remit the matter 
back to the RPD for redetermination. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the RAD grant 
any other order that the Division deems reasona ble and expedient having regard to the peculiar 
facts and circumstances of this case.   
DETERMINATION  
[4] Pursuant to Section 111(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the 
RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neithe r a Convention refugee (CR) 
nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.  
[5] This appeal is dismissed.  
Background:  
[6] The Appellant alleged before the RPD that her husband’s famil y members want to carry 
out female circumcision (female genital mutilation) on her infant daughter who was born in 
Canada  on XXX, 2014. XXXXXXXXXXXXXX and her husband oppose this practice. The Appellant is 
afraid that she would personally face serious harm, torture or death due to her op posi tion to this 
practice. The A ppellant’s husband remains in Ghana and he does not believe that he could protect 
his wife or daughter in these circumstances. The  Appellant also alleged that all female family 
members of her husband have undergone this procedur e and her father -in-law in particular wishes 
to preserve this custom .

[10]  Section 110(4) of IRPA provides that an Appellant may present only evidence that arose

claim by the RPD. Therefore , I am not satisfied that these documents meet the expre ss statutory

[13]  I also have serious concerns about the credibility of t hese documents because the author of

libia majora and libia minora .

Appellant’s c ousin informing her that her father -in-law wants to have the XXXXXXXXX’s daughter 
undergo FGM. The RPD found the inconsistency regarding the date of this call. The Appellant

The Appellant clearly testifie d that the alleged call was on June 4, 2014 (at 58:43 minute mark in 
the audio recording of the hearing). The RPD cannot be found to have erred in this respect.  
[27]  Moreover, her narrative states that her father -in-law  called her on June 28 ; however, the  
Appellant testified that he called her on July 28,  2014  (at 1hr 3:30 minute mark) .  
[28]  The XXXXXXXXX ’s whole story is based on two alleged and calls from Ghana, both recent at 
the time of the hearing and yet the Appellant provided contradicto ry informat ion. The Appellant

testimony at the hearing that she indeed has a short -term memory challenge which was giving her

 counsel urged her to get help of the psychologist and to ma ke her claim for refugee protection ”. I 
cannot find that the RPD ignored the report, however  it was open to the RPD to assign the weight 
it considered appropriate. It is the RPD’s responsibility to determine whether the Appellants are 
credible, and the RPD  is not required to defer to a psychologist’s report when making findings of

[30]  A psychological report presented by a refugee claimant does not serve to prove the alleged 
persecution suffered in the past or fu ture persecution. S uch reports  may establish that the 
Appellant suffers from a condition or exhibits symptoms that are consi stent with the alleged 
trauma. Further, a psychological report might assist the RPD in conducting the hearing in an 
appropriately se nsitive manner or to consider whether apparent credibility problems are , instead , 
the result of a psychological condition.   
[31]  The Federal Court in Mico5 stated:  “Just because a patient is suffering from psychological 
problems and manifests symptoms associated with those problems does not mean that the 
patient’s account of past persecution as the cause of th ose problems can be believed.” The RPD 
noted in its reaso ns, “Having reviewed Dr. XX ’s report, I find that there is nothing in the 
document to suggest that the psychologist independently verified any of the allegations reported 
by the Appellant ”. I find that the RPD’s finding is supportable . 
[32]  I am aware that  the Federal Court6 has accepted that a claimant's inconsistency in 
recollecting specific dates may well be peripheral to the central issues in the case at hand. 
However, in this case, the whole basis of the claim is based on two calls; first, a call about  an 
alleged argument in the family and, second, another alleged call from her father -in-law. This was 
not a case of historic persecution.  
[33]  The RPD questioned the Appellant about her husband; the RAD finds him to be a 
similarly situated person because he also is against FGM practice allegedly dear to her father -in-
law. No harm has happened to him.

[37]  Having considered the totality of the evi dence before me, I find that the Appellant is

[38]  The RPD also considered state protection. It  is trite law that the burden is on the Appellant 
to provide clear and convincing evidence that the state is either unable or unwilling to provide 
adequate protection to the Appellant.  
[39]  The RPD’s stated in its reasons, “I cannot find on a balance of p robabilities the police in

[41]  I note that the RPD considered contradictory evidence that the police ha ve high levels of

protection analysis. I would have preferred to see a more detailed analysis on the issue of 
effectiveness of the state’s efforts to eradicate the heinous practice of the female genital 
mutilation; however , even though the RPD’s analysis is rather brief , it is supportable.  
[42]  I note that RPD correctly identified that this practice was outlawed in 1994. I also note 
that the government strengthened its efforts by ratifying the Maputo Protocol of 2007. In ad dition 
to the above, the Ghana D omes tic Violence Act of 2007 provides protective orders for wom en

[43]  The effectiveness of the governmen t’s efforts  to curb this practice become more apparent 
when one considers the percentage of persons who have undergone the FGM procedure by age 
groups. The World Health Organization states that 3.8% of the females have undergone this 
procedure ; however , when it is broken down by age groups ,7 age group 15 to 19 years , shows the

 The claimant alleges that he worked as a XXXXX at his XXXXX XXXXX during the daytime and worked as a XXXXX salesperson in the evenings.  An individual known as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, who belonged to a gang involved in drugs, wanted the claimant to work with him.  By doing so, XXXX told the cl aimant that he would be able to turn his XXXXX XXXXX business into a franchise and would personally become rich.  Because the claimant refused to work with XXXXX, he was targeted by him and his accomplices.  XXXXX and his accomplices used guns to issu e death threats to the claimant.  Towards the end of XXXXX 2006, the claimant made one attempt to file a report against XXXXX and his accomplices with the judiciary police, but he received no assistance from them because of lack of sufficient evidence.  The clai mant felt that state protection from Mexican state authorities would not be forthcoming since XXXX was associated with corrupt members of the security forces.  ANALYSIS
 The determinative issue in this case is state protection.  In making the assessment in this claim, the panel considered the claimant’s oral  and written testimony, his counsel’s submissions and all of the other documentary evidence entered at the hearing.  The panel particularly considered the documentary evidence pertaining to  measures dealing with crime, including drug related crime and corruption, as well as evidence about the police, the availability of mechanisms for lodging complaints and, in general, the level of democracy in Mexico.   
State Protection  
Based on the evidence adduced and for the follo wing reasons, the panel finds that there is adequate state protection for the claimant should he be returned to Mexico.  The panel finds that the claimant has not met the burden of establishing  “clear and convincing” proof of lack of state protection for individuals like him in Mexico.

representative for the Appellant as the XXXXX lant is a minor. The Appellant has not submitted new 
evidence in support of her appeal and does not request an oral hearing. She asks the Refugee 
Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own determination. 
In the altern ative, the Appellants ask the RAD return the matter to a differently -constituted panel 
of the RPD for re -determination.  
DETERMINATION  
[2] Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (IRPA), the 
RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a 
person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.  
Background  
[3] The Appellant alleged before the RPD that, upon return to Austria, she will be kidnapped 
by her father and forced to undergo fe male genital mutilation.  
[4] The XXXXXXXXX’s claim for refugee protection was heard on October 28, 2015. By a 
decision of October 30, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD found that the Appellant 
failed to rebut the presumption of state protection in Austria.  
[5] The Appellant submi ts that the RPD erred in its state protection analysis and ignored 
evidence.  
ANALYSIS  
Role of the RAD  
[6] What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD? 
While the Appellant makes no argument with respect to the role of the  RAD, the RAD notes that

 the Federal Court, in Huruglica ,1 considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and 
the RPD. It found that the RAD had erred in simply reviewing the RPD’s decision on a standard 
of reasonableness, rather than conducting its own independent assessment of the Appellant’s 
refugee c laim. The Court held that the RAD’s application of a reasonableness standard curtailed

In the Court’s view, the RAD should not even engage in a standard of re view analysis; rather, it 
should consider the purpose of the appellate tribunal, the statutory provisions, comparable 
expertise, and comparative appellate regimes.   
[7] Justice XXXXXX stated the following in Huruglica : 
Having concluded that the RAD erred in r eviewing the RPD’s decision on the 
standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the 
RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the 
RPD’s decision and come to an independent assessment of wh ether the claimant is 
a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment 
departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.   
In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the 
RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular 
advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate 
court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an “overriding and palpable 
error.”   
[8] Consideri ng the recent jurisprudence, including the Court’s decision in Huruglica , the 
RAD will review all aspects of the RPD’s decision and come to an independent assessment of the 
Appellant’s refugee claim, recognizing and respecting the conclusion of the RPD on such issues 
as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. 
Where the RAD’s assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD will substitute its own 
determination.

[16]  Further, the RAD finds that the Appellant’s argument that the RPD applied irrelevant and

[17]  The Appellant has submitted that the RPD mischaracterized her profile and did not take 
into consideration that she is a child of African descent . The RAD does not agree. The RPD 
accurately characterized the Appellant as a child with Austrian citizenship of African descent at 
risk of kidnapping and forced genital mutilation by her father. It not only considered her profile, it

 [18]  The Appellant has submitted that the RPD’s expectation of reporting to the police is 
unreasonable. The RAD disagrees.  
[19]  It is important to note some state protection principles set out by the Courts. A refugee 
claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting 
only a subjective re luctance to engage the state.  Doubting the effectiveness of the protection 
offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption 
of state protection. Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate prot ection to be invoked 
only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of 
their home state. The onus is on the refugee claimant to approach the state for protection in 
situations where state protection might be re asonably forthcoming.  In the absence of a 
compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state 
will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a 
willingness and  the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.  The 
refugee claimant’s burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in  
question: the more democratic the state’s institutions, the more the ref ugee claimant must have 
done to exhaust all courses of action open to them. In a functioning democracy, a refugee 
claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been 
required to exhaust all of the recourses available to  them domestically before claiming refugee 
status. A refugee claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the 
circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the 
steps taken and the refugee cla imant’s interactions with the authorities.    
[20]  The RPD noted that the Appellant’s mother did not approach police in Austria because she 
heard from individuals in the African community that there is discrimination against Africans in 
Austria. She also indica ted that she heard police would not help her because she does not speak 
German. However, the RAD finds, based on the documentary evidence, some of which is noted 
above, that state protection would have been reasonably forthcoming had the XXXXXXXXX’s mother  
reported her problem to police in Austria. The evidence establishes that Austria is a functioning 
democracy with the willingness and apparatus necessary to provide protection to its citizens. The 
RPD was not wrong in its view that had the Appellant’s moth er sought state protection in Austria, 
she would have received an adequate response. The RPD was not wrong to find that the 
Appellant’s mother, and by extension the Appellant, failed to take all objectively reasonable

 efforts to exhaust all courses of acti on reasonably available to her. It was not wrong to find that 
the XXXXXXXXX’s subjective reluctance to engage the state had no objective basis.  The RAD agrees 
with these findings.  
[21]  The XXXXXXXXX has also alleged that the RPD mischaracterized her profile by holding her to 
the standard of an adult (her mother) and based its determination on the actions and expectations 
of her mother. The Appellant’s argument has no merit. In assessing the adequacy of state 
protection, the RPD must consider the steps taken by t he refugee claimant to seek protection in 
their home country and the refugee claimant’s interactions with the authorities in their home 
country. In the case of a minor, especially an infant as in this case, the Board must consider the 
steps taken by his or  her parents or caregivers. The Appellant’s mother in this case is the best 
possible witness to support the Appellant’s claim for protection. She has cared for the Appellant 
since birth and initiated her claim for protection in Canada. The Board cannot ign ore her 
experience in Austria with respect to the Appellant’s allegations and the RPD was not wrong to 
consider her experience in Austria in the determination of the Appellant’s claim.            
[22]  The Appellant has alleged that the RPD mischaracterized the risk she faces in Austria. The 
RAD disagrees. As noted above, the RPD clearly set out the risk the Appellant alleges she faces 
in Austria and conducted an analysis of the evidence regarding the availability of state protection 
for Austrians with that parti cular risk profile. It considered the issue of racial discrimination in 
Austria. It noted the Austrian law that prohibits female genital mutilation and cutting. It noted that 
there were no reports of police or judicial reluctance to pursue such cases. It n oted the 
government’s continued efforts to monitor child abuse and prosecute offenders. The RPD 
correctly characterized the risk the Appellant alleges to face in Austria and correctly interpreted 
the evidence on the availability of state protection for tho se who face such a risk.  
[23]  The Appellant has alleged that the RPD ignored evidence. The RPD is presumed to have 
considered all of the evidence before it, and there is no requirement for the panel to refer to each 
document in the record.  Notwithstanding this  presumption, the Appellant argues that the RPD 
made very selective usage of an Amnesty International (AI) report by relying on only two 
paragraphs of the 60 page report to support its conclusion while ignoring hundreds of paragraphs 
that contradict its co nclusion. However, the Appellant only presented excerpts of two AI reports 
to the RPD and the RPD addressed those excerpts in its reasons. The RPD is unable to consider
