 evidence that is not before it. Nonetheless, the RPD does acknowledge from the excerpts , 
information about institutional racism in the Austrian justice system and discriminatory practices 
in law enforcement structures. The RAD notes that the 60 page AI report the Appellant refers to is 
dated April 2009 while the AI report in the National Doc umentation Package is from 2015. As 
noted above, a reflection of Austria’s success in dealing with racial discrimination is the absence 
of this as an issue of concern in AI’s annual report on Austria from 2015. The RAD gives more 
weight to AI’s 2015 report  as it more accurately reflects the current situation in Austria.                  
CONCLUSION  
[24]  After reviewing all the evidence in the record the RAD has reached the same conclusion as 
the RPD. The RAD concurs with the RPD that the Appellant has failed to r ebut the presumption 
of state protection. The RAD finds that the Appellant has adequate state protection available to 
her in Austria. The RAD finds that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in 
need of protection.  
[25]  Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA , the RAD  confirms the decision of the RPD  and 
dismisses the appeal.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
[1] XXXX XXXX  (the Appellant,)  and her daughter XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXthe minor) are

[23]  The Appellant did not make any submissions on standard of review.  
[24]  The RPD wrote on the issue of credibility the following: “I find the principal claimant to

[25]  An Appellan t found to be credible is not necessarily a Convention refugee (CR) or a 
person in need of protection. Alternatively, under certain circumstances, an incredible person with 
a specific profile and country condition may be a CR or a person in need of protect ion. However, 
the issue of state protection can be determinative in most circumstances.  
[26]  Thus , in my opinion, the determinative issue is “state protection”.  In state protection, th e 
panel is required to consider  particular circumstances of the Appellant. Th ose “circumstances” are 
defined by the findings of fact.  Thus , the issue in this case is  - did the RPD’s analysed state 
protection reasonably consider the particular situation of the Appellant? This is an issue of mixed 
facts and law, and the following ana lysis is regarding the appropriate standard of review to be 
applied.  
[27]  The standard of review regarding appeals before the RAD is not specifically addressed in 
the Act.  
[28]  In assessing and selecting the appropriate standard of review, the RAD considered the 
factors outlined in XXXXXX v. Criminal Trial Lawyers’ Association,4 which take into account the 
list of factors in XXXXXXXX .5

[35]  The RPD, the tribunal of the first instance, derives its authority from the Act to make a 
decision on whether to accept or reje ct a claim for refugee protection.7 The RPD members have 
the expertise to interpret and apply the Act and are experts in assessing claims based on the 
particulars of the claimant. The RPD must conduct a hearing8 and thus it hears directly from 
claimants (a nd witnesses if appropriate) in making its finding on credibility. The RPD has the 
expertise in making findings of fact after considering the totality of evidence before it , including 
the country conditions after hearing and evaluating all the evidence bef ore it.

must proceed without a hearing in most cases on the basis of the record, submissions by the 
parties and new evidence if any are accepted by it.9 RAD's authority to  consider new evidence

evidence or evidence submitted in response to the Minister’s evidence, under subsection 110(5).

in all the circumstances, including those particular to the appellants, for them to seek refuge there .20 
[33]  To assess the possibility of an IFA, the appel lants’ personal situation must be considered, as

communities, including against XXXXXXXXXXXX I believe  the Appellants do not have a viable IFA in Chile.

 REASONS FOR DECISION  
 
INTRODUCTION  
 
[1] These are my reasons and decision  with respect to an appeal by XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX , 
(the “appellant ”) pursuant to subsection 63(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act  (the 
“Act ”).1 He is appealing from a decision made outside of Canada regarding his residency 
obligation.  
 
[2] Section 28 of  the Act  requires a permanent resident to be physically present in Canada for 
at least 730 days in the five -year period imm ediately prior to an assess ment  for a travel 
document. In a May 11, 2011 decision,2 the officer concluded that the appellant had not met the 
residency obligation and also determined that there were not sufficient humanitarian and 
compassionate considerations to justify the retention  of permanent resident status.  
 
ISSUE  
 
[3] The relevant five year period for assessment in this case is the five years immediately 
prior to April 20, 2011 . The appellant challenged the legal validity of the refusal and alleges that 
he has been physically prese nt in Canada for a total number of days well above the requirement.  
 
[4] The Minister of Cit izenship and Immigration (the “respondent”)  asks me to dismiss the 
appeal  regarding legal validity and took no position on humanitarian and compassionate relief , 
which  can be granted if, taking into account the best interest of a child or children directly 
affected by the decision, sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations exist which 
warrant special relief circumstances of the case.3

 ANALYSIS  
 
Legal Val idity  
 
[5] The appellant was landed in Canada on June 22, 2005 with his wife, two daughters and a 
son. His application for a travel document that was signed on April 20, 20114 states that he was 
last physically present in Canada on December 18, 2006. At the he aring the appellant indicated 
this was an error and should have been the year 2010.  
 
[6] Information in the application form alleges substantial periods of time spent in Canada. At 
the hearing the appellant offered similar information , alleging that from the time of landing in 
June 2005 until December 2006 he resided in Brampton, with departures from Canada for only 
two weeks in Dec 2005 and another visit to India from Feb 2006 – June 30, 2006, for a total of 
127 day s out of the country. He alleged  that he rem ained in Canada from Dec 2006 to Dec 2010 
without any departures and returned to India in December 2010. He applied for his travel 
document and to return and pick up his Permanent resident Card in April 2011 but the application 
for a travel document genera ted the negative decision regarding his residency obligation.  
 
[7] In support of this appeal the appellant provided disclosure that includes employment and 
income information, documents related to a house in Canada, and an Alberta Operator ’s license  
and perso nal health card.  
 
[8] I find that the appellant has not established the extent of physical presence alleged. The 
appellant relied mainly on employment and income information in support of his allegation of 
extensive physical presence in Canada  but that evidenc e failed to establish his allegation  on a 
balance of probabilities. I find that the appellant has had some periods of residence in Canada 
since landing and some employment activities in Canada. However, the documentary material 
submitted is not independent ly probative of the extent alleged and his oral testimony at the 
hearing did not credibly supplement that evidence. His testimony was, on balance, not credible in 
material areas. He was vague and unclear about the nature and specifics of his employment and  
income in Canada  and  not reasonably consistent or able to provide clear detail s that would

 suggest participation in the alleged ongoing and full time employment.  The appellant’ s testimony 
was vague and at times evasive , for example with respect to questio ns about where he lived in 
Canada at material times. Finally, he failed to resolve contradictory residence and income 
information in his application. The information in his application form cannot be relied on 
because the appellant conceded that it contain ed errors about his physical presence and his 
income.  
 
[9] Notably lacking from the appellant’s disclosure and evidence at the hearing is the type of 
evidence that arises from and is inevitably incidental to daily presence in Canada. The appellant  
had opportun ity to provide supportive evidence prior to the hearing but failed to produce some of 
the simple and obvious, such as photographs of participation in family events  in Canada , 
documents generated by school, home and community participation, bank records, cr edit card 
bills, receipts related to daily living, home utility bills, rental agreements, evidence of medical 
appointments, charity contributions, etc. which is the inevitable paper trail that emerges from 
home ownership , work, children and participation  in community. I acknowledge the presence of a 
co-worker at the hearing who attested to the appellant’s work and community relationships but in 
the circumstances that was not sufficient to overcome the dearth of reliable documentary 
evidence of physical pres ence in Canada for the amount of time alleged by the appellant. He has 
relied substantially on employment information, which is not sufficient for reasons indicated 
above, and he has failed to provide the type of evidence that ought to be reasonably availa ble 
from daily presence in Canada.  
 
[10]  At the close of the hearing and in response to the questions he was asked during the 
course of the hearing, the appellant indicated that he could obtain additional documents such as 
evidence of community involvement etc . I characterized the appellant’s submission as an 
application to submit  late disclosure. I am denying that application because there has been ample 
opportunity for the appellant to provide supportive documentation in response to the visa 
officer’s decisio n and in preparation for this appeal. Reasonable explanation was not provided for 
failure to submit such documentation earlier. Rather, the application arises as a belated attempt to 
rehabilitate the gaps in his testimony and evidence that became apparent during the course of the 
hearing.

Humanitarian and Compassionate Considerations  
 
[11]  I turn now to consideration of whether there are sufficient humanitarian and 
compassionate considerations in this case that would warrant relief from the legally valid 
dec ision concerning failure to meet the residency obligation.  
 
[12]  The courts have indicated that discretionary relief may be granted when circumstances 
“would excite in a reasonable [person] in a civilized community, a desire to relieve the 
misfortunes of anothe r… ”5 The courts have confirmed that it is not sufficient to merely identify 
goals such as family unity or a general desire to live in Canada, which are always present to a 
lesser or greater degree. The Supreme Court of Canada endorsed the concepts of “unus ual, 
undeserved or disproportionate” hardship as a guide for the proper application of discretionary 
relief from the requirements of the Act .6 
 
[13]  A number of factors have been established from the many cases that have considered this 
issue in the past and I have used those factors to evaluate whether there are humanitarian and 
compassionate grounds for relief in this case.  
 
[14]  I find that the available evidence in this case does not support the granting of 
discretionary relief . The appellant does not come with c lean hands, having been found not 
credible in relation to his alleged physical presence in Canada. The appellant has some 
establishment in Canada but given the lack of credibility about physical presence, there is not 
reliable evidence that he is establish ed in terms of employment or assets. He testified that he 
owns some rental properties but the evidence about this was unclear. He did not provide reliable 
evidence of family ties in Canada. I accept that he is somewhat connected to community based on 
the p resence and information from his co -worker at the hearing. It was not established that there 
are children whose best interests are negatively affected by the appellant’s loss of permanent 
resident status.

[15]  In conclusion, the factors for discretionary re lief do not weigh in f avour of the appellant.  
 
[16]  Based on the evidence before me I find that the visa officer’s decision regarding the 
appellant’s residency obligation failure is legally valid. I also find that there are not sufficient 
humanitarian and comp assionate considerations in this case that would warrant relief from the 
legally valid decision concerning failure to meet the residency obligation.   
 
DECISION  
 
The appeal is dismissed.

OVERVIEW  
[1] XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the Appellant , is a 44 -year -old citizen of Pakistan and permanent 
resident (PR) of Canada.  Twenty -one days after landing in Canada as a PR in April 20 07, the 
Appellant  returned to Pakistan.  He has not been back to Canada since.  
[2] In October 2020, the Appellant  applied for a PR travel document to re turn to Canada, 
which was refused in the decision underlying this appeal.  The application was refused as the 
Appellant  had failed to meet the residency obligation, with zero days of residency in Canada in the 
five years preceding the application, well sho rt of the 730 days required.  It was also determined 
that the Appellant  had not established that his personal circumstances involve humanitarian and 
compassionate (H&C) considerations that justify the retention of his PR status .1 
[3] On appeal, the Appellant  concedes the legal validity of the refusal but is seeking special 
relief on H&C grounds.  The burden lies with him to establish sufficient grounds to warrant special 
relief.  His request for special relief rests largely on his explanation of the breach, nam ely that he 
was required to remain in Pakistan due to family obligations, which have now been resolved, 
leaving him in a position to now return to Canada.  Testimony was heard from the Appellant and 
his mother , with the assistance of  an accredited Urdu -Eng lish interpreter.  
[4] For the reasons set out in more detail below, I find that the Appellant  has not established 
sufficient H&C grounds to warrant special relief and so this appeal is dismissed.  
ANALYSIS  
[5] The Appellant  bears the burden of proof to establish th at, taking into account the best 
interests of any child directly affected by the decision, there are sufficient H&C considerations to 
warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case.  
[6] The larger the shortfall in days, the more H&C is r equired to allow the appeal.  The extent 
of non -compliance in this case is significant, with the Appellant  in absolute breach of the residency 
obligation.  As such, the threshold to warrant special relief is high.
